articles.title: Epoch Raises $4.25 Million to Help SMEs Comply with EUDR Supply Chain Deforestation Regulation - ESG Today
articles.summary: Epoch Raises $4.25 Million to Help SMEs Comply with EUDR Supply Chain Deforestation Regulation  ESG Today
articles.full_text:
Supply chain intelligence platform Epoch announced today that it has raised $4.25 million in a seed funding round, alongside the launch of a new solution aimed at automating compliance for small and mid-sized businesses (SMBs), starting with the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR).
According to Epoch, the funding and new launch come as businesses face increasing regulatory requirements to trace the origins of raw materials. The EUDR, for example, requires companies placing products including cattle, cocoa, coffee, palm oil, rubber, soy and wood on the EU market to demonstrate that they are deforestation-free and legally produced. The regulation will apply to large and medium-sized operators beginning December 30, 2026, and to most micro and small operators from June 30, 2027.
Founded in 2023 by CEO Jinal Surti and CTO William Ouellette, London-based Epoch develops AI-powered supply chain intelligence technology designed to help businesses trace raw materials to their origins and assess environmental and regulatory risks The company uses geospatial AI and automated research to analyze supply chains, reducing reliance on supplier questionnaires.
The company said that its technology identifies supplier facilities, locates plots where raw materials originate and assesses deforestation and legality risks. Its platform enables businesses to use the resulting information to address multiple regulatory requirements, including the EUDR.
According to Epoch, the new self-service solution allows SMBs to begin with existing supplier information and use AI assistants, including ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, to organize data and assess supply chain risks. The platform can generate Due Diligence Statements with supporting evidence for submission to the EU Information System (TRACES), the company added.
Surti said:
“We’ve built a compliance solution for the AI era. One sweep across a supply chain, using geospatial AI and agentic research, produces evidence that can be packaged for every regulation a company faces, including the ones not written yet. Enterprises get it inside the platforms they already run, and from today on, so does any SMB.”
The $4.25M seed round was led by Burnt Island Ventures and Sand River, and brings the total Epoch has raised to $6.26M. The company said that the new capital will go into product, infrastructure and the commercial team.
Christine Boyle, Partner, Burnt Island Ventures, said:
“Large companies rely on their supply chains to operate their businesses, and they are often operating in the dark as to the local conditions around drought, flood, and forest health. The Epoch platform leverages AI, earth observation data and proprietary models to enable visibility into risk mitigation, and compliance.”

articles.title: France’s debt woes in focus as ECB meets - Kuwait Times
articles.summary: France’s debt woes in focus as ECB meets  Kuwait Times
articles.full_text:
FRANKFURT: France’s deteriorating public finances will take centre stage when the European Central Bank meets this week, but policymakers are not expected to throw a lifeline to the eurozone’s second-biggest economy just yet. The ECB is set to keep interest rates on hold, having already hiked them twice this year, walking a fine line between tamping down inflation fuelled by the Iran war energy shock and supporting the eurozone economy.
But the focus of Thursday’s meeting is likely to shift quickly to France and "how the ECB will respond to the ongoing fiscal and political crisis,” said Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics. French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, surged to their highest level since 2002 last week amid a standoff over next year’s budget, which aims to reduce the country’s vast debts.
Concerns have also been fuelled after protests, driven in part by demands for more spending on public services, degenerated into the worst street violence in years.
There has been speculation that the ECB could, for the first time, use a crisis-fighting tool aimed at combating sharp movements in markets to push down French bond yields. However, the criteria to activate the so-called Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) are strict, and most observers believe France’s problems do not meet the threshold. The ECB stipulates that the tool can only be used to counter "unwarranted” moves in markets, where there is a risk of financial stress spreading—but not in cases where problems stem from poor fiscal policy.
So far ECB President Christine Lagarde, who also once served as France’s finance minister, has sounded cool about the idea. Asked about France’s rising yields earlier this month, she responded: "The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies.”
France’s central bank chief, who sits on the ECB’s governing council, also downplayed the prospect of an intervention, saying that "conditions are not met” for the central bank to step in.
Kenningham of Capital Economics predicted there would be "no lifeline for France” at Thursday’s meeting, saying spreads between French and German bonds, the eurozone benchmark, would need to widen far more to justify any action.
Despite rising inflation caused by higher energy prices, the central bank for the 21 nations that use the euro is expected to keep its benchmark rate steady at 2.5 percent. The ECB’s rate call will come a day after the Federal Reserve announces its latest decision, with the US central bank also expected to stay on hold following a hike in September. Eurozone inflation rose to a three-year high of 3.8 percent in September, although closely watched core inflation—excluding volatile energy and food prices—hardly changed. There have so far been "very little knock-on effects from higher energy prices,” ING economist Carsten Brzeski told AFP.
And France’s crisis had "actually lowered chances of another rate hike,” he said, adding that the "bond markets have taken over the ECB’s task”. Rising bond yields cause tighter financing conditions and can push up borrowing costs for businesses and households, similar to the impact of higher rates.
Most economists predict the ECB will make the final hike of its current tightening cycle in December when it will be armed with updated growth and inflation forecasts.
Lagarde is also likely to face questions about her future as speculation intensifies she will step down before her term as ECB chief officially ends in October next year. She has been linked to the top job at the World Economic Forum, which hosts a gathering of the global elite every year in the Swiss Alps resort of Davos. But she has been tight-lipped so far, saying at the ECB’s last meeting in September there was "nothing to report” on the matter. --AFP

articles.title: Britain To Unveil Plan To Meet NATO Defence Spending Targets By 2035 - Arise News
articles.summary: Britain To Unveil Plan To Meet NATO Defence Spending Targets By 2035  Arise News
articles.full_text:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government will outline a plan to fully fund its existing defence commitments and meet its NATO spending targets by 2035.
Burnham said Finance Minister John Healey would provide details of the funding plan on Wednesday when he delivers his first budget, as the defence industry seeks assurances that Britain has a clear strategy for increasing military spending.
Speaking on ITV’s Good Morning Britain on Monday, Burnham said the government’s immediate priority was to fully fund its previously announced defence investment plan.
“We’ve been working hard to do that,” he said. “It’s crucial that we have a funded plan that we can then implement, and we will set out more details on Wednesday as to how we’ve done that.”
Asked whether the plan would include increasing defence spending to three per cent of gross domestic product by 2030 and 3.5 per cent by 2035, Burnham confirmed that the targets would be included.
“It is, and we will set out a plan as to how we think is the right way to do that,” he said, adding that Britain would meet its NATO commitments.
Britain currently spends about 2.6 per cent of its GDP on defence and has previously pledged to reach the three per cent target during the next parliamentary term. The country’s next general election is due by mid-2029 at the latest.
Last year, NATO members agreed to spend 3.5 per cent of GDP on core defence requirements by 2035, alongside an additional 1.5 per cent on broader defence and security measures.
The British defence industry has called for a clear and gradual increase in military spending, warning that delaying the planned rise until after 2030 could undermine the country’s credibility with allies and investors.

articles.title: UK PM Andy Burnham signals youth jobs support changes as John Healey prepares NATO spending plan - Business Upturn
articles.summary: UK PM Andy Burnham signals youth jobs support changes as John Healey prepares NATO spending plan  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has signalled changes to government support for young people seeking work, saying savings could be made while improving how employment assistance is delivered. He has also confirmed that Defence Secretary turned finance minister John Healey will set out the government's plan for meeting its NATO commitments on Wednesday.
The two announcements come ahead of the UK government's budget on October 28, when ministers are expected to explain how they intend to manage public spending while addressing youth unemployment and national security.
Burnham has made helping young people into employment a priority for his government. At the same time, his administration faces pressure to meet defence spending commitments without putting additional strain on public finances.
The upcoming budget is expected to provide more detail on how the government plans to balance these competing priorities.
Andy Burnham signals changes to youth employment support
Burnham has indicated that the government's approach to supporting young people who are out of work needs to change. He also suggested that money could be saved by reviewing how existing support is provided.
The issue is significant for the UK, where youth unemployment and the number of young people outside education, employment or training have become major policy concerns.
Government figures cited in recent reporting show that close to one million people aged between 16 and 24 are classified as not in education, employment or training. The group is commonly referred to as NEET.
Burnham has argued that the government should invest in helping young people develop skills and find jobs instead of relying primarily on benefits after they struggle to enter the workforce.
His approach places greater emphasis on employment opportunities, training and practical assistance. The aim is to help young people move into work while reducing long-term dependence on government support.
However, changes to youth employment programmes could raise questions about which services will receive funding and how any savings will be achieved. Burnham's latest remarks indicate that the government wants to review the current system, but the precise changes and their financial impact will depend on the details announced by ministers.
The budget could therefore offer a clearer picture of how the government intends to support young jobseekers while controlling expenditure.
John Healey to outline Britain's NATO spending commitments
Burnham has also confirmed that John Healey will set out the government's path towards meeting Britain's NATO defence spending commitments on Wednesday.
The announcement is important because the government faces pressure to explain how it will finance the country's military requirements over the coming years. NATO allies have agreed to a higher long-term defence spending target, increasing the importance of clear funding plans.
According to Reuters, the UK government intends to outline a pathway towards allocating 3.5% of gross domestic product to core defence spending by 2035. The budget is expected to explain how Britain plans to work towards that commitment.
The challenge is finding the money while maintaining the government's other spending priorities. Burnham has previously stressed that national security must be protected without ignoring social security needs.
Healey's budget will therefore be closely watched by defence officials and policymakers looking for clarity on future military investment. A clear spending pathway could provide greater certainty about the resources available to the armed forces and the timetable for meeting NATO's targets.
Wednesday's budget will test the government's spending priorities
The youth employment announcement and the NATO spending plan highlight two major challenges facing Burnham's government: improving opportunities for young people and maintaining Britain's defence commitments.
Both priorities require funding, but the government also has to manage borrowing and meet its wider fiscal objectives. That makes decisions about departmental budgets and potential savings particularly important.
The government has indicated that existing resources will need to be used carefully, with new commitments requiring decisions about spending elsewhere. The budget is expected to show how that approach will work in practice.
For young people, the key question is whether changes to employment support will create clearer routes into work and training. For the defence sector, attention will focus on whether Healey provides a credible timetable for meeting Britain's NATO obligations.
Wednesday's budget should offer the first detailed indication of how Burnham and Healey intend to bring those priorities together. The figures and policy measures announced will determine whether the government's promises are matched by a practical funding plan.

articles.title: Sovereignty and scale: How industry Is delivering ‘Made in NATO’ - EU Reporter
articles.summary: Sovereignty and scale: How industry Is delivering ‘Made in NATO’  EU Reporter
articles.full_text:
The security of the world is at a critical juncture. The conflicts in Ukraine, the Middle East and tensions in the Indo-Pacific are only part of the challenge. At precisely the moment we face a renewed great power competition, we may be less equipped than ever to meet it, writes George Whittier, CEO Fairbanks Morse Defense.
Decades of post-Cold War military downsizing have hollowed out defence industrial capacity across Europe and the United States. Euro-Atlantic governments are now realising that they must rapidly rebuild their industrial bases to address a complex geopolitical environment. Defence spending in Europe has grown by 90% nominally since 2022 and the U.S. 2027 defence budget is expected to top €1.3 trillion ($1.5 trillion). Across the NATO alliance, members are signing contracts for equipment that industry is struggling to produce at the speed of need. The weak point is not demand, it’s the capacity to meet demand.
This tension is especially clear in the maritime domain. The largest shipyards in Europe and the United States are currently reporting tens of billions of euros in backlogs along with a shortage of skilled labour and aging port infrastructure. According to the European Commission, manufacturing output has grown by a mere 1% for frigates and 7% for attack submarines over the last decade. Meanwhile, Russia is maintaining a steady pace of warship construction, despite crippling western sanctions, and China produces roughly the equivalent tonnage of the entire French Navy every four years.
While the focus of NATO members has been on strategic autonomy, the fact is that no nation on its own has the industrial capacity to confront the geopolitical crises at hand. The days when strategic industrial capacity was centered on a broad supplier base of tens to thousands of machine shops and suppliers is gone. Industry is now playing a vital role in reviving it.
The challenge of reviving the allied defence industrial base has been a central theme of recent NATO summits. The war in Ukraine, which triggered a survival instinct amongst members, has helped catalyse increased cooperation between members and industry. The Defense Production Act Plan and Industrial Capacity Expansion Pledge, initiated in 2023 and 2024, created a framework for joint procurement and increased interoperability to achieve production at scale across the alliance. The Strategy for Industry-NATO Cooperation (SYNC), signed by heads of state in Ankara this year, further emphasised the importance of industry in collective security and deterrence, as did the announcement of $54 billion in allied defence procurement. As NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte rightly said, these “Made in NATO” capabilities represent “transatlantic cooperation in action.”
Sovereignty, however, is a sticking point. Many allies are concerned that NATO is dominated by the United States. According to European Parliamentary Research Service reports, three-quarters of European defence procurement now flows to non-European suppliers, and more than half of that is to the United States. At a time of heightened global conflict, EU nations and the UK fear that a NATO-integrated supply chain will leave them structurally dependent on, or dominated by, America, and therefore vulnerable to crises, disruptions or political-economic disputes. But allied production is not either-or, it’s all of the above.
Nations do not have to choose between sovereignty and the ability to defend themselves. Allies must build more of their own defence capacity, not just for NATO, but to support sovereign military demand and national economic strength. A go-it-alone approach is not tenable for either side of the Atlantic. In fact, nationally-isolated procurement strategies have left Europe's defence industry fragmented, especially smaller, specialized suppliers critical to naval construction. This fragmentation is the enemy of scale. It is why NATO has increasingly stepped into its role as an aggregator of demand, providing standards and requirements for interoperability and a multinational buy signal so suppliers can serve a broader, more predictable market.
When I emphasise that we are better off working together, I speak from experience. Two months ago, the company I lead broke ground on a manufacturing centre of excellence in the Słupsk region in Poland. Working in partnership with the local government, and using the advanced engineering of our Norwegian subsidiary, the new centre will increase annual production of handling equipment for allied autonomous and crewed vessels by up to 80%. Opening this facility allows us to tap into a skilled workforce in Europe, in a strategic location for Europe, to provide NATO and European forces with the equipment they need to defend themselves.
Ultimately, countries should control the capabilities and decisions essential to their security. They also need equipment delivered at speed. Allied production can help achieve both if nations identify clearly which capabilities must be local and which can be complementary and accessed from close partners.
A nation doesn't need to be able to build a warship or platform end-to-end to have a thriving defence sector. Shoring up the NATO arsenal depends on expanding the capacity and depth of allied suppliers. By specialising in critical ship equipment and plugging those components into the broader allied market, local economies gain larger, steadier demand than any single domestic government could ever guarantee on its own.

articles.summary: Temu falls into line as EU backs its action plan after €200m fine  Euronews.comEU accepts Temu plan to remedy Digital Services Act breach  ReutersEU forces Temu to act after €200m fine under European digital law  The Brussels TimesNo more toxic toys? Temu promises to clean up its shelves as Brussels watches  EU PerspectivesWhat Temu plans to change after a €200 million EU fine  FashionNetwork France
articles.full_text:
The Chinese-owned online retailer has promised stronger action to address several violations of the EU’s Digital Services Act, the European Commission said on Monday, following a €200 million fine in May.
The European Commission has said it has accepted Temu's action plan to address several violations of the bloc's Digital Services Act (DSA).
Temu has promised to carry out a risk analysis, to keep a close eye on measures to prevent the sale of illegal products on its platform and to step up its efforts if needed.
The Chinese retailer will also review how its recommender systems "may amplify the spread of illegal goods", the Commission said.
In May this year, Temu was fined €200 million by the EU for allowing the sale of illegal products like dangerous baby toys and faulty chargers on its platform.
The fine came after a formal investigation launched in October 2024 into whether Temu was meeting its obligations as a designated Very Large Online Platform under the EU's Digital Services Act.
Commission investigators said the platform failed to properly identify and address the risks posed by illegal and unsafe products sold to European consumers.
Today, Temu welcomed the approval of its action plan by European regulators. “We appreciate the Commission's constructive engagement with us throughout the process,“ the company said in a statement.
The plan "stands as a clear testament to Temu's commitment to investing in robust compliance infrastructure to ensure a safe, trustworthy shopping environment for all EU users”, it added.
The Chinese retail giant has 130 million users in the 27-nation EU, nearly a third of the bloc's population, making it one of the biggest online retailers in Europe.
Temu is one of several ecommerce platforms dealing with the EU’s new €3 fees on low-value packages since July, while those worth less €150 had entered the bloc duty free beforehand.
The new packaging rules have seen imports, especially from China, slump by 30% to 40% since coming into force.

articles.title: The EU is seeking to finalize a €45 billion loan for Ukraine. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The EU is seeking to finalize a €45 billion loan for Ukraine.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
European Union (EU) member states are seeking to reach an agreement by the end of 2026 on a loan of approximately 45 billion euros for Ukraine to meet its financial needs and strengthen its defense capabilities in 2027.
 However, the Czech Republic and Slovakia are unwilling to participate in the new financial mechanism, according to information published by Politico on October 26 (Prague time), citing diplomatic sources and EU officials.
 According to the VNA correspondent in Prague, the option being considered is to raise capital on the financial market, using the current EU budget as collateral for the loan. This is considered one of the feasible options to support Ukraine in the context of continuously increasing financial needs. However, the specific mechanism and final scale of the support package have not yet been decided.
 EU leaders are expected to discuss this issue at their meeting on November 26, after the European Commission presents its options.
 The Czech Republic and Slovakia's position follows their decision not to participate in the 90 billion euro loan mechanism for Ukraine in 2026-2027, which was agreed upon by the EU in December 2025.
 According to the European Parliament's Research Service, the previous loan was raised through EU borrowing on financial markets, with the EU budget as collateral; the Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Hungary were not required to bear any related financial obligations under the enhanced cooperation mechanism.
 Under this mechanism, a group of member states can cooperate within the EU framework without requiring all countries to participate. However, for the new €45 billion loan, the legal and financial conditions still need to be discussed.
 The fact that the Czech Republic and Slovakia do not want to participate does not mean that they can automatically prevent other countries from implementing a mechanism that complies with EU regulations.
 The need for new assistance stems from the prolonged conflict and the pressure on Ukraine's defense spending. 
 In October 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky requested an additional 70 billion euros from partners for 2027. If approved as planned, the 45 billion euro loan would cover approximately two-thirds of Kyiv's request. The EU is also seeking additional contributions from the UK and Canada.
 Some member states have also continued to propose using frozen Russian assets in Europe, but Belgium remains opposed to this option due to related concerns.
 According to Politico, the debate over the loan to Ukraine could also affect the EU's long-term budget negotiations for the period 2028-2034.
 Some countries supporting Ukraine have warned they may reconsider their support for proposals to increase funding for cohesion policies, which support regional development and reduce economic disparities among member states, if the countries benefiting from these funds do not share the burden of supporting Kyiv.
 However, some EU diplomats also warned that linking aid to Ukraine's budget for internal EU policies could complicate negotiations, as many member states depend significantly on cohesion funds. The EU must therefore find a balance between the need to support Ukraine and maintaining resources for programs serving its citizens.

articles.summary: Russian Refiners Ramp Up Diesel Output to Supply Trump Deal  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comEXCLUSIVE: First Russian diesel from Putin-Trump deal heading for US, data shows  ReutersRussia has increased diesel production due to sanctions relief, Reuters says  Українська правдаUkraine war briefing: Russian diesel tankers headed for North America, says Moscow, as US tries to revive peace talks  The GuardianU.S. Diesel at $6.30 a Gallon as First Russian ...
articles.full_text:
Russian refiners have raised diesel output for October after Moscow issued export quotas under the Kremlin’s supply agreement with the United States, two industry sources told Reuters on Monday. Daily production fell to about 160,000 metric tons in the first half of the month, from 175,000 tons in September. It began climbing toward 180,000 tons a day once the quotas arrived in mid-October.
Russia’s domestic diesel consumption typically drops to about 140,000 tons a day in October, after the grain harvest and the summer driving season end, leaving at least 40,000 tons a day, more than 1 million tons a month, available for export, according to the sources. Between 200,000 and 300,000 tons of that is likely to go to neighbouring countries under intergovernmental agreements.
Moscow is expected to keep its diesel export ban, which took effect in August, in place and to use quotas to control how much leaves the country.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on October 9 that Russia would ship more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that. A further 3 million tons would depend on the condition of Russia’s refineries. Washington has temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel to allow the trade, with a six-month Treasury waiver issued the same day.
The waiver goes beyond pre-election price relief, and is seen by some analysts as a first step toward easing sanctions on Russian energy and pulling Moscow’s supplies back toward the West and away from China, which has come to rely on Russia since the Hormuz closure cut off Gulf oil.
The first cargo on the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes left Primorsk on October 23 with about 40,000 tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel and is due in New York on November 7, four days after the midterm elections. The average U.S. diesel price stood at $6.32 a gallon that day, up from $3.63 a year earlier.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said shipments to the United States would continue regularly. At least two other tankers carrying Russian diesel have signaled destinations in Turkey and Brazil.
Analysts doubt the volumes will move the market. Standard Chartered has warned that Russia will struggle to raise diesel output in the near term because Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged its refineries, which will take months to repair. The bank adds that barrels redirected to U.S. buyers come out of supply to Russia’s existing customers. Kyiv resumed refinery strikes on October 15 after a three-day pause, which puts the October recovery at risk.

articles.title: Animal rights campaigners claim victory on stunning of pigs - The Telegraph
articles.summary: Animal rights campaigners claim victory on stunning of pigs  The TelegraphNew plans to end carbon dioxide stunning of pigs to prevent suffering  GOV.UKStunning pigs before slaughter to be banned in victory for animal rights campaigners  LBCWe need a 'realistic timeline' – Katie sets out NPA position on CO2 in Farming Today interview  National Pig AssociationAIMS calls on Defra secretary to suspend CO2 consultation until EU-UK deal agreed  Pig Wor...
articles.full_text:
Animal rights campaigners have claimed victory after ministers moved to ban the stunning of pigs with carbon dioxide.
The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) unveiled proposals on Monday to outlaw using CO2 to subdue pigs before they are slaughtered, saying it causes them “unnecessary pain and distress”.
In England and Wales, more than 90 per cent of pigs are slaughtered using CO2. But ministers have said the system must change as part of their official Animal Welfare Strategy.
Defra said in a statement: “Pigs are highly sentient and intelligent animals, capable of experiencing pain and fear. Minimising distress during handling and slaughter is an important part of safeguarding their welfare.”
Project Slingshot, a pressure group that has in the past been funded by Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, said the move vindicated a recent high-profile campaign calling for an end to the practice.
Thousands of adverts featuring comedian Diane Morgan ran on the London Underground as part of the push, and the group also projected campaign videos onto Buckingham Palace and the Houses of Parliament.
Naomi Hallum, the head of Project Slingshot, said: “We are relieved that the horrors of CO2 are coming to an end, and are glad to have played our part in that.
“When the public was given the information about what CO2 slaughter means for pigs through our ads, stunts and social media posts, they were horrified too.”
However, the National Pig Association and the British Meat Processors Association (BMPA) warned against the move.
Jonathan Powell, from the BMPA, said a rapid transition away from CO2 would put the UK’s food security at risk.
He said: “It’s a major food security issue. Ninety per cent of pigs are killed using CO2 but there’s no viable alternative on the table at the moment.”

articles.title: ‘Preparing for a wider EU’ is only half the challenge for Ukraine - PubAffairs Bruxelles
articles.summary: ‘Preparing for a wider EU’ is only half the challenge for Ukraine  PubAffairs Bruxelles
articles.full_text:
The EU and its member states increasingly recognise enlargement as a geopolitical imperative, as discussions at last week’s European Council demonstrated. Amandine Sabourin and Sara Gianesello address a question that remains largely unresolved: Can the EU make enlargement work for candidates, existing members and itself?
More than four years after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine accelerated enlargement discussions, the debate has since then clearly shifted. The EU and member states increasingly recognise enlargement as a geopolitical imperative, with High Representative Kallas describing it as ‘the EU’s most successful foreign policy tool for decades’ at the Foreign Affairs Council last week, a view echoed by EU leaders at the European Council on 15–16 October. The question now is whether the EU can make enlargement work for candidates, existing members and itself.
The European Commission’s package ‘Preparing for a wider Union’, shared in October 2026, marks a significant attempt to put enlargement and EU internal reform on the same agenda. For too long, these have been largely treated as separate questions: conditionality and reform benchmarks on the candidate side, governance and decision-making on the EU side. The Commission’s package acknowledges that a larger Union will work only if the EU itself is willing to change how it operates.
This is a welcome, long-overdue step, but the Commission’s package only partially addresses the challenges posed by the accession of Ukraine, arguably the candidate that makes EU internal reform most pressing, and the only one for which the EU is simultaneously running three agendas, now accelerated in parallel.
A larger Union, but still functional
A larger EU needs to be governable and politically functioning. But years of internal blockages, often fueled by the (over-)use of vetoes by individual member states, have left scars. It is therefore understandable that member states want to avoid importing new sources of paralysis into an already complex, often criticised slow decision-making system.
Yet concerns about the EU’s capacity to act are one side of the story. Member states are also weighing the political, economic and financial implications of a country like Ukraine: its large agricultural sector could impact the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy and distribution of EU funds significantly, increase competition within the single market, including labour mobility, and a possible backsliding of democratic standards and the rule of law.
“The harder task is reconciling competing national interests and spending priorities, as enlargement could shift the EU’s political and strategic priorities further eastwards.”
Current members also fear they may face higher contributions or a redistribution of funding towards new beneficiaries after accession. Yet past experiences show that the overall costs of enlargement are more manageable than often assumed. The harder task is reconciling competing national interests and spending priorities, as enlargement could shift the EU’s political and strategic priorities further eastwards, with implications for how attention and resources are allocated across different regions and policy areas.
These concerns surfaced in five ‘non-papers’ circulated by member states this year. Proposed changes range from gradual integration before accession to longer transition periods and temporary limitations on certain decision-making rights for new members. The Commission’s package meets them halfway while keeping enlargement politically credible on three fronts.
First, to prevent further veto blockages, the Commission proposes greater use of the ‘passerelle clause’, which would help move to qualified majority voting in selected areas (including opening of negotiating clusters in accession processes) and of the ‘constructive abstention’, which allows a country to step back from a unanimous decision on foreign or security policy without blocking it. Yet activating the passerelle clause still requires unanimity, leaving the EU dependent on the very mechanism it is trying to circumvent.
Second, to address concerns about the EU’s ability to enforce its democratic standards and the rule of law after accession, the package includes stronger safeguards and follow-up under Article 7 (the EU’s existing rule of law procedure) and possible cuts in financial support or suspension of voting rights for serious breaches of democratic principles and the rule of law during the first 15 years of membership.
Finally, the package promotes gradual integration, offering candidates earlier access to selected EU policies and sectors (energy, transport, digital, defence). This could deliver tangible benefits to candidate countries and their citizens, while building the capacity needed for membership, provided that integration remains conditional and reversible.
Why Ukraine is the stress test
These proposals prepare the EU for future enlargements, but they do not address a central challenge in the EU’s existing relationship with Ukraine, namely how to manage reconstruction, accession and security as parts of a coherent long-term partnership.
“Ukraine is not simply the largest accession candidate, or the most geopolitically complex, it is the only candidate for which the EU’s partnership already operates simultaneously across three different institutional tracks.”
Ukraine is not simply the largest accession candidate, or the most geopolitically complex, it is the only candidate for which the EU’s partnership already operates simultaneously across three different institutional tracks. The €50 billion Ukraine facility runs through the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood (DG ENEST) and combines financial support, investment and reforms through three pillars with their own governance arrangements. The accession process instead follows a separate institutional track involving the Council of the EU’s enlargement working party (COELA), accession cluster negotiations, and the Commission’s enlargement directorate. Lastly, security and defence cooperation, including the European Peace Facility, the €150 billion SAFE instrument, the EU military assistance mission, as well as several member states’ bilateral contributions, operates through yet another set of mechanisms, largely outside the civilian architecture.
Each track has its own priorities, institutional interlocutors (in Kyiv, in Brussels, and in the capitals) and accountability structures, with no single Council working party or European Commissioner holding a comprehensive view across all three.
The package works for a regular candidate to the EU: gradual integration, stronger safeguards and more effective decision-making are all key. But for Ukraine, it would be necessary to limit the costs of institutional fragmentation. For instance, the reform conditionality under the facility and accession conditionality under the enlargement process would benefit from greater alignment, as they are currently developed through separate processes, creating confusion.
Similarly, the security and defence dimension of Ukraine’s relationship with the EU remains largely disconnected from the reconstruction and accession architecture. Last week’s EU Foreign Affairs Council meeting could have been the opportunity to put perspective on both the opening of two additional enlargement clusters and the financing gap for 2027. The October European Council acknowledged this concern only implicitly, calling for timely disbursement of 2026 commitments without addressing what comes next.
Treating these tracks separately is a structural problem that further discussions on the reform of the EU in the perspective of enlargement must address.
Roadmaps: Differentiation vs coherence?
The Commission’s roadmaps for Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine, expected in early November, will offer another opportunity to assess how the EU intends to translate its renewed enlargement ambitions into practice. Each roadmap is supposed to provide a clearer plan in terms of timelines and deliverables, which allows differentiation and coping with the countries’ respective political realities, as well as their various levels of preparedness.
EU leaders reaffirmed this differentiated approach at the last European Council and it seems the most productive and honest way. Montenegro is the most advanced candidate and could conclude negotiations in the coming years, while Ukraine’s accession trajectory remains closely connected to the evolution of the war.
For Ukraine, however, a roadmap could go beyond defining reform benchmarks and accession milestones. It is an opportunity to identify how the different strands of EU engagement should reinforce each other, including how conditionality under the Ukraine Facility can be better aligned with accession requirements, how reconstruction investments can support Ukraine’s longer-term integration and how security and resilience considerations can be reflected more systematically across relevant accession chapters.
Two tests, one partnership
The Commission’s package asks the right question: how can the EU enlarge without weakening its capacity to function? Enlargement is becoming a test of the EU’s capacity to reform itself; for Ukraine, it is also a test of the EU’s capacity to act coherently and strategically across the different dimensions of its partnership. The upcoming roadmap in November is the first place to show progress.
About the Authors:
Dr Amandine Sabourin is a senior policy analyst in ECDPM’s European foreign and development policy and Inclusive governance and accountability teams.
Sara Gianesello is a policy analyst and gender and youth focal point in ECDPM’s inclusive governance and accountability and peace, security and resilience teams. She is also the coordinator of the gender task force.

articles.title: UK and EU age assurance laws mean a single compliance strategy may not work across Europe - Osborne Clarke
articles.summary: UK and EU age assurance laws mean a single compliance strategy may not work across Europe  Osborne Clarke
articles.full_text:
Published on 26 October 2026
Varying age limits and verification standards are a challenge for services seeking to comply with all child safety rules
At a glance
- The UK Online Safety Act and EU Digital Services Act share principles but differ on age thresholds, scope and age assurance standards.
- The proposed UK social media restrictions and EU KIDS ACT, alongside member's national measures, add complexity and likely uneven enforcement.
- The viability of a single cross-border age assurance model will depend on the type of service, its functionality, the applicable age thresholds and the risks it presents to different age groups.
Online services face different age assurance requirements across the United Kingdom and European Union, despite a shared focus on child safety. Differences in age limits, verification standards and the services covered mean that a single European compliance strategy is unlikely to satisfy every requirement.
Shared principles
UK and EU age assurance frameworks, however, share certain principles: two of the most important are that online services should account for the different risks faced by children of different ages, and the assurance method used should be proportionate to the relevant risk and legal obligation. These principles underpin two areas of overlap: age-based risk duties and recognition of different forms of age assurance.
Age-based risk duties
The fact that risks can vary by age group means there is a need to provide an age-appropriate experience for child users. Ofcom’s guidance under the Online Safety Act requires risk assessments to consider how risks will manifest for children of different ages.
The European Commission’s guideline under article 28 of the Digital Services Act (DSA) take a similar approach. They require platforms accessible to minors to put in place appropriate and proportionate, risk-based and privacy-preserving measures that take into account children’s age and evolving capacities.
Many forms of age assurance
Legal frameworks in both the UK and EU recognise that there are different forms of age assurance, each with different levels of accuracy and robustness. Self-declaration, or a minimum age stated only in terms and conditions, are generally judged as insufficient to meet core child-safety obligations.
Points of difference
The similarities, however, do not amount to a single compliance standard, and the UK and EU approaches will continue to have points of difference. New or emerging laws also increase the complexity that platforms must navigate. The main differences concern age thresholds, methods of age assurance and the services within scope.
Different age thresholds
There remains a lack of harmonisation in the age limits that age assurance is intended to uphold. Proposed UK social media restrictions will focus on under-16s, with separate protections for 16- and 17-year-olds. The proposed EU KIDS ACT takes a different approach: restrictions for some social media and video-sharing services below the age of 15, guardian-controlled accounts from 13, and safety-by-design protections for all under-18s.
Methods of age assurance
There is also divergence between legal frameworks in the form that age assurance must take, with standards also differing within single territories. In the UK, the Online Safety Act sets a high bar with "highly effective age assurance"; while the Information Commissioner’s Office takes a more flexible, risk-based approach permitted under its Age Appropriate Design Code.
The individual proposed laws also provide for different methods. The EU KIDS ACT would require the use of an EU-approved age-verification solution to prevent under-13s accessing certain social media and video-sharing services. The same type of solution would be required to prevent 13- to 14-year-olds creating autonomous accounts rather than via a guardian. However, other age assurance methods would be possible when applying safety-by-design default settings to under-18s.
Services within scope
The type of platform and its functions will be a central consideration when determining whether and how to implement age assurance obligations. A service may find itself heavily regulated in one jurisdiction and outside the scope of the rules in another.
The OSA applies to user-to-user and search services, while the DSA regulates a potentially broader category of online platforms. The EU KIDS ACT and UK social media restriction proposals would overlay service-specific obligations for different and often more granular categories of service, such as online games, artificial intelligence companions and chatbots.
The regulatory burden will therefore vary between platforms depending on service type, functionality and risk of harm. Social media, gaming and artificial intelligence chatbot providers may need to reconcile current broad OSA, DSA or General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) obligations with specific proposed EU and UK requirements. The key question is which rules apply to the whole service and which apply only to particular functions.
Continued fragmentation
The EU KIDS ACT is intended to reduce fragmentation in rules governing minors' access to higher-risk services, but its implementation will not be immediate. France, Austria, Germany, Greece and Spain are among the countries considering interim national measures. Other member states may wait for the EU KIDS ACT to come into force.
The Commission’s response to a French proposal earlier this year illustrates the legal complexity. It indicated that the DSA does not prevent national law from setting a minimum age for access to certain products or services on an online platform, provided the measure complies with EU law, including the DSA and e-Commerce Directive. The Commission also suggested that national legislation could provide a transitional solution if it contains a mechanism allowing the measure to be suspended or repealed once EU rules are adopted.
Member states do not have unrestricted power to impose any obligations in this area. France’s recent experience shows that a national proposal can be struck down where it is too broad or conflicts with the existing position under the DSA. Proposals from member states therefore remain subject to scrutiny not only in comparison with the emerging KIDS ACT model, but also against EU rules already in force.
Osborne Clarke comment
Uncertainty remains over which member states will legislate, what their interim measures will contain and whether they will withstand scrutiny under existing EU law. The EU KIDS ACT and UK social media proposals may also change during the legislative process. Adoption will not guarantee uniformity: experience under the GDPR and DSA suggests that interpretation and enforcement may still differ between countries.
This is the first Insight in Osborne Clarke's series on age assurance for digital platforms in the UK and EU, mapping where the principal legal frameworks overlap and diverge. Our next Insight in the series will examine practical approaches for platforms as they look to implement age assurance across Europe.

articles.title: Euro zone firms find it harder to get credit, ECB survey shows - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Euro zone firms find it harder to get credit, ECB survey shows  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
FRANKFURT, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Euro zone firms are having a harder time getting credit from their banks just as their finances are squeezed by more expensive fuel and higher costs, a European Central Bank survey showed on Monday.
The ECB has been gradually raising interest rates to stem an energy-driven rise in inflation, though it is expected to stay put this week to garner more evidence on how higher borrowing costs, including on the bond market, are affecting the economy.
Its quarterly Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises in the euro area showed some strains were becoming visible, with firms reporting higher interest rates and a decrease in the availability of bank loans.
Firms said they needed more credit lines just as these were becoming harder to get.
"The continued simultaneous increase in the need for both trade credit and credit lines suggests that firms are facing broader pressures on their working capital, potentially driven by higher input costs," the ECB said.
"However, the decrease in credit line availability signals that banks are becoming more cautious in extending this type of financing, which could further constrain firms' ability to meet their short-term funding needs," it added.
The share of firms reporting obstacles to obtaining a bank loan increased to 7% in the three months to September from 5% in the previous quarter.
The survey also showed large increases in firms' expectations for prices, wages and other costs, but the ECB said this was skewed by a large number of first-time respondents.
Firms that took part in both of the last two rounds of the poll expected prices to rise on average by 3.6% in the coming 12 months, compared with 2.5% in the second quarter's survey.
Across the full sample of 12,822 enterprises, firms expected selling prices to rise by 7.1%, compared with 3.2% in the previous poll.
(Reporting by Francesco Canepa; Editing by Andrew Heavens)

articles.summary: Truce begins in wartorn Ukraine city after it was announced by Melania Trump  BBCUkraine war latest: Starlink access restored in Ukraine - as Kyiv's forces 'posing long-term threat' to Russia  Sky NewsUkrainian who fled Oleshky views US-brokered ceasefire with deep scepticism  ReutersRussia open to local truces but will not stop offensive  RTE.ieRussia Accuses Ukraine of Launching Strikes Against Oleshky Ahead of Ceasefire  The Moscow Times
articles.full_text:
A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, a week after it was announced by US First Lady, Melania Trump.
The ceasefire is meant to allow aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians.
Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram it had stopped firing toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson - across the river from Oleshky - at 04:00 Moscow time (01:00 GMT) in preparation for the humanitarian operation.
Oleshky is on the south bank of the river Dnipro, which forms the front line in the Kherson region. The remaining residents have been desperately short of food and other essential supplies.
Ukraine's parliament commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed in a social media post that the ceasefire had begun.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.
Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Residents were trapped with scarce food between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east.
The city was home to 24,000 people before the war. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.
The White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured the ceasefire in Oleshky.
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she said in a press release.
While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.
In August 2025, she penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".

articles.summary: Zelenskyy Mocks Trump Envoy's Claim Putin Is A 'Humanitarian'  HuffPost UKUkraine war briefing: Russia strikes Kyiv hours before truce begins in war-ravaged city Oleshky  The GuardianUkraine must 'unblock' Patriot missile delivery, Zelenskyy says after deadly strikes  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosRussian strikes on Ukraine kill four and injure 28, authorities say  Euronews.comRussia drops cluster warheads on Kyiv after Witkoff-Putin peac...

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has mocked Donald Trump’s special envoy after Steve Witkoff described Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian”.
The US representative stunned international allies when he praised the wartime dictator during a face-to-face meeting in St Petersburg last week.
American delegates were meant to be putting forward their latest plan to secure peace in Ukraine for the Kremlin’s consideration.
It came after a particularly alarming few weeks where the US started to fully align itself completely with Russia, apparently forgetting how the Ukraine war began when Putin invaded back in 2022.
Trump agreed to a sanctions-busting diesel deal with Putin, called for Zelenskyy to be ousted as Ukraine’s president, ignored Russia’s repeated breaches of the US’s “energy ceasefire” and was accused of restricting Kyiv’s access to US intelligence.
Witkoff then added salt to the wound when he told Putin: “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian.
“You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again.”
Asked to respond to the US claim that Ukraine is not “grateful” for the help it has received so far from America, Zelenskyy told ABC News: “They have a right to say what they think about what they want.”
“You don’t get insulted when people say that?” Journalist James Longman asked.
“No, of course – yes,” the Ukrainian president said. “I’m a normal person.
“Maybe not such a big humanitarian as Putin, of course, we are different.
“But in any way, I try my best, really.”
Zelenskyy also said Trump is “cautious” over the phone, but when asked if Trump was “polite”, Zelenskyy hesitated and joked: “Up to you!”
“Like between friends, like in the family, you have to be honest, not to play games. I don’t play games with Trump,” the Ukrainian leader said.
“This is my difference between me and Putin. I don’t play with him any games. I’m direct, honest.”
Zelenskyy said he does not feel betrayed by the US – despite saying otherwise recently – but did express sadness over the lack of US assistance.
“I feel what I feel. It’s not supportive,” he said.

US tech giant Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to employees around the globe, its chief people officer announced on Monday.
In a memo sent to staff, Amy Coleman called the "Voluntary Exit Offer" an "important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter."
The offer will be made available to employees on select teams across the US, Canada, India and the United Kingdom "at level 70 and below," meaning some senior staff could be included.
"This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources," the memo continued.
It added that eligible employees would receive an email with a link to their offers in the coming hours.
Around 60,000 staff are reported to be eligible.
In July, Microsoft announced it was eliminating around 4,800 roles, or roughly 2.1% of its global workforce at the time, as the company sought to shift its focus and cut costs as the AI era continues to take hold. Those cuts mostly affected the firm's commercial and Xbox gaming divisions.
Microsoft also offered some staff the option to retire early this year.
The company has said that more than 30% of those eligible for the early retirement scheme chose to participate and that it would "continue exploring similar approaches in the future."

articles.title: Trump considers Orbán as UN chief, WSJ reports - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Trump considers Orbán as UN chief, WSJ reports  Euronews.comOpinion | Viktor Orbán, U.N. Secretary-General?  WSJ'Funny': Tusk laughs off report that MAGA is eyeing Orbán for UN top job  Politico'MAGA conservatives' dream candidate': Trump administration eyes Orban as next UN chief - report  The Jerusalem PostAs Orbán is encouraged to run for UN secretary-general, Ukraine's foreign minister reveals trick for dealing with him  Українська правда
articles.full_text:
Trump administration officials are reportedly floating former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán for UN secretary-general, potentially backed by the US, Russia and China, though nothing is confirmed and his selection remains uncertain.
Officials in the Trump administration are advocating the nomination of former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán for the post of UN secretary-general, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal.
The newspaper reports that Orbán could be a joint American, Russian and Chinese candidate, and that sources in all three countries have confirmed the Trump administration is backing his bid.
Orbán lost power in Hungary’s parliamentary election in April, when Péter Magyar’s Tisza party defeated him after 16 years of governing with an absolute majority.
His hard-right, fiercely anti-migration and eurosceptic policies, together with the rule of law backsliding in Hungary, strained relations with Western allies, including the European Union and NATO. Nevertheless, Orbán maintained close ties with Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Since the election, Hungarian authorities have launched fraud and corruption investigations into several members of Orbán’s former government. Two former ministers and the former governor of Hungary’s National Bank are under arrest, and authorities could also examine Orbán’s potential involvement in those cases.
According to the WSJ, no final decision has been taken on the plan. A US State Department official admitted that the idea sounds crazy at first, but said previous talks with Washington suggest Russia and China also support it. The aim is for Orbán to be the joint candidate of the three countries.
“If the United States, Russia and China want the same thing in the UN Security Council, they usually achieve it,” officials from the United States and another country told the newspaper. The second five-year term of the current secretary-general, António Guterres, ends on 31 December.
The White House, and Beijing have not confirmed the information.
According to Russian deputy foreign minister Aleksandr Alimov, the US, China or Russia will not nominate Orbán, as permanent members of the UN's Security Council can not do so.
"Neither Russia, the United States, nor China will nominate Orbán because we are permanent members of the UN Security Council and we do not nominate anyone for the position of UN Secretary-General," Alimov told the Interfax news agency, adding that if press reports are true, those behind the idea need to find a nominating country.
"We will discuss all the people officially nominated for the post of Secretary General" Alimov noted.
Euronews has contacted Orbán’s spokesperson for comment but has not yet received a response. The spokesperson previously dismissed press reports about Orbán’s candidacy for the post of deputy secretary-general as “fake news”.
In May, the VSquare investigative newsletter reported that a UN position could be important for the former prime minister because of the diplomatic immunity attached to the role.
According to the WSJ, Orbán would only run if his victory were assured, a scenario that currently seems unlikely.
A candidate must secure the support of at least nine of the 15 Security Council members, while any of the five permanent members can veto the nomination. Besides the US, Russia and China, France and the United Kingdom are also permanent members.
Two European governments have already spoken out against the idea of putting forward Orbán as a potential candidate.
"I do not foresee Poland supporting Viktor Orbán's candidacy for UN Secretary-General," Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said in a social media post.
His Ukrainian counterpart, Andrij Sbyha, also posted on X, saying:
"Viktor Orbán, as UN Secretary-General, would put to good use the masterful veto and blackmail skills he has developed over years of derailing major EU decisions."

articles.title: Elon Musk's Dust-up With Ukraine on Starlink Isn't Over yet - Business Insider
articles.summary: Elon Musk's Dust-up With Ukraine on Starlink Isn't Over yet  Business InsiderMusk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored  BBCU.S. Allies Race to Escape SpaceX’s Orbit  WSJUkraine says Starshield back to normal, Musk says Kyiv violated terms  ReutersWhy is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?  BBC
articles.full_text:
Ukraine said its access to Starshield was restored this weekend, but Elon Musk isn't finished with Kyiv yet.
In an X post on Sunday, Musk accused Ukrainian forces of breaching Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian platform in drone attacks.
"Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," wrote the SpaceX owner.
"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," he added.
Musk made it clear he was talking about the commercial platform and not Starshield, the military version of the satellite communications service owned and controlled by the US government.
"Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," Musk added.
Ukrainian drone advisors hit back
Two prominent Ukrainian drone figures, however, disputed Musk's statement, saying that it was technically impossible for any of Kyiv's troops to have independently used Starlink in drone strikes.
"As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say for sure that this is not true," wrote Serhii Sternenko, a former advisor for drones to Ukraine's defense ministry, on his Telegram channel.
"It is very strange that Elon Musk does not know about the restrictions on Starlink operation in Ukraine," wrote Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, another former advisor.
Both worked in the ministry in early 2026, when it negotiated with SpaceX to prevent Russia from using black-market Starlink terminals in the war. SpaceX agreed in February to block Starlink over Ukraine and Russia, allowing access only to whitelisted Ukrainian terminals.
Sternenko said that Ukrainian civilians and troops could register their terminals on the whitelist, but that these would only work while subject to a speed requirement.
For one to connect while moving, it would have to be put on a special list that uses Starshield instead, he said.
"That is, it was technically impossible to use civilian Starlink to perform missions on drones. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield," Sternenko added.
Beskrestnov said the Ukrainian Starlink terminals were subject to a speed limit of 90 kmph, or about 55 mph. The civilian service is also completely cut off over Russia, he added.
"Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and middle strikes," Beskrestnov wrote.
Starshield vs Starlink
Tactical drones operating on the Ukrainian battlefield at speeds below 55 mph, such as first-person-view attack drones, typically use radio-frequency signals rather than satellite communication to maintain contact with an operator. These are also often too small and lack enough onboard power to reliably carry even a Starlink Mini terminal.
What Ukraine usually uses satellite internet for — hence its reliance on Starshield — is mid-range and deep strikes on Russia's rear or Russian territory, with larger, more powerful drones that fly much faster.
Kyiv also relies on satellite communications for its small interceptor drones, which fly at up to 265 mph to catch incoming attack drones.
Musk followed up on his Sunday X post with a screenshot of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy writing on social media in mid-October that Kyiv's forces "also use Starlink for mid-range strikes" against Russian targets.
However, Zelenskyy's post was describing Ukraine's recent troubles with Starshield, and he repeatedly used the term "Starlink" to refer broadly to the military satellite service instead.
Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider.
Earlier this month, Ukraine raised the alarm that its access to Starshield was being throttled at high speeds, reducing its ability to conduct deeper strikes and to control interceptor drones.
The crisis lasted 10 days and came as President Donald Trump and Musk openly criticized Ukraine for targeting Russian oil facilities at a time when the White House was trying to ease fuel prices.
The Wall Street Journal reported, citing unnamed US officials and sources, that Musk had personally ordered the speed cap. Musk and Trump have separately said they were not responsible for the slowdown.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Starshield services were running normally again.
