articles.summary: Mecca defence alliance members in Tehran to defuse Iran-US, Yemen tensions  Al JazeeraIran hosts Saudi Arabia and regional powers as fears grow of return to war  CNNOil ticks lower as Saudi defense minister meets with Iran's president in Tehran to de-escalate  CNBCSaudi defence pact countries push for peace in Tehran as Houthis launch more attacks  ReutersIran hosts regional powers for talks to prevent fresh escalation  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Tehran, Iran – Ministers and senior security officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye – the three nations that signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement – are in Tehran to discuss regional security issues amid threats of new US strikes on Iran.
Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, Pakistani military chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and will discuss tensions with security chief Mohsen Rezaei.
The meetings are among the highest-profile dialogues held in Tehran in recent months. While there is still little information on what might be discussed, the meetings come amid a flurry of diplomatic activity to deal with a new escalation between the United States and Iran.
“The Mecca pact’s 11th-hour visit to Tehran is an attempt to tip the balance in favour of those willing to compromise before the guns start blazing again,” said Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group.
“But unless they arrive with a credible formula to bridge the US-Iran divide, they may find themselves with little more than goodwill in a race against the clock.”
The talks are expected to address the waves of missile and drone attacks carried out by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, who are allied with Tehran, on Saudi Arabia, which supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
“I believe that parties to the Mecca agreement lack options of military engagement with the Houthis, but Riyadh is certainly asserting greater pressure for more, and its expectation of its partners has grown in parallel with the offensive from Yemen,” Ayesha Siddiqa, a senior research fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
But despite the collective security arrangement in the Mecca defence pact, Saudi Arabia’s allies Turkiye and Pakistan cannot “afford to commit troops on the ground” in Yemen, said Siddiqa.
The latest diplomatic push is likely linked to visits by Pakistani army chief Asim Munir to Saudi Arabia and Iran last week, Siddiqa said, and coincides with Islamabad’s restrictions on overland border trade with Tehran amid the US blockade on Iran.
Iranian authorities have said they favoured “security originating from within the region” as they prepared for the meetings.
Umer Karim, who researches Saudi foreign policy and its implications for regional security, said the Tehran meetings are unlikely to reduce the risk of a renewed war between Iran and the US, which would likely lead to more regional turmoil.
“Therefore, these talks perhaps are more concerned about the security of Saudi Arabia and involve an attempt by Turkiye and Pakistan to compel Iran to reach a compromise,” he told Al Jazeera.
Sanam Vakil, the director of Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa programme, said she was “cautiously optimistic” about the impact of the immediate meeting, but “less positive” about a lasting breakthrough.
“Iran has strong incentives to avoid another major confrontation, and there may be room for limited understandings, particularly concerning Yemen,” she said. “However, the Houthis have their own calculations, and Iran’s influence over them is not absolute. Preventing renewed US-Israeli attacks will be even more difficult because the fundamental disagreements between Tehran and Washington remain unresolved.”
US President Donald Trump is said to be considering new attacks to break the diplomatic deadlock with Iran, which has refused to agree to any peace agreement with Washington unless several of its demands are met.
The US and regional powers want international shipping and transit through the Strait of Hormuz to resume without impediments or attacks. Washington also wants to rein in Tehran’s nuclear programme and bring in international inspectors to assess Iran’s highly enriched uranium. Israel says it wants to overthrow the Islamic Republic.
Tehran wants to lift the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports, which has halted crude oil exports and disrupted most trade, and return to a memorandum of understanding agreed between the two countries in June.
The US has refused this, with President Trump saying he is left with a choice to “finish the job” by launching major strikes on Iran’s civilian infrastructure. This could prompt Iran to lash out at its neighbours, as it did earlier in the war with strikes on US bases in Arab states and infrastructure.
Meanwhile, the US Department of State issued an October 21 order for nonemergency US government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia for their safety’s sake, given the Houthi threat.
As talks involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye continue in Iran, analysts say these Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signatories will likely try to minimise the impact on Saudi Arabia if war does break out again.
“However, since little has changed from an Iranian strategic calculus and the actors involved don’t have the kind of leverage needed to affect Iran’s strategic thinking, these negotiations are going to yield little,” Karim said.

articles.title: Turkish Trade Minister slams tighter EU steel quotas as exports fall 6.7% - Türkiye Today
articles.summary: Turkish Trade Minister slams tighter EU steel quotas as exports fall 6.7%  Türkiye Today
articles.full_text:
Türkiye's steel exports to the European Union fell as tighter import quotas and new carbon rules weighed on trade, with shipments of steel products covered by the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) declining 1.7% in the first nine months of 2026, Trade Minister Omer Bolat said on Friday.
Speaking at the Steel Networking Summits 2026, Bolat highlighted the impact of European trade measures on Turkish steelmakers, warning that unilateral restrictions could raise costs for exporters and disrupt the supply of lower-carbon steel.
Türkiye's overall iron and steel exports to the EU dropped 6.7% in January-September, while shipments to destinations outside the bloc rose 10%, according to figures cited by Bolat.
The EU narrowed its steel import quotas by 50% from July 1, 2026, while the CBAM began taking effect at the start of the year, requiring companies to measure and verify emissions and pushing producers toward lower-carbon manufacturing.
"Our priority is to support the green transition while ensuring that exporters do not face disproportionate costs and additional trade barriers," Bolat said.
Türkiye produced 38.1 million tons of crude steel in 2025, ranking seventh globally and first in Europe, Bolat said.
The country exported $17.1 billion worth of steel to more than 200 countries, becoming the world's 10th-largest steel exporter. Global steel trade reached $615 billion, with the EU accounting for 42.3% of Türkiye's steel exports.
Bolat highlighted steel's role in construction, automotive manufacturing, machinery, energy, transportation, shipbuilding and defense.
About 78% of Türkiye's steelmaking capacity relies on scrap-based electric arc furnaces. The country imported 18.8 million tons of steel scrap while producing 27.5 million tons of crude steel through this technology, according to Bolat.
He criticized U.S. and EU steel trade restrictions, arguing that unilateral measures hurt exporters, manufacturers reliant on steel inputs and consumers while disrupting the supply of low-carbon steel.
Bolat reiterated Türkiye's support for fair, rules-based trade, noting that the EU is Türkiye's largest trading partner and Türkiye is the bloc's fifth-largest.
Annual bilateral trade reached $233 billion (€204 billion), while trade over the past five years exceeded €900 billion, or $1 trillion, he said.
Türkiye's goods exports rose from $36 billion in 2002 to $273.2 billion in 2025, reaching an annualized $283.7 billion as of September 2026, Bolat said.
Over the same 12-month period, the country imported $380 billion worth of goods, including steel, oil, natural gas, coal, gold and industrial products.
Including services, total exports reached $409 billion, comprising $283.7 billion in goods and $125 billion in services. Service imports stood at $63 billion-$64 billion, bringing total foreign trade to $860 billion, according to Bolat.
He said Türkiye's economy grew by an average of 5.35% annually in real terms over the past 24 years. Excluding 2009, the country recorded positive growth in 15 of the past 16 years and expanded for 24 consecutive quarters following the second quarter of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The economy grew 2.5% in the first half of 2026, expanding 2.6% in the first quarter and 2.3% in the second. Net exports of goods and services contributed strongly to growth, Bolat added.
Gross domestic product rose from $238 billion 24 years ago to $1.7 trillion, with the economy expected to reach around $1.8 trillion by the end of 2026. Per capita income stood at $18,000 in 2025 and was expected to exceed $20,000 this year, he said.

articles.title: UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises - The Guardian
articles.summary: UK shop price inflation ‘highest since 2024’ as retailers struggle to limit price rises  The GuardianInflation and government borrowing highest for a year ahead of next week's Budget  BBCInflation jumps in run-up to Healey’s maiden Budget  The TelegraphAct now or face rising food prices, BRC warns Chancellor ahead of budget  The GrocerWe need a genuine cost of living budget  Third Force News
articles.full_text:
Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers.
The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out.
It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday.
Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year.
The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month.
Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly.
Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. If the rise in retail prices persists, it is likely to persuade many of the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee to raise rates still further in December or the new year.
Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years.”
She said that while there was heavy discounting to attract shoppers ahead of Halloween celebrations, supermarkets could no longer keep the prices of tins and packets on their shelves from going up.
The chancellor is expected to come under intense pressure from his own backbenchers concerned that the high cost of living is harming many of their constituents.
The impact of cost of living pressures on low-income families is the subject of a report by Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow.
Based on a long-term study, it shows that high petrol and diesel prices are hitting families who need to transport disabled children to and from school and health appointments, and workers who use a car to travel to and from their jobs.
Petrol prices above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre can mean that work doesn’t pay, according to Patrick, who leads Changing Realities, an online project tracking 100 low-income families.
She said that in the last month almost three-quarters (73%) of participants in the project had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold.
One respondent, Rosie L, who lives in rural Scotland, said: “It’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car.” She added: “Public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are [and] not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly as my children are disabled.”
The report involves in-depth interviews with 70 participants, of which 67 shared strategies they had taken to reduce costs over the previous month.
Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities so far did not match the scale of the problem. “The budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’,” she argued.
“Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of child benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”

articles.title: Canada, UK to develop separate defense financing institutions - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Canada, UK to develop separate defense financing institutions  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
Investing.com -- Canada and Britain agreed on Sunday to develop separate but complementary defence financing institutions, rather than merge their rival proposals, in a bid to speed up funding for military procurement.
The two countries said in a joint statement issued by the Department of Finance Canada that they had agreed to develop a framework of cooperation that works in the interest of both institutions.
The institutions are the Multilateral Defence Mechanism and the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank. Canada and Britain said they had "mutually concluded that it is best to develop two distinct but complementary institutions that work in partnership."
The countries said they were working to strengthen defence financing and improve the efficiency of spending.
Once the institutions are set up, they will be designed to work in close partnership so they can support each other on emerging industrial priorities, investment opportunities and strategic financing challenges, the statement said.
Together, they will offer complementary tools to strengthen the defence industrial base and improve collective defence readiness.

articles.title: Clean Energy Boom Is Driven by Security, Not Climate Targets - Discovery Alert
articles.summary: Clean Energy Boom Is Driven by Security, Not Climate Targets  Discovery Alert
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- Renewables supplied 33.8% of global electricity in 2025 against 33.0% for coal, the first crossover in the modern power system, though coal generation fell only 0.6%.
- UNEP's lowest-overshoot pathway needs cuts of 18% by 2030 and 45% by 2035, while current NDCs deliver only about 5-8% by 2030 and 11-15% by 2035.
- Clean energy attracts about US$2.2 trillion of 2026 investment against US$1.2 trillion for fossil fuels, driven mainly by security and affordability rather than climate targets.
- Grid investment of about US$550 billion has not cleared the bottleneck, as transmission, transformers, permitting and interconnection queues now constrain deployment more than panel or turbine costs.
- Security logic also supports gas, with US$330 billion of spending at a decade high, so clean energy gets built only where import exposure points that way.
Renewables now generate more of the world’s electricity than coal. Yet in the same year, the United Nations has concluded that holding warming to 1.5°C is no longer attainable without overshooting it first. Both facts are true, and the tension between them is the signal most clean energy investors are missing: the record investment boom is not being driven mainly by climate ambition.
The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) launched its Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return on 21 October 2026. It projects roughly 2.6-2.8°C of warming by 2100 under current pledges and policies.
That matters for your portfolio because the motive behind spending shapes how durable it is. If you assume clean energy demand rests on climate targets, the UN’s verdict looks like a threat. If you see that security and price stability are doing the heavy lifting, the picture changes.
Here is whether security-led deployment can move at the pace UNEP says is needed, and where the investment risk actually sits.
What UNEP’s overshoot verdict actually says (and what it does not)
The headline shorthand, “1.5°C is dead”, misstates the finding. UNEP is not saying the target is physically impossible. It is saying that staying below 1.5°C the whole way is no longer a plausible route, and that countries can still limit how high warming peaks and how long the overshoot lasts.
The spread between pathways shows how much is still in play.
| Pathway | Warming by 2100 | Key condition | 
|---|---|---|
| Current policies | ~2.8°C | Warming keeps rising after 2100 | 
| Full NDC implementation | ~2.6°C | All national pledges delivered | 
| Most optimistic scenario | ~2.1°C | NDCs plus extra net-zero commitments | 
| Lowest-overshoot pathway | Peak ~1.7-1.8°C mid-century, about 50% chance of returning to 1.5°C | Steep cuts plus large-scale CO₂ removal | 
Nationally determined contributions (NDCs) are the emissions-cut pledges each country submits under the Paris Agreement. The lowest-overshoot route requires cuts relative to 2025 of:
- 18% by 2030
- 45% by 2035
- 69% by 2040
Reporting on the assessment puts current NDCs at only about 5-8% by 2030 and 11-15% by 2035. Meanwhile, Carbon Brief estimates fossil CO₂ rose 0.4-1.1% in 2025, methane held roughly flat, and total emissions reached about 58.4 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent.
The removal bill The lowest-overshoot pathway needs roughly 320 GtCO₂ removed and permanently stored this century, about eight years of 2024 global CO₂ emissions.
That gap tells you policy alone is not on track. You cannot treat climate commitments as the main support for clean energy demand.
When big ASX news breaks, our subscribers know first
Record deployment, but is it fast enough? Power, EVs and oil in 2025
If pledges are falling short, the hardware tells a more encouraging story, at least at first.
The power sector
The crossover Renewables supplied 33.8% of global electricity in 2025 (about 10,730 TWh), against 33.0% for coal (about 10,476 TWh), according to Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026, published 22 June 2026.
It is the first time renewables have beaten coal in the modern power system, and coal generation slipped 63 TWh (0.6%). One caveat: Ember measures generation share, so the milestone holds for electricity, not for total final energy, which still includes oil-heavy transport and industry.
EVs, oil and rising demand
The headline 2025 numbers from the International Energy Agency (IEA):
- Over 20 million electric cars sold, up more than 20%
- Roughly one quarter of global new-car sales
- Clean technologies deployed since 2019 avoided over 35 exajoules of annual fossil demand
How much oil EVs displaced depends on which figure you use. Earlier reporting citing the IEA put it at about 1.2 million barrels per day, while the IEA’s Global EV Outlook 2026 says the global fleet avoided about 1.7 million barrels per day; the gap may reflect different scopes (new sales versus the whole fleet) or publication timing. The IEA credits most of it to fuel standards and industrial policy in China and the EU.
Then the stubborn data arrives. Global oil demand still grew about 0.65 million barrels per day, led by petrochemicals and aviation, and AI growth plus development in the Global South keeps pushing energy demand up.
Because oil and emissions both rose in a record clean energy year, you should read this boom as displacement at the margin, not yet as decline in the fossil system.
Differences between IEA scenarios on demand growth and policy ambition help explain why investment forecasts diverge so widely, and why the same 2025 data can support opposing readings of the transition.
Why security, not climate, is now steering the capital
So who is paying for the build-out, and why? Follow the money first.
Where the money is going
| Category | Approx. 2026 figure | Note | 
|---|---|---|
| Total energy investment | US$3.4T | Up about 5% | 
| Clean energy | US$2.2T | Renewables, nuclear, grids, storage, efficiency | 
| Fossil fuels | US$1.2T | Still substantial | 
| Renewable power | US$665B | Includes about US$365B solar | 
| Grids | US$550B | Bottleneck spending | 
| Gas | US$330B | Decade high, partly tied to AI demand | 
Source: IEA, World Energy Investment 2026. That is almost US$2 of clean spending for every US$1 on fossil fuels, a major shift in capital allocation but not an end to fossil investment.
The security logic, and its limits
The IEA attributes the reshuffle to security concerns, geopolitical uncertainty and affordability, and estimates about US$260 billion of fuel-import spending was avoided across five major importing regions in 2025. The mechanism is simple: renewables cost a lot to build but almost nothing to run, so each project reduces exposure to imported fuel.
Energy security capital allocation now explains much of the reshuffle, with boards weighing import exposure and price stability alongside returns when choosing between renewables, grids and gas.
Wind and solar, argues David Frykman of Norrsken in a Fortune op-ed, cannot be embargoed, blockaded or cut off by a foreign power.
Fortune reported that over 90% of new renewable capacity added in 2025 was cheaper than the fossil alternative, and Forbes has framed clean energy as an economic and geopolitical necessity. Even so, IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol told Reuters on 17 September 2026 that grid capacity and affordability remain the main barriers.
Security cuts both ways. The same logic justifies domestic gas, nuclear, coal retention and LNG terminals, which the gas figure above already shows.
If clean energy is bought for resilience and price, you can expect it to survive climate backlash. You should also expect it to be built only where security logic points, and that sometimes points to gas.
How security-led clean energy works in practice, and where it has already worked
The basic mechanism
Think of a power source as two bills: the cost to build it and the cost to fuel it. A gas plant is cheaper to build but needs fuel bought every day, often from abroad, at whatever price the market sets. A solar farm costs more upfront, then its fuel is free.
Once built, it insulates you from the next price shock. Batteries extend that by storing cheap output, while heat pumps, efficiency upgrades and EVs move heating and transport onto the same domestic electricity.
Four precedents
- Europe after 2022: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine triggered a gas price shock; the response mixed efficiency, LNG diversification, heat pumps, solar, wind and storage, and with over 90% of new 2025 renewables cheaper than fossil options, it became self-reinforcing.
- China: Industrial policy, security and export competitiveness drive rapid solar, battery, EV and grid build, though Asia remains the main region where coal stays significant.
- India: Solar and efficiency reduce exposure to imported coal, oil and gas while meeting fast-growing demand; the IEA names India, China and the EU among the importers benefiting from avoided imports.
- Import-dependent developing economies: Solar-plus-storage goes up faster than large fossil or nuclear projects and avoids expensive diesel and LNG bills.
Transport follows the same pattern: EVs in China and the EU drove most of the roughly 1.7 million barrels per day the IEA says was avoided in 2025. The case is strongest where imported fuel is expensive and sunshine is plentiful.
These outcomes rest on local fuel costs and policy, so judge any clean energy exposure by how import-dependent and policy-supported its home market is.
Can security-driven deployment close the gap, and where is the investor risk?
You might expect a yes or no. The more useful answer sits in between.
Is the pace enough?
Some forces are structural: falling solar and wind costs, rapid EV uptake and lasting worries about import exposure. Others are cyclical, because fuel shocks linked to the Ukraine and Iran wars lifted urgency that could fade if prices normalise. Against both stand AI-driven demand, new fossil infrastructure and the risk of policy reversal.

articles.full_text:
LONDON — U.K. Chancellor John Healey is set to deliver an unexpected increase in defense spending at his first budget on Wednesday, as Britain strains to reach its NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035.
Healey — who quit as defense secretary in the dying days of Keir Starmer’s government over a funding row — hopes he can show how Britain will start to reach that target now that he's safely ensconced in the powerful Treasury.
Until last week, it was assumed that the top finance minister would defer decisions on ramping up funding until next year’s multi-year, government-wide spending review. So Wednesday’s move could represent an early win for the Ministry of Defence in Prime Minister Andy Burnham's new government.

Epoch Blue (t/a Epoch) secures £3.2 million Seed funding led by Burnt Island Ventures and Sand River
EPOCH RAISES $6.26M TO EQUIP SUPPLY CHAIN COMPLIANCE PROFESSIONALS WITH AI
The first-mile data platform, already available to more than 30,000 enterprises through partners including Altana, Assent, Resilinc and 3E, now opens directly to small and mid-sized businesses.
London, 26 October 2026 – Epoch, the first-mile supply chain intelligence platform, has today launched a self-serve product that automates compliance for small and mid-sized businesses (SMBs), starting with the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR)*. The launch follows the close of a $4.25M seed round led by Burnt Island Ventures and Sand River, bringing Epoch’s total funding to $6.26M.
Rather than relying solely on supplier questionnaires, Epoch uses geospatial AI and agentic research to map the first mile of a supply chain: the farms, plantations and mines where raw materials originate. Companies can see independently where their goods come from, and focus supplier outreach where it is genuinely needed.
Reporting requirements on supply chains have increased significantly in recent years, and more regulations are on the way. For SMBs, one of the most pressing is the EUDR. The EUDR applies to large and medium operators from 30 December 2026, and to most micro and small operators from 30 June 2027. From those dates, companies of every size must show where their raw materials were produced, yet most suppliers cannot provide this. Smallholders growing cocoa, coffee and rubber rarely hold plot-level coordinates, and countries including China and Indonesia now restrict what companies may share, even with their own customers abroad.
SMBs are particularly exposed to the risk of non-compliance. They lack the purchasing power of larger operators, making them more vulnerable to supplier questionnaires going unanswered. Epoch’s answer is to analyse a supply chain once and use the results across multiple regulatory requirements. As the number of supply chain regulations grows, sending suppliers a fresh questionnaire for each regulation becomes harder to sustain. A single first-mile analysis produces evidence that serves the EUDR today and can also be tailored to new regulations as they arrive, so the burden no longer falls on suppliers alone.
“Supply chain compliance has been built on questionnaires, audits and certifications, and that toolkit is incomplete: regulations keep multiplying while suppliers increasingly can’t, or aren’t allowed to answer, ”
said Jinal Surti, co-founder and CEO of Epoch.
“We’ve built a compliance solution for the AI era. One sweep across a supply chain, using geospatial AI and agentic research, produces evidence that can be packaged for every regulation a company faces, including the ones not written yet. Enterprises get it inside the platforms they already run, and from today on, so does any SMB.”
The EU Deforestation Regulation requires companies placing cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya or wood products on the EU market to prove they are deforestation-free and legally produced, traced to the plot where the commodity was grown, and covered by a Due Diligence StatementBy enabling enhanced visibility of supply chains Epoch also allows businesses to manage these supply chains more proactively creating positive outcomes both for supply chain resilience and the health of the environments from which products are sourced.
Self-serve compliance for SMBs Companies can start with whatever supplier information they already hold, even a simple list of supplier names. Compliance teams can work in Epoch’s self-serve platform, or through AI assistants they already use, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, to clean their data and ask questions about risk in plain language. Sensitive business information stays private within their own environment.
Epoch then does the rest, without asking suppliers for plot data. It locates supplier facilities, identifies the plots where goods are produced, and assesses deforestation and legality risk. The result is a Due Diligence Statement, with every finding cited, ready to submit to the EU Information System (TRACES).
Enterprise access through partner platforms Larger companies can use Epoch inside the software they already run. Epoch has signed partnerships with Altana, Assent, Resilinc and 3E, each of which has integrated Epoch or is in the process of doing so. Together they give more than 30,000 enterprises access to first-mile data without changing systems. Epoch supplies the data; the partner platform handles the workflow.
Over the past six months, Epoch has screened more than 12,000 suppliers for enterprise customers.
What partners say
“European importers need to know not just who their suppliers are, but where their goods actually come from. Altana is the AI network for global trade, where eight of the world’s ten largest logistics providers, Fortune 1000 companies and their suppliers, and governments work together. Epoch’s first-mile intelligence is helping extend our network to the source, so our customers can meet EUDR and CBAM and keep their products trade-ready for Europe. ”
– Evan Smith, CEO and Co-Founder, Altana
“Adding AI-enabled first-mile intelligence to the Assent Network with Epoch helps our customers and suppliers better identify where risk may be concentrated, spot gaps in their data and build visibility into their supply chain across multiple tiers. We want to equip our customers with the most complete product intelligence network to allow them to make better informed decisions based on a reusable data foundation they can trust, giving them confidence they are meeting their regulatory and compliance requirements in the markets they serve. Our partnership with Epoch is one of many ways we are helping them do that. ”
Catherine Cormier, Chief Innovation Officer, Assent
“Resilinc’s platform works hand-in-hand with Epoch’s verified first-mile data to help our customers identify exposure, prioritize supplier actions and streamline due diligence submission, creating a foundation for evolving EU compliance requirements and more. ”
– Ranjit Jose, Head of Product and Partner Marketing,
Resilinc
“Combining Epoch’s first-mile intelligence with 3E’s breadth of regulatory content enables our customers to move beyond data collection to power full-scale compliance strategy across regulations, including EUDR.”
– Meredith Bearden, Managing Director, Supply Chain and Sustainability, 3ECustomers of each platform can ask their account manager about enabling Epoch.
Growing the team
Jinal Surti and William Ouellette (Co-founder and CTO) built the product on their deep technical skills. Drawing on their extensive experience of growing businesses, the Epoch team has built out its commercial capability across North America and EMEA. Dave Shanteler has joined as Head of Partnerships, Mario Romero Garoz leads EMEA Sales, and Tony Dawson leads North American Sales.
Funding
The $4.25M seed round was led by Burnt Island Ventures and Sand River, and brings the total Epoch has raised to $6.26M. Christine Boyle, Partner at Burnt Island Ventures, has joined Epoch’s board. The funding will go into product, infrastructure and the commercial team.
“Large companies rely on their supply chains to operate their businesses, and they are often operating in the dark as to the local conditions around drought, flood, and forest health. The Epoch platform leverages AI, earth observation data and proprietary models to enable visibility into risk mitigation, and compliance. Epoch is a team of 14 that operates like a team of 140, punching way above their weight! It’s a transformative approach to managing supply chain risk and compliance. ”

articles.title: Omnibus V — Defense Readiness: Simplification of EU Rules on Defense Procurement, Permitting and Intra-EU Transfers - Freshfields
articles.summary: Omnibus V — Defense Readiness: Simplification of EU Rules on Defense Procurement, Permitting and Intra-EU Transfers  Freshfields
articles.full_text:
Oct 26 2026
On 9 October 2026, the Council of the European Union (the Council) formally approved the “Omnibus V” defense simplification package. This followed the political agreement reached with the European Parliament (Parliament) in June 2026 and Parliament’s first-reading position of 16 September 2026. For defense companies operating in the European Union (EU), the package will result in important changes to EU rules on defense procurement, permitting and intra-EU transfers, including:
higher thresholds to fall within scope of the EU Defence and Security Procurement Directive (up to EUR 2 million for supply and service contracts and EUR 10 million for works contracts);
faster permitting for defense readiness projects such as munitions plants, testing facilities and factory expansions; and
General Transfer Licences for moving defense equipment between certified suppliers, under EU-funded defense programmes, and within structured intra-EU industrial partnerships — reshaping how cross-border contracts and supply chains are structured.
The package comprises three new legislative acts: two Regulations and one Directive. Following the Council’s final approval[RC1] , the legislative phase is complete, and the Regulations will take effect next month with direct EU-wide application, while the Directive triggers the national transposition period for procurement and transfer rules.
In our previous blog post, we explored the antitrust and state aid considerations arising from the European Commission (Commission)’s proposal for the Defence Readiness Omnibus. These antitrust and state aid proposals were not covered in the Omnibus V legislative package; we cover where they currently stand further below.
Context
The Omnibus V package is the legislative pillar of the EU’s Rearm/Readiness 2030 agenda (see our previous blog posthere). It aims to eliminate administrative drag, compress timelines and create the legal framework needed to scale defense manufacturing across Europe — forging, in the Commission’s words, a “Pax Europaea for the 21st century.”
The package comprises: (i) an amending Directive on transfers and defense procurement, (ii) a new Regulation on fast-track permitting and (iii) an amending Regulation on defense readiness and investments. We explore each of these below.
Defense procurement and intra-EU transfers of defense equipment
Higher procurement thresholds: The financial threshold above which contracts fall within the scope of the Defence and Security Procurement Directive has been raised from EUR 432,000 to EUR 2 million for supply and service contracts, and from EUR 5.404 million to EUR 10 million for works contracts. A EUR 1.5 million ammunition contract, for example, now falls outside of the Defence and Security Procurement Directive’s scope and may be awarded under national rules.
New General Transfer Licences: The existing certified-supplier/recipient licence under the Intra-EU Transfers Directive is reinforced so it covers at least the same products as the EU, NATO or intergovernmental licence; and two new licences are created: (i) for European Defence Fund or EU programme-funded transfers, and (ii) for structured intra-EU industrial partnerships. This replaces case-by-case national permits with a pre-approved framework for moving defense components across EU borders.
Cross-border joint procurement: Cross-border joint procurement was already possible under the Defence and Security Directive, including through a ‘lead nation’ central purchasing body. It relied on Article 10 and the non-binding 2019 Commission guidance. New Articles 10a and 10b make this binding and add detail. They prevent Member States from blocking the use of central purchasing bodies in other Member States. They require joint purchasers to agree responsibilities and applicable national law, and to record this in the procurement documents. They also deem participants compliant when they buy from the responsible authority. These reforms build on the momentum of other recent initiatives to promote more cross-border joint procurement — including the UK, Finland, Poland and the Netherlands’ proposals for a joint defense financing mechanism (see our previous blog here).
Accelerated tendering and flexible purchasing: The package introduces dedicated rules for Dynamic Purchasing Systems (Article 29a) for fast, recurring electronic purchases of defense goods and Innovation Partnerships (Article 27a) to co-develop innovative tech from R&D to procurement. It also shortens the minimum bidding window from 40 days to 37 days (Article 33). This helps speed up contract awards for critical defense equipment.
A temporary “reporting holiday” to cut red tape: Member States’ annual procurement statistical reporting obligations to the European Commission are suspended until 31 December 2030 to free up administrative resources for defense ramp-up.
Importantly, the amendments to the Defence and Security Procurement Directive described above are separate from the Commission's ongoing review of that Directive, which is expected to be finalised by the end of 2026.
Acceleration of permit-granting procedures
A new, standalone EU Permit-Granting Regulation creates a fast-track pathway for “defense readiness projects,” such as munitions plants, testing facilities, and factory expansions. Each Member State must designate a Single Point of Contact (SPOC) to coordinate all environmental, safety, and planning approvals and notify final approval. The process is capped at 42 working days (extendable to a maximum of 102 working days in complex cases) and introduces the principle of tacit approval, meaning permits are deemed automatically granted if authorities fail to meet the deadline. Unlike the Commission’s original proposal for blanket automatic approvals, the final text allows Member States to derogate from tacit approval and issue a formal written decision if a project poses a serious risk to human health or national security.
Targeted chemical exemptions: Article 2 of REACH is amended to allow Member States to exempt chemical substances where necessary for defense, with corresponding adaptions to other biological and environmental EU rules.
Protecting defense intellectual property rights (IPR) and bolstering SME incentives: The Regulation caps the repayment clawback for non-EU technology transfers to three years after final project payment, while restricting IPR ownership claims of Member States co-financing EDF projects. In parallel, the Regulation increases the proposed funding bonus for SME participation in EDF projects.
Streamlining EDF management: Multi-annual work programmes (Article 24), more flexible indirect management and simplified SME application procedures make EU co-financing easier to access.
Supporting cooperation with Ukraine: Strategic industrial partnerships will become more integrated by explicitly making costs for defense testing activities carried out in Ukraine eligible for funding under the EDF.
Antitrust and State aid
Alongside this legislative package, the Commission’s original Defence Readiness Omnibus set out a parallel, non-legislative agenda for antitrust and State aid, explored in more detail in our Roadmap for EU Defence Consolidation blog (see here). These commitments do not change the legal framework but signal a Commission supportive of certain defense sector consolidation and cooperation.
Draft Merger Guidelines: the Commission’s draft Merger Guidelines commit to weighing the changed security environment and the benefits of enhanced EU defense and security. The draft Guidelines also for the first time explicitly recognise EU Defence Readiness as part of the competitive assessment. The Commission is expected to finalise its Guidelines by the end of 2026 or the start of 2027.
Antitrust: the Commission has signalled it is willing to provide guidance to parties on defense-sector cooperation needed to scale up production, weighing efficiencies and readiness benefits.
State aid: the Commission stated in its Defence Readiness Omnibus that it will prioritise defense-readiness State aid casesand also highlighted that certain aid for defense production capacity may be exempted under the Article 346 TFEU “essential security interests” exemption (though EU courts require narrow, case-by-case application of this exemptions).
Outlook
A theme across all three of the Omnibus V acts is the balance struck between defense single-market integration and national sovereignty. While fully endorsing the Commission’s deregulatory aim, the Parliament and the Council were careful to recognise through targeted opt-out provisions the Member States’ authority over their national security interests under Article 346 TFEU and Article 4(2) TEU.
For European defense businesses, the focus now turns from the legislative process to operational implementation. The practical value of Omnibus V will depend on how quickly, and to what extent, its reforms can be translated into commercial advantage. Companies that have already mapped these reforms against their procurement, supply chain and investment strategies with the new rules now will be best placed to capture the benefits as the Regulations enter into force and Member States transpose the Directive.
Importantly, these reforms are only one part of a wider process of change: the Commission's separate review of the Defence and Security Procurement Directive, due to conclude by the end of 2026, is expected to bring further reform, which may include reforms on participation restrictions (such as a ‘Buy European’ requirement) and the ‘defence exemption’ under Article 346 TFEU. For defence companies active in Europe, it will be critical to prepare for and navigate both the immediate changes — including to procurement thresholds, transfer licensing and permitting — as well as this further wave of reform to the Defence and Security Procurement Directive.

articles.summary: Cornish bride given 'potentially deadly' wedding cake  Cornwall LiveCornwall baker to pay £3,963 over plastic in wedding cake and false nut-free claim  Falmouth PacketUK bride gets 'potentially deadly' wedding cake - then maker refuses refund  The MirrorWadebridge baker fined after plastic found inside wedding cake  CornishStuff
articles.full_text:
The baker refused to provide a refund
A bride in Cornwall avoided a catastrophe after being given a wedding cake containing "potentially deadly" traces of nuts.
It was only discovered after the cake was found to be the wrong colour and had imperfections on the icing when it was delivered to the venue on the day of the wedding.
Faye Selway of the Natural Cake Company, based in Wadebridge, pleaded guilty at Bodmin Magistrates Court to four charges under the Food Safety Act 1990 and the Food Safety and Hygiene (England) Regulations 2013.
The case was brought by Cornwall Council following a complaint from a customer relating to plastic contamination in a wedding cake supplied by Ms Selway in April of this year.
The kitchen staff at the wedding venue had discovered pieces of plastic between the icing layers when the cake was cut in the kitchen to serve to the guests.
As a result of this, the cake was not served for fear of further pieces of plastic being in the cake posing a risk to health.
The customer contacted Cornwall Council, following Selway’s refusal to provide a refund.
On investigation, it was discovered that Selway, aged 49 and of Glen Road, Wadebridge, had also given the customer both written and verbal assurance that the cake would be nut free and made in a completely nut free environment at her cake studio, which was vital as one of the brides has a severe nut allergy and, in the past, had been hospitalised with anaphylaxis.
Don't let an algorithm decide what Cornwall news you see - click here to add CornwallLive as your preferred Google source.
Given the concerns not only around the plastic, but also the standard of the cake, further investigations revealed that the cake was not made in the studio, but in a domestic kitchen, which could not be the nut free environment that was crucial to the brides.
The court heard Selway vacated the cake studio nine months before she took the order for the cake, knowing full well that it would not be made in a dedicated studio.
Neither the cake studio or Selway’s domestic kitchen were registered with Cornwall Council as a food business, which is required by law and therefore had not been subjected to any food safety interventions, which would have included allergen control and assessing allergen claims.
Selway had been advised in writing by the council when she was considering setting up the cake studio that she would need to register as a food business if she pursued the venture and was therefore fully aware of the requirement.
The council said that had the plastic not been in the cake, and it was served at the wedding, the potential for nut contamination could have had catastrophic results.
The magistrates, in line with sentencing guidelines fined Selway £896 ordered her to pay the council’s costs of £3,067 totalling £3963.
Nick Kelly, group leader, food safety, health and safety and port health said: “The legislation around allergens in food are there to ensure consumers have accurate advice to enable them to make an informed decision in respect of the foods they consume. In this case, the misleading information could have had life threatening consequences.
“Where businesses fail to meet their legal obligations and put people at risk, the Council will not hesitate to take formal enforcement action.”
Councillor Thalia Marrington, cabinet member with responsibility for community safety and public protection at Cornwall Council, added: “This case highlights the importance of ensuring businesses provide accurate information in relation to the foods they sell.
"Making misleading claims is totally unacceptable and in instances like this can be life threatening to the consumer.
“When businesses blatantly disregard their legal obligations and put their customers at risk, we have no choice but to take action.”

articles.summary: Smoke and Fires in Voronezh: Drone Hits 25-Story Business Center as 7 Fuel Tankers Burn in Russia  Kyiv PostUkraine-Russia war latest: Drone strikes kill three in Belgorod and injure five at Russian industrial plant  The IndependentUkrainian Attacks Kill 5 in Belgorod and Lipetsk, Hit Perm Industrial Plant  The Moscow TimesDrone attack sparks fires at industrial facilities in Russia’s Voronezh region  UkrinformDrone Attack Damages Moscow-Bound Passenger Tr...
articles.full_text:
A drone attack reportedly hit a 25-story business center and residential buildings in Russia’s Voronezh, while a separate train derailment in Sverdlovsk Region left seven fuel tankers burning.
The independent Russian outlet Astra reported that a drone struck the Chizhova Gallery business center at 35A Koltsovskaya Street. The complex includes a 25-story high-rise that is one of the city center’s prominent architectural landmarks, according to the facility’s website.
The attack prompted reports of numerous explosions and fires across Voronezh. Astra said a drone threat was declared in the region at around 3 a.m., followed by a missile threat approximately two hours later. Residents told the outlet that they had heard explosions but that no air-raid sirens had sounded.
Residential buildings, vehicles reportedly damaged
An Astra OSINT analysis of photographs and videos identified several locations where damage or fires were reported.
According to the outlet, a residential complex at 4K Arkhitektora Troitskogo Street was struck, while the newly built Uritsky residential complex at 135 Uritskogo Street also sustained damage. The latter building was completed last year, Astra reported.
At least 10 cars were reportedly on fire in a parking area at 275/1 45-y Strelkovoy Divizii Street. The outlet also reported fires in residential areas and smoke spreading across the city.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ claimed that some of the impacts resulted from Russian electronic warfare systems operating inside the city, alleging that Russian air defenses caused damage while attempting to counter the drones. The claim has not been independently verified.
Another monitoring channel, Supernova+, reported that the Severny Bridge in Voronezh may also have been targeted, citing reports that the bridge was closed and smoke was visible nearby.
Industrial and aviation facilities possibly targeted
Supernova+, citing their own open-source intelligence analysis, suggested that the Voronezhsintezkauchuk synthetic rubber plant and the Voronezh Aircraft Joint-Stock Company (VASO) may also have been targeted.
Voronezhsintezkauchuk, part of Russian petrochemical group SIBUR, produces synthetic rubber and thermoplastic elastomers. VASO is part of Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation and participates in the production of Il-96 long-haul aircraft and components for other aircraft.
Killed and injured in Voronezh drone attack, governor says
A drone attack reportedly killed two people and injured 17 others in Voronezh.
Voronezh Region Governor Alexander Gusev said the two people killed were men born in 1960 and 1973. One child was among the injured, and two of the wounded were in serious condition.
A significant number of those injured were traveling on a train passing through Voronezh’s left-bank suburbs when drone debris fell onto it, Gusev said. Emergency services were working at the scene.
The attack also sparked fires at several industrial facilities, a business center, an apartment building, two dacha settlements, a school stadium, and a garage cooperative, according to the governor. He said the industrial fires had no major consequences.
Building facades and windows were damaged in nearly every district of the city, Gusev added.
According to the governor, air defense forces shot down more than 70 drones over Voronezh, while 113 were intercepted across the metropolitan area and several districts of the region. These figures have not been independently verified.
Neither the Russian defense ministry nor Ukrainian officials have commented on the reported attack.
Freight train derails in Sverdlovsk Region
Separately, 20 freight train cars derailed in Russia’s Sverdlovsk Region, with seven fuel tankers catching fire, according to reports cited by Astra. The cause of the incident has not been disclosed, and no casualties have been reported.
The Sverdlovsk Railway said traffic on the Reshety-Aramil section had been suspended after the derailment compromised clearance of an adjacent track. Firefighting and recovery trains were dispatched to the scene.
Local residents reported seeing flames and thick black smoke, with one witness telling media that an explosion had illuminated the area near the Chusovsky Tract.
Russia’s consumer rights watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said it would test air quality in nearby residential areas.
The derailment comes amid a series of reported disruptions to Russian railway infrastructure in recent months.
The Moscow Times reported that Ukrainian drone attacks on railway infrastructure in the Bryansk Region on Sept. 28 caused 10 railcars to derail after a railway bridge section collapsed, while a separate incident derailed 18 empty freight cars.
Other reported railway incidents in September and July caused train delays and damage, although the causes differed.
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian officials have publicly attributed the Sverdlovsk derailment to an attack.

The Hague [Netherlands], October 26 (ANI): Netherlands' Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation Sjoerd Sjoerdsma has said he wants India-Netherlands trade to double as soon as possible, identifying semiconductor cooperation, port connectivity and green transport corridors as key areas for expanding bilateral economic ties.
Sjoerdsma said the potential for economic cooperation between the two countries was substantial and pointed to the semiconductor industry as an important driver of future growth.
"The potential is almost unlimited, and I would like to see it double as soon as possible," he said.
Highlighting the Netherlands' strength in semiconductor technology, the minister cited Dutch company ASML and its cooperation with India's Tata group as an example of the opportunities emerging between the two countries.
He said the combination of India's semiconductor ambitions and Dutch technological expertise could create a major new dimension in bilateral economic relations.
"We all know, looking at the tremendous potential within India when it comes to the semiconductor industry, if we look at the tremendous quality and innovation that we can provide, this partnership can be huge," he said.

He said both countries depended significantly on the movement of goods and would pursue opportunities to deepen port-to-port links and develop green transport corridors.
"Wherever we see the possibility to tie our ports to ports in India, to deepen our relationship, to ensure green corridors of transport, we will do so," he said.
The minister added that concrete steps could follow Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal's recent visit to the Port of Rotterdam.
Sjoerdsma also underlined the importance of political trust in expanding commercial engagement, saying relations between India and the Netherlands were at an all-time high.

"We'll be happy to bring our companies to India again because we, just as your minister is bringing Indian companies to us, know that we stand to benefit from our relationship," he said.

articles.summary: Chinese automakers expand manufacturing in Europe to avoid EU tariffs amid rising domestic competition: Repo..  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
Chinese automotive giants, such as BYD and Geely, are setting up production plants in Europe. This strategic initiative helps them sidestep steep EU import taxes on electric vehicles, significantly lowering costs. By investing more in local manufacturing, they cultivate better connections with European suppliers, boosting operational efficiency.
According to the report, Chinese automakers, including BYD, Chery and Geely, are shifting production closer to European markets amid intense domestic competition and excess manufacturing capacity. Beyond avoiding European Union (EU) tariffs, these companies are leveraging underutilised factories and local partnerships to establish a long-term presence in Europe's automotive industry.
"The expansion marks a new phase in China's global automotive ambitions, testing whether its advantages in cost, scale and electric vehicle technology can be replicated overseas," the report said.
At the same time, it noted, for Hyundai Motor Group, which has spent decades building a European manufacturing network, the transformation brings a "formidable new challenge" as Chinese rivals increasingly compete on its turf.
Hence, local production offers a significant advantage in navigating EU trade restrictions, it noted.
Chinese-made battery electric vehicles (EVs) are subject to a standard 10 per cent import duty in the European Union (EU), along with additional countervailing tariffs ranging from 7.8 per cent to 35.3 per cent, depending on the manufacturer.
BYD faces an additional tariff of 17 per cent, while Geely and SAIC Motor face levies of 18.8 per cent and 35.3 per cent, respectively.
Thus, setting up manufacturing facilities within the EU would enable Chinese automakers to avoid these additional import tariffs, lower shipping costs and strengthen ties with local suppliers.
Notably, other Chinese manufacturers are pursuing similar strategies. SAIC Motor, which sells vehicles primarily under its MG brand, has explored plans for a European production facility as it seeks to reduce reliance on imports from China, the report said.
Additionally, "Chinese automakers are increasingly forming alliances with established manufacturers that are struggling with sluggish demand, costly electrification investments and underused production capacity."
It should also be noted that Chinese brands' European sales jumped 90.6 per cent year-on-year to 531,862 vehicles in the first half of 2026, The Korea Herald reported, citing market research firm MarkLines.
"Chinese manufacturers are expanding beyond battery-electric vehicles into plug-in hybrids and conventional hybrids," it noted.
While this shift may help the struggling European factories stay open, it also raises questions about the region's growing reliance on China.

The ECB faces a challenging policy environment, with oil prices remaining above $100 a barrel and inflation risks elevated even as tighter financial conditions threaten to weigh on economic growth. Political instability in France and rising government borrowing costs have added to uncertainty surrounding the euro zone economy, the report stated.
Also Read |Global Market: China's yuan hits four-year high as dollar weakens ahead of policy meetings
ECB expected to keep rates unchanged
Economists polled by Reuters expect the central bank to raise rates by 25 basis points in December, reflecting concerns that inflation could remain elevated if energy costs continue to rise.
Eurozone inflation reached 3.8% in September, well above the ECB's 2% target. At the same time, rising government bond yields are tightening financial conditions and could constrain economic activity, complicating the central bank's efforts to balance price stability with growth.
Also Read |Global Market: South Korean shares fall over 1% as AI trade concerns weigh; won strengthens
Energy prices keep inflation risks elevated
The ECB is likely to remain alert to the possibility that higher energy costs could spread to other goods and services, eventually pushing up wages and broader inflation.
However, recent inflation data suggest that these second-round effects remain relatively contained. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, edged up to 2.5% in September from 2.4% previously, indicating that higher energy costs have yet to trigger a more widespread acceleration in prices.
The report stated that comments from ECB officials, including Chief Economist Philip Lane, suggest policymakers are not yet overly concerned about an energy-driven inflation spiral.
Nevertheless, oil prices have risen sharply this year, while a survey released on Friday showed that euro zone consumers increased their inflation expectations for the next 12 months in September.
Markets are pricing in at least two additional rate increases by mid-2027. Further escalation of the Iran war or renewed pressure on energy prices could strengthen the case for additional tightening, even next year.
French bond selloff adds to ECB's challenges
The deterioration in France's public finances and political stability presents another challenge for the ECB as it prepares for its policy meeting.
French 10-year government bond yields have climbed above 5%, reaching their highest levels in 24 years, while political tensions and protests have complicated the government's efforts to address the country's fragile fiscal position.
The premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over German government debt has widened to 167 basis points, compared with 92 basis points at the ECB's previous meeting.
The widening spread reflects growing investor concerns about France's fiscal outlook and the risk that political uncertainty could undermine efforts to control public debt.
However, the ECB is not expected to intervene immediately through its Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which allows it to purchase government bonds to counter unwarranted and disorderly tightening in financing conditions across euro zone member states.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has argued that France must address its debt problems through fiscal consolidation.
The central bank could, however, reconsider the pace of monetary tightening if financial instability in France threatens to significantly weaken economic growth. The report by Reuters stated that the ECB could also use its bond-buying mechanism to prevent a French crisis from spreading to other euro zone economies with stronger public finances, according to the report.
Lagarde's succession emerges as another focus
Investors are also likely to watch for developments concerning Lagarde's future and the succession process at the ECB.
Lagarde could be appointed as the next chair of the World Economic Forum as early as November, potentially bringing forward discussions about who might succeed her as ECB president.
Former central bank governors Klaas Knot of the Netherlands and Pablo Hernandez de Cos of Spain are considered leading candidates for the position.
Her departure would come amid broader changes to the ECB's leadership. The resignation of Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel has opened another vacancy, while Chief Economist Philip Lane is scheduled to step down in May.
Lagarde's current term is due to end in October next year. An earlier departure could allow European leaders to appoint a successor before France's spring presidential election, reducing the risk that domestic political developments could complicate the selection process.
A possible snap election in Spain could also influence the political dynamics surrounding the appointment.
Policy uncertainty likely to persist
The ECB's October meeting comes at a time when policymakers must navigate competing risks from persistent inflation, higher borrowing costs, geopolitical uncertainty and political instability in a major euro zone economy.
Although a pause in interest rates is widely anticipated, investors will scrutinise the central bank's assessment of energy prices, underlying inflation and financial conditions for clues about its next move.
The immediate decision may be straightforward, but the outlook for monetary policy remains uncertain, with the trajectory of the Iran war, oil prices and France's fiscal situation likely to shape the ECB's decisions in the coming months, according to the report.

articles.title: It’s hard breaking up with Washington: Why Canada’s European defense turn has limits - POLITICO.eu
articles.summary: It’s hard breaking up with Washington: Why Canada’s European defense turn has limits  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
Canada and Europe both want an insurance policy against Donald Trump — and they are turning to defense partnerships to do so.
The military and industrial relationship between Ottawa and Europeans is accelerating, driven by the U.S. president's repeated threats to annex Canada and his undermining of the traditional American commitment to European security.
But European officials, diplomats and analysts who spoke to POLITICO describe a welcome with conditions. Neither side, for one thing, wants a total rupture with Washington, highlighting how delicate reshuffling alliances can be.

articles.full_text:
“What we want to gain from cooperation with South Korea is not a growth rate, but an industrial ecosystem. The new nuclear power plant at Dukovany could be a catalyst for boosting the competitiveness of the Czech manufacturing sector as a whole.”
In an interview with Financial News on the 26th, Czech Ambassador to South Korea Ivan Jančárek said the new nuclear power plant project at Dukovany in the Czech Republic was not “a contract to build two power plants,” but “an industrial cooperation platform combining the Czech Republic’s manufacturing base with South Korea’s nuclear technology and project delivery experience.” Team Korea, led by Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power, was selected as the preferred bidder for the Dukovany Units 5 and 6 project in July 2024 and signed the final contract last year. The project involves building two APR1000 units in the 1,000-MW class, with a total cost of around 400 billion koruna, or well over 20 trillion won. The Czech Republic already operates four units at Dukovany and two at Temelín, generating about 40% of its electricity from nuclear power. 
“The energy industry is a growth engine ... the two countries are alike”
Ambassador Jančárek pointed to manufacturing, particularly heavy industry and mechanical engineering, as common ground between the two countries. He said, “What the Czech Republic is focused on is not simply economic growth, but the creation of a strong industrial ecosystem,” and praised South Korea for “making manufacturing a central pillar of national development while pursuing technology development, workforce training and supply chain development at the same time, thereby raising competitiveness across the industry.”
He added, “If a high level of localization enables Czech companies to participate meaningfully in the supply chain and build new capabilities, this project could become a turning point that transforms the manufacturing sector as a whole, extending beyond nuclear power.” He stressed that “the ultimate goal is to build a long-term partnership in which the two countries grow together and pursue projects together in third-country markets.”
Nuclear power projects in Europe have recently been plagued by construction delays and cost overruns. Finland’s Olkiluoto 3, France’s Flamanville 3 and the United Kingdom’s Hinkley Point C are prominent examples. It is widely believed that South Korea’s on-time, on-budget track record was decisive in the Czech Republic’s choice of South Korea.
He said, “The ability to meet schedules and budgets was one of the most important factors in the evaluation process,” adding that “we examined not only technical excellence but also actual project delivery capabilities in detail.”
He summarized the strengths of South Korea’s proposal in two points: a project schedule that clearly specified the start and completion dates, and a contract structure that imposed liquidated damages for delays if those dates were not met. He said, “It gave us a high level of confidence in project management and commitment to delivery.”
That was further supported by South Korea’s domestic nuclear power projects and its track record at the Barakah Nuclear Power Plant in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). He stressed, “What the Czech Republic valued was not just price competitiveness or technological superiority, but the confidence that comes from a proven track record of completing projects on schedule and within budget.”
Many analysts say the strength of South Korea’s nuclear industry comes not from any single company, but from the concentration within the country of an industrial ecosystem spanning design, manufacture of major components, construction, operation and maintenance, along with a skilled workforce. Only a handful of countries can manufacture key equipment such as reactors, steam generators and turbines all at one plant.
He said, “A closely integrated industrial ecosystem is one of the key competitive strengths of South Korea’s nuclear industry,” explaining that “because its core capabilities are organically connected, both quality control and project predictability are enhanced.” He added, “What the Czech Republic particularly values is that these manufacturing capabilities are integrated into a broader industrial ecosystem.” He stressed that “we could expect reliable project delivery from South Korea, which has built new nuclear power plants for decades, developed its technology, workforce and industrial base, and plans to build additional new nuclear plants at home to sustain them.” 
A century of turbines in Plzeň: Doosan Škoda Power
The fact that a Korean company already has Doosan Škoda Power, a turbine manufacturer in Plzeň, Czech Republic, as an affiliate is seen as evidence that it had taken root in the local industrial ecosystem even before technology transfer was discussed. He said, “Cases like Doosan Škoda Power show that industrial cooperation between the two countries did not emerge suddenly, but has built up over a long period,” also citing investment and job creation by Doosan, Hyundai Motor, Hyundai Mobis and Nexen Tire.
He said, “The evaluation took into account technological capability, safety, project delivery capability, economic viability and the potential for long-term cooperation,” adding that “experience with existing industrial cooperation provided a meaningful foundation for understanding each other’s industrial environments and corporate cultures.”
On the Škoda brand, he said it was “a name that symbolizes the Czech Republic’s industrial tradition and engineering heritage,” and praised Doosan Škoda Power’s participation, saying it “shows that the technological and manufacturing capabilities the Czech Republic has built up over a long period remain competitive in future energy projects.”
Hydrogen and renewable energy are seen as areas for expanding cooperation. He said, “In Europe’s energy transition, nuclear power, renewable energy and hydrogen are complementary, not competing,” adding that “if renewable energy is at the heart of decarbonization, nuclear power supports the grid with stable, predictable electricity, and clean hydrogen produced using that electricity could become an important field for the future.”
Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power and the Czech Hydrogen Technology Platform (HYTEP) agreed to cooperate on nuclear-based clean hydrogen production and technology development. Hydrogen and nuclear power were also discussed at the Korea-Czech Republic Industrial and Energy Technology Cooperation Forum held in Prague that same year.
Ambassador Jančárek predicted, “If cooperation expands to include small modular reactors (SMRs), hydrogen, energy storage and renewable energy, the two countries can develop beyond nuclear power partners into comprehensive energy partners.”

articles.full_text:
The UK's "number one binman" has shared the rules of disposing of shredded paper at home.
Many households have been guilty of placing every piece of paper, plastic, metal or glass in their recycling bins, presuming it can probably be recycled. Regrettably, recycling is more complex than that, given the wide variation in recycling standards throughout the country.
While ordinary sheets of paper can certainly be recycled at home, the situation differs when it comes to shredded paper. Although shredded paper appears to be recyclable, numerous local authorities actually refuse to accept it.
Ashley, the viral sensation known as The No1 Binman on TikTok, has urged households to "stop putting shredded paper in your paper bin".
In a social media post, the binman explained: "It's [shredded paper] not recyclable because you broke it down too much. It's too much effort and costs too much money to recycle it in your normal [recycling] bins. So don't put it in there."
Ashley also highlighted that shredded paper in recycling bins makes the work of bin collectors more difficult. He said: "When we tip it when it's cold, windy, and wet, it goes everywhere, and then we have to try and get it off the floor, sweeping it up - it all sticks to the floor. It's horrible."
Instead, the binman advises households to dispose of shredded paper in their general waste bins, as in most cases it cannot be recycled anyway.
However, if your local authority does accept shredded paper, Ashley suggests: "Put it [the shredded paper] in a Primark bag or something like a paper bag so it doesn't go everywhere."

Why can't I recycle shredded paper at home?
Shredded paper can be recycled in certain instances, but not all local authorities will accept it for recycling, as some paper mills are unable to process it.
This is because the shredding process weakens paper, and it can create difficulties at paper mills, such as maintenance and fire hazard concerns.
If your council won't collect it for recycling, you can simply place it in your general waste bin as advised by The No1 Binman, take it to a paper bank, or put non-glossy shredded paper at the bottom of your food waste recycling bin to absorb any liquid and help stop dripping.
Households can also add it to their home compost heap, though not if it's coloured or glossy paper, as these can contain chemicals that are damaging to plants.
