Europe mostly protects gas and data revenue it already earns
Frigates get billions; cable repair gets tens of millions
Accidents, not sabotage, cause most seabed damage so far
According to figures from the European Commission, Norway accounted for 31% of natural gas imports to the EU in 2025. This number has been steadily increasing from 24% in 2021 and positions Norway as the biggest natural gas exporter to the EU from outside the union. The majority of this gas is transported via pipeline. In 2025, 86 billion cubic metres were sent to EU customers via Norwegian pipelines. That represents 54% of all natural gas sent by pipeline to the EU. Gassco, the state-owned pipeline operator for the 8,800 kilometres of pipeline running across the North Sea, sent a combined total of 114.9 billion cubic metres to Germany, the UK, Belgium, France and Denmark. There is a clear distinction between the debate over North Atlantic security and that of the Bering Strait. The commercial benefit of the Bering Strait comes from increased trade in the Arctic. Right now, that is just speculation. Whereas the benefit to the North Atlantic between Norway and the UK is already built and in use on the ocean floor.
There is an implication that if money is spent on defence in these areas, most of that money is going towards assets that would earn money regardless. The question becomes: is it lowering the expected costs of not making that money by more than what is spent on defence? When talking about defence spending in these areas, there are many numbers being mixed together. First are actual amounts that are being spent. For example, Norway recently placed a £10 billion order with the UK for Type 26 Frigates. Next are plans that have no attached cost. The EU recently released its Arctic Strategy on the 20th of October 2026. Much of that plan fits this description. The last number is how much would be lost if a certain event occurred. With these three numbers in mind, Europe is spending more money on ships and less money on the ability to fix things when they break.
Norwegian Gas Is Something Europe Cannot Replace
Not only is Europe dependent on Norway for gas. Norway is also dependent on Europe. Crude oil, natural gas, natural gas liquids and condensate made up 1,000 billion NOK of Norwegian exports in 2025, according to information released by the Ministry of Energy and the Norwegian Offshore Directorate. This represented 57% of the total amount of goods exported from Norway. Gas brought in more than oil. Almost all of this gas travels through a few key points. The refining facilities in Kollsnes, Kårstø and Nyhamna. Various pipes travel through the North Sea. And the ports in the UK and Germany. The addition of the Arctic has allowed for gas to be shipped to ports by tanker from Hammerfest. Around 6.5 billion cubic meters are shipped from here each year. This is efficient when everything is working but can be devastating if one of these points fails. No matter what causes the issue (which is likely to be a mechanical failure).
Europe has already seen the impact that one of these failures can have. At the beginning of June 2024, Gassco announced that a pipe had cracked on the Sleipner riser platform. This caused Nyhamna and Easington to shut down production. This removed 56 million cubic metres of gas from production that day. According to Argus Media, the Dutch TTF future price for gas to be delivered in July jumped from 34.43 euros per megawatt hour to 38.60 euros at one point that day. That is an increase of 12% because of a cracked pipe. No bad actor was involved. This can be extrapolated to what Europe would lose if a large gas supplier stopped sending gas to Europe. A good comparable would be the loss of Russia from the equation. After Russia stopped sending gas to Europe, governments across Europe allocated approximately 651 billion euros to protect their citizens from rising prices, according to Bruegel's fiscal response tracker. Norway has many more fail-safes in its pipeline network. So this is a high estimate of what Europe would lose if Norway stopped sending gas.
Data Cables Carry Risks Insurers Will No Longer Cover
There is less information available on the costs of failing data cables. They are just as vulnerable as the pipelines. The European Commission released its Action Plan on Cable Security in February 2025. It states that 99% of all trans-oceanic internet traffic travels through undersea cables. Many of these travel to and from Ireland, the UK, Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Norway. Information on undersea cables in the Arctic is limited. On the 7th of January 2022, one of the two cables that ran from mainland Norway to Svalbard lost power. This cable also serves the SvalSat ground station. It houses over 100 antennas to receive satellite information. Norwegian police stated that they found evidence that humans may have been involved but later dropped the case. The other cable continued to send traffic during this time. About nine months later, the SHEFA-2 cable that goes around Shetland lost power on both ends. Leaving many on the island without phone and internet. It took until the 23rd of October to repair. The cable company Faroese Telecom believes that a fishing boat caused the damage.
While both of these could have been the work of a state, it is unlikely that every time a cable breaks, it's because of the Russians. By labeling these attacks, governments funnel money towards deterrence. The last two incidents in the Arctic could have easily been caused by fishing boats. Attribution no longer matters to one group of people. On the 6th of July 2026, the High Court in London ruled that Nord Stream AG would not be able to collect the 580 million euros it claimed from Lloyd's Insurance Company and Arch Insurance. They determined that the explosion that occurred in 2022 was covered under the policy's war exclusion. The court did not have to determine who was responsible for the attack. Companies that provide insurance for fixed structures that are on the ocean floor may not offer coverage for sabotage in the future. Gallagher Re warned of this in 2025. If a structure breaks in the Norwegian Sea, the owner may not be able to prove who did it or get reimbursed for the damage. This leaves companies and the public to pay for these losses.
Repair Ships Are the Weak Point in North Atlantic Security
If a cable breaks, a ship is needed to fix it. There will not be enough ships in 10-15 years, according to a study commissioned by the SubOptic Association in 2025. TeleGeography calculated that two-thirds of the ships that repair cables will reach the end of their lifespan by 2040. Maintaining current repair times would cost around $3 billion to build 15 new ships. And have another 5 as backups. Europe is spending very little on the ability to repair its cables. In the spring of 2026, the EU opened a 20 million euro project to develop modules to repair cables in the Baltic Sea. Then in June opened another call for proposals worth 40 million euros. To develop modules that can be used to repair cables in the Atlantic, Mediterranean and other seas. They also committed 5.8 million euros to two cable hubs. One in the Baltic and one in the Mediterranean. According to The Brussels Times. No cable hub yet covers the Norwegian Sea. Or off the coast of Shetland. The new Arctic Strategy mentions the development of an Arctic Cable Hub that can be used to monitor, defend, and help repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. But the document did not mention how much they would spend on any of these.
The EU has committed 66 million euros so far to help repair cables. Norway is spending £10 billion on frigates. The EU has committed 533 million euros to help with submarine cables for 2024-2027. They have awarded 186 million to 25 projects so far. It would only pay for a fraction of one frigate. Defence planners argue that the ships will be there to deter attacks on infrastructure. That is true. But the evidence shows that most damage will likely come from fishing boats or old pipes. Deterrence will not help. The Centre for Eastern Studies said that Norway will receive its first Type 26 in 2030. That leaves a few years where, if something breaks off the coast of Scotland, it will be in line with the rest of the world's aging repair ships.

Norway will also receive a promise that Norwegian companies will receive industry benefits equal to the amount spent on frigates. These two nations will also lead NATO in the development of autonomous systems. This will open up a market for these types of technology. Companies from Norway and the UK are sure to benefit from this.

Vietnam’s Communist Party chief and president, To Lam, arrived in Brussels on Wednesday for an official visit to the European Union (EU) and Belgium in another sign that relations continue to expand.
The visit comes just days after Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
Trade ties between Vietnam and Europe have deepened in recent years. The EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), which took effect in August 2020, substantially expanded Vietnam’s commercial ties with most European states.
Amid global tariff wars, the EU-Vietnam relationship “is a welcome advertisement for keeping markets open,” Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told DW.
“This is a win-win for both sides,” he said. “Vietnam offers Europe an established manufacturing base and another foothold in Asian supply chains. Europe offers Vietnam capital, technology and a large market, helping Hanoi reduce its exposure to American demand and Chinese industrial inputs.”
Vietnam-EU ties deepen
Vietnam is now the EU’s largest goods-trading partner in Southeast Asia and its 14th-largest globally. The EU is Vietnam’s fourth-largest trading partner and a major source of foreign investment.
Noneconomic relations are also advancing. In January, both sides upgraded ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership — the first such agreement between the EU and a Southeast Asian country.
Vietnam has become a key strategic partner for the EU in the Indo-Pacific, Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW.
“The cooperation is crucial for advancing the EU’s economic security agenda and its strategy of de-risking from China,” he said, referring to the European Union’s efforts to diversify its supply chains and reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing.
Several EU states have signed defense agreements with Vietnam. Bloc foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas held talks with Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung on Wednesday to discuss ways to improve security cooperation, including in the South China Sea, where Hanoi is locked in territorial disputes with China.
Concerns over Vietnam’s human rights record
The relationship has also faced difficulties. Questions remain over whether European companies are benefiting sufficiently from Vietnam’s economic boom and whether Brussels is overlooking Hanoi’s worsening human rights record.
Vietnam remains a one-party communist state that severely restricts political opposition, independent journalism and civil society. Rights organizations say repression has intensified under To Lam, who previously headed the country’s powerful public security ministry.
In an open letter sent this week to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa, 12 international human rights organizations raised “grave concerns over the Vietnamese government’s intensifying repression” and urged EU leaders to demand meaningful reforms.
When negotiating the EVFTA and the accompanying political agreements, Hanoi agreed to obligations on human rights, labor protections and environmental standards.
These included commitments to reform labor legislation to permit independent worker organizations and align domestic regulations more closely with International Labour Organization (ILO) standards.
Rights groups say Hanoi has failed to deliver. Vietnam has still not ratified the ILO convention on freedom of association, and independent trade unions remain prohibited.
“The EU has taken no action in response to Vietnam’s repeated breaches of its EVFTA-related obligations and pledges; instead, in January it upgraded bilateral relations,” the joint letter read.
Benefits ‘distributed unevenly’
There are also questions about which Vietnamese companies have benefited most from the EU’s trade liberalization.
Large foreign-invested manufacturers and established exporters have been better placed to exploit tariff reductions than smaller domestic businesses, which often lack the resources to navigate Europe’s complex import requirements.
Vietnamese exporters also face growing demands from the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and its deforestation regulations, which require businesses in affected sectors to provide more detailed information about their production processes and supply chains.
“It is quite clear that the EVFTA’s benefits have been distributed unevenly across sectors, firms and social groups, while political, regulatory, and economic challenges may complicate the next phase of the relationship,” Hai Thiem Bui, a researcher at the Stockholm Center for Global Asia, Stockholm University, told DW.
READ: EU must raise its game with Asean
“The next phase of EU-Vietnam trade relations is likely to depend less on tariff liberalization and more on whether Vietnam can adapt to increasingly demanding EU standards concerning labor rights, sustainability, and regulatory governance,” he added.
Better for EU?
Another challenge concerns how much European businesses are gaining from Vietnam’s expanding export economy.
Although the EVFTA has considerably strengthened bilateral commerce, it has been far more successful at increasing Vietnamese exports to Europe than EU sales to Vietnam.
The EU’s goods-trade deficit with Vietnam reached €51.7 billion ($57.9 billion) in 2025 — up from roughly €24 billion in 2019.
This imbalance is becoming more conspicuous as Brussels seeks greater economic security and new export opportunities for EU industries.
Another obstacle is the EU-Vietnam Investment Protection Agreement, signed in 2019, which has still not entered into force.
“We have also seen an uptick in investments by European businesses in Vietnam, despite the lack of an Investment Protection Agreement being in place,” Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.
Germany ratified it in February and Poland followed in April, but France, the Netherlands and several other member states have yet to complete ratification.
The agreement will strengthen legal protections for investors and establish a permanent mechanism for resolving investment disputes, potentially encouraging greater EU investment in Vietnam.
“With a new government in Vietnam pursuing an ambitious legislative program but with an overall target of maintaining Vietnam’s extraordinary growth path, we would expect trade to continue to flourish,” Humphrey said.
“That said, many European businesses are looking carefully at what the legislative program may bring in terms of reform,” he added.
For Brussels, the next phase of relations is about ensuring that EU businesses benefit from that growth, while demonstrating that its commitments to human rights and sustainable trade are more than diplomatic promises. /dl

In the same action, Treasury sanctioned Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore PTE. Ltd. and UAE-based Whales Shipping Line LLC for allegedly providing shipping and logistics services that supported Iranian petroleum shipments and sanctions-evasion activities, while two vessels owned by Whales were identified as blocked property.
In connection with the designations, the U.S. Department of the Treasury Office of Foreign Assets Control (“OFAC”) issued Iran-related General License (“GL”) GG and GL HH, both authorizing certain wind-down activities through November 20, 2026.
- GL GG permits transactions ordinarily incident and necessary to the wind-down of dealings involving Karnakis and Karnakis and any entity which it owns, directly or indirectly, a 50% or greater interest, including transactions involving the firm’s blocked employees and representatives acting in their official capacities.
- GL HH authorizes the wind down of transactions involving Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading S.A. and its blocked vessels, as well as limited safety, environmental, and port-related activities outside Iranian and Russian ports, including vessel management, crewing, insurance, emergency repairs, and the delivery and offloading of non-Iranian cargo loaded on or before October 21, 2026.
US Imposes Sanctions to Counter IP Theft
On October 19, the Department of State sanctioned five entities connected to Chinese national Linwei Ding, founder of Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Co. Ltd. (“Zhisuan”). According to the State Department, Zhisuan “has knowingly engaged in, or benefited from, significant theft of trade secrets of United States persons.” This action was taken pursuant to the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (“PAIPA”). A Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson opposed the move and warned that it may retaliate if the US does not correct its actions.
The sanctions follow Ding’s earlier conviction of IP theft. On January 29, 2026, a federal jury in San Francisco found Ding guilty on seven counts of economic espionage and seven counts of theft of trade secrets. Ding was convicted of stealing thousands of pages of confidential information containing Google’s trade secrets related to artificial intelligence technology to benefit China-based tech companies. According to von der Leyen, this experience is a lesson that Europe “will certainly not forget.”
The Commission President’s speech comes amid emerging transatlantic differences over the future role of Russian energy in global markets following U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to authorize the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel until April 7, 2027. Germany Tooling Materials Market 2026 Analysis and Forecast to 2035
Executive Summary
Key Findings
- Germany’s Tooling Materials market serves a technically advanced machining and forming base, spanning carbide, HSS, tool steel, cermet, ceramics, CBN, PCD, and cobalt alloys.
- Carbide likely represents roughly 35–50% of value, while HSS retains a substantial 20–30% role in general-purpose, lower-speed, and resharpenable applications.
- Demand growth is expected around 2–5% annually to 2035, with specialty materials and reconditioning outperforming basic grades as users seek productivity and longer tool life.
Market Trends
- Automotive, aerospace, machinery, and precision engineering sustain demand, while electric-vehicle and lightweighting transitions alter machining requirements rather than eliminate them.
- Premium hard materials can cost roughly 3–10 times commodity tool steel on a weight basis, but their economics depend on cycle time, scrap risk, and usable tool life.
- Regrinding and coating extend the service life of many tools, often through one to five reconditioning cycles depending on geometry, material, and application.
Key Challenges
- Specialty powders, tungsten-bearing inputs, cobalt, and certain hard-material grades expose German processors to global supply and price volatility.
- Demand is cyclical: weak automotive or capital-goods production quickly pressures standard material orders and distributor inventories.
- Material substitutions require process trials because hardness, toughness, heat resistance, coating compatibility, and workpiece geometry interact.
Market Overview
Germany’s Tooling Materials market is an industrial intermediate-input market serving cutting tools, dies, molds, forming equipment, drills, and specialized wear parts. It includes raw and alloyed tool steels, high-speed steel, cemented carbide, cermet, ceramic, cubic boron nitride, polycrystalline diamond, and cobalt alloys. Materials may be sold as bars, blanks, powder, inserts, tips, or finished tool components; market boundaries shift depending on whether the accounting point is raw material, tool blank, or completed tool.
Germany’s strong machinery, automotive, aerospace, medical technology, and metalworking industries support a sophisticated buyer base. Buyers balance purchase price against machining speed, tool life, downtime, workpiece quality, and regrindability. The market has both commodity grades and application-engineered materials: a standard steel bar is relatively substitutable, while a coated carbide grade or PCD cutting edge may be tightly tied to a particular process. Material suppliers, toolmakers, coating specialists, distributors, and reconditioning shops all influence the competitive outcome.
Market Size and Growth
Germany’s market is difficult to isolate from finished cutting tools and tool services, so growth is more informative than a standalone monetary estimate. A reasonable structural range is 2–5% annual demand growth through 2035. The lower end reflects industrial cyclicality, mature machining practices, and pressure on European production costs; the upper end assumes sustained investment in precision machining, automation, aerospace, medical devices, and higher-value engineering. Nominal spending can diverge from physical material use when energy, alloying elements, and specialty powder prices move sharply.
Value growth may exceed volume growth as users shift toward more capable grades and engineered blanks, even if total metal removal activity grows slowly. Carbide and superhard materials benefit from harder workpieces, tighter tolerances, and faster machining, while HSS and tool steel remain important in established applications and tool bodies. German demand is tied to both domestic production and export-oriented manufacturing. Through 2035, a broad cumulative expansion of 20–55% from the 2026 baseline is plausible, with recessions and plant relocations creating meaningful downside variance.
Demand by Segment and End Use
Carbide is likely the largest value segment, at about 35–50%, because it combines high cutting performance with broad use in inserts, drills, and milling tools. HSS may account for roughly 20–30%, supported by general-purpose tools, lower-speed applications, and geometries that benefit from resharpening. Tool steel is central to precision molds, dies, and stamping; ceramic, CBN, and PCD serve specialized high-temperature, hardened-material, or non-ferrous machining tasks. Cermet and cobalt alloys fill narrower process-specific roles.
End-use demand spans automotive stamping and component machining, aerospace parts, general industrial fabrication, woodworking, mining and drilling, precision molds, and medical-device manufacturing. Automotive remains a major source of cyclical volumes, but the transition to electric drivetrains changes the mix of workpieces and processes. Aerospace and medical applications are smaller but have demanding material and quality requirements. Regrinding, recoating, and tool refurbishment help moderate virgin material consumption, while short production runs and complex geometries can increase use of premium inserts and specialized blanks.
Prices and Cost Drivers
Prices vary by alloy composition, powder metallurgy route, sintering, material purity, geometry, heat treatment, and the degree of finishing. Premium carbide, CBN, or PCD can cost roughly 3–10 times commodity tool steel by weight, though the comparison is only illustrative because buyers purchase different forms and performance outcomes. Tungsten and cobalt exposure affects carbide economics; alloying elements, energy, and processing yield affect tool steel and HSS. Tight tolerances and low-volume custom blanks increase conversion costs.
Buyers assess cost per part or cutting edge rather than raw material cost alone. A material that supports higher feed rates or fewer tool changes can justify a price premium, while a high-value blank that is difficult to regrind may not suit low-volume work. Supplier quotations often reflect alloy surcharges and contract terms, while spot markets influence some powder and alloy inputs. Energy-intensive melting, powder production, heat treatment, coating, and sintering add cost sensitivity. German buyers also weigh inventory carrying cost against delivery certainty, especially for imported specialty grades.
Suppliers, Manufacturers and Competition
Germany combines domestic steelmakers, tool manufacturers, carbide and powder specialists, coating providers, distributors, and global suppliers. Recognized participants across the broader tooling ecosystem include Kennametal, Sandvik, Ceratizit, Plansee, Walter, and voestalpine, alongside German specialist firms and local service providers. Their positions differ by material and product form; not every participant supplies every class of Tooling Materials. Competition is shaped by material performance, application engineering, availability, and integration with finished tooling.
At the raw-material end, scale and process consistency matter; closer to the customer, technical application support and local stock can be decisive. Large users may qualify multiple steel and carbide sources but standardize critical inserts or superhard grades within a production line. Distributors and toolmakers bundle material with geometry, coating, and reconditioning services. This makes competitive boundaries fluid: suppliers can win through longer life or productivity even if material cost is higher, while commodity grades face stronger price competition and substitution pressure.
Domestic Production and Supply
Germany has a substantial industrial base for tool steels, specialty alloys, cutting tools, powder processing, and downstream tool manufacturing. Domestic capability supports short technical feedback loops and a broad range of precision grades. Production depends on alloying elements, steelmaking and powder-metallurgy capacity, heat treatment, sintering, and coating. Specialty carbide and superhard inputs are more exposed to global upstream supply than conventional tool steels, so local finishing does not imply locally sourced raw material.
Supply bottlenecks arise from concentrated mineral inputs, energy costs, qualification lead times, and the specialized nature of certain powder and blank processes. Buyers often use contracts and rolling forecasts for high-value or critical grades, with planning horizons of roughly 3–12 months for some custom requirements. Regrinding and recoating preserve value and reduce reliance on new material; many geometries may be refurbished one to five times before replacement, although this varies widely. Local service capacity is a competitive asset because it reduces turnaround and production interruption risk.
Imports, Exports and Trade
Germany both imports and exports Tooling Materials and semi-finished tooling inputs within an integrated European and global supply chain. Intra-European movement supports steel, carbide blanks, powders, and finished inserts, while East Asian and North American suppliers contribute specialist materials and components. Imports may supply approximately 30–50% of selected specialty inputs, but this is not a single share for the broad market; conventional grades have more domestic or regional alternatives than some hard-material and powder categories.
Exports are supported by Germany’s manufacturing and toolmaking base, particularly in processed materials, finished tools, and engineered components. Trade classification is fragmented across steel products, carbides, ceramics, and diamond materials, so customs values do not map neatly to the market definition. Tariff treatment depends on origin, code, and applicable trade arrangements. Currency changes, logistics disruptions, and export controls on particular upstream materials can affect availability or lead times, while supplier diversification and recycled or reclaimed inputs provide partial resilience.

Defence spending should go to five per cent of gross domestic product immediately, the country should be prepared for a wider European war and planning should assume Britain may have to fight without the United States, according to a security academic at the University of Leicester.
Dr Simon Bennett, director of the Civil Safety and Security Unit in the university’s School of Business and author of a 2025 book on security lessons from the war in Ukraine, set out the argument in comments issued through the university press office.
Bennett said: “Given these facts, we must prepare ourselves to fight alone. Like Keir Starmer, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is in denial about Trump. The American president is a lost cause. Better to focus finite energies and budgets first, on supporting Ukraine, and secondly, on preparing this country for a wider European war. Defence spending must be increased to 5% of Gross Domestic Product immediately and, as suggested by former Secretary of State for Defence Lord Hutton of Furness in the 17 October edition of The i Paper, the British public must be told the truth about Russia’s hybrid warfare campaign.”
On the range of threats he believes the country is exposed to, Bennett said: “The United Kingdom faces a spectrum of threats. The country has suffered two Kremlin-initiated chemical warfare attacks, in London in 2006 (Polonium) and in Salisbury in 2018 (Novichok). The Council on Strategic Risks recently highlighted the UK’s vulnerability to biological weapons. Prime Minister Burnham, it is time to focus on what really matters – giving Ukraine the weapons it needs and securing a vulnerable United Kingdom. Do not prostrate yourself before Trump, as your predecessor did. As Volodymyr Zelensky and Mark Carney have shown, the only way to deal with Trump is to stand up to him.”
Bennett is asking for far more than the government has signed up to. Ministers have committed to NATO’s target of three and a half per cent of gross domestic product on core defence by 2035, with a further one and a half per cent on defence-related resilience and infrastructure making up the alliance’s headline five per cent figure. Bennett is calling for core defence spending itself to reach five per cent now, a distinction ministers have had to set out repeatedly.
Lord Hutton of Furness, whose intervention Bennett cites, was Secretary of State for Defence from 2008 to 2009. His argument that the public must be told the truth about Russian hybrid warfare runs close to what ministers have themselves begun saying. Wes Streeting told the Defence Committee this month that hybrid activity of this kind amounts to state backed terrorism, and Louise Sandher-Jones confirmed in a written answer last week that “we know Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe.”
Ministers have also confirmed that government messaging on defence and security will build ahead of Exercise ALBISTON SHADOW and NATO’s crisis management exercise in spring 2027, and the Cabinet Office launched its Be Ready campaign this month asking households to prepare to look after themselves for three days.
The two chemical incidents Bennett refers to are the poisoning of Alexander Litvinenko with polonium-210 in London in 2006, which a public inquiry found was probably approved by the Russian president, and the Novichok attack on Sergei and Yulia Skripal in Salisbury in 2018, which killed Dawn Sturgess and which Britain attributed to the GRU. The Council on Strategic Risks is a Washington-based institute publishing on biological, climate and nuclear security.

articles.full_text:
In mid-October 2026, Western sanctions policy toward Russia revealed a striking contradiction. On October 12, the European Union approved the largest single expansion of its sanctions listings since the start of the full-scale war, adding nearly 1,600 Russian companies and executives from the military-industrial complex. Almost simultaneously, Washington moved in the opposite direction: the United States authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel until April 7, 2027, extended sanctions exceptions for overseas filling stations and certain Lukoil assets until April 24, 2027, and President Donald Trump used his executive authority to decline to impose the “hell sanctions” envisaged under the recently passed Lindsey Graham Act.
These contradictions—signals of which we noted as early as this spring—point to a more fundamental problem: the EU and the United States are increasingly diverging over how much economic pain sanctions pressure on Russia can reasonably inflict. What is especially notable is that this divergence has emerged just as sanctions against Russia appeared to be producing more tangible results. By the end of 2025, the cumulative effect of European restrictions, reinforced by U.S. sanctions against Rosneft and Lukoil, had coincided with market conditions unfavorable to Russia. Discounts on Russian crude, increasingly complicated export logistics and payments, declining oil and gas revenues, and a growing budget deficit were creating conditions for further pressure on the Kremlin.
The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, which began in late February 2026, dramatically changed the situation. Disruptions to supplies through the Strait of Hormuz pushed global prices higher and narrowed the discounts on Russian oil. At the same time, Washington began expanding exceptions to its sanctions regime, justifying the move by the need to stabilize energy markets. Russia unexpectedly received a reprieve precisely when accumulated restrictions might have created more serious financial difficulties.
This does not mean, of course, that U.S. sanctions have ceased to work, or that favorable oil market conditions have erased all the effects of sanctions pressure. Despite higher oil prices, Russia’s oil and gas budget revenues fell by 17 percent year on year in the first nine months of 2026. But what is happening raises questions that go far beyond individual general licenses issued by the U.S. Treasury. How sustainable can sanctions policy remain if one of its key participants begins to ease restrictions? How do such decisions affect the behavior of third countries and businesses’ assessment of sanctions risk? And can the European Union offset the consequences of American concessions, or is the divergence between the two strategies gradually becoming an independent factor weakening sanctions pressure on Russia?
From temporary relief to a new U.S. approach
In spring 2026, the first U.S. relaxations of oil sanctions looked like a forced response to the energy crisis triggered by the war with Iran. Washington sought to increase the supply of oil on the world market and prevent prices from rising further. The concessions were initially narrow: general licenses from the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) permitted the sale of Russian oil and petroleum products already loaded onto tankers by specified dates. This made it possible to release existing volumes without opening the way to new supplies. Yet the Treasury repeatedly extended and adjusted the exceptions, the latest phase of which ran only until June.
By autumn, U.S. policy had gone beyond the original emergency measure. The relaxation of restrictions on Russian diesel, the extension of exceptions for Lukoil’s overseas assets, and the decision not to impose the new sanctions and tariffs envisaged under the Graham Act suggest a more durable practice of easing restrictions. The contradictions are evident not only between the United States and the EU, but also within the American political system: the Graham Act won bipartisan support in Congress, while the authorization of trade in Russian diesel drew criticism from Democrats and some Republicans. Moreover, a bipartisan bill has been introduced in Congress to block the relevant OFAC authorizations.
The most significant consequences of these decisions may be felt far beyond the United States. As early as August 2025, Washington imposed an additional 25 percent tariff on Indian imports in response to India’s purchases of Russian oil, while subsequent sanctions against Rosneft and Lukoil forced India’s largest refiners to reassess their relationships with Russian suppliers. In January 2026, India’s imports of Russian oil fell to roughly 1.2 million barrels per day, but by July they had risen again to nearly 2.5 million. This was helped both by supply disruptions in the Middle East and by the temporary U.S. sanctions relief. Purchases recovered even though India had committed in February to stop buying Russian oil in exchange for Washington’s removal of the additional tariff.
Trump’s decision not to impose the new sanctions and 100 percent tariffs envisaged under the Graham Act against the largest buyers of Russian oil now removes the immediate threat of another major source of pressure. That does not mean, however, that sanctions risks have disappeared for Indian, Chinese, or other foreign companies: restrictions on Russian oil companies remain in place, as does the possibility of secondary sanctions for transactions with designated entities.
Consistent American concessions can change how international buyers assess these risks. There is also a problem with the political credibility of Washington’s demands on third countries: only recently, the United States was pressing them to reduce purchases of Russian oil under the threat of sanctions and tariffs; now it is itself authorizing transactions involving Russian energy products, including imports into the United States. Formally, these involve different commodities and legal regimes, but for India, China, Turkey, and other market participants, that is not necessarily a compelling reason to incur additional costs and forgo new opportunities. Tellingly, such arguments are now being made not only by traditional Asian buyers of Russian oil, but within the EU itself. Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has explicitly linked the Russian-American diesel arrangement to Budapest’s intention to secure an extension of the U.S. sanctions exception for imports of Russian oil.
Taken together, these decisions point to the emergence of a new approach by the Trump administration. Sanctions against Russia are not being lifted, but their application is becoming more selective, and Washington’s willingness to impose additional restrictions less resolute. For Russia, this means an opportunity to preserve certain channels of oil trade and potentially weaken the deterrent effect of sanctions threats on international buyers and intermediaries. The scale of these consequences remains an open question.
Europe’s response: the possibilities and limits of unilateral pressure
Against the backdrop of American concessions, the European Union continues to expand sanctions against Russia. What matters more, however, is not the number of new measures but the change in Brussels’ approach to their application. In 2026, the EU intensified pressure not only on Russian companies and banks, but also on foreign infrastructure used to circumvent sanctions. The April twentieth package, for example, was the first to invoke the special anti-circumvention tool, restricting supplies of certain categories of industrial equipment to Kyrgyzstan because of the risk of re-export to Russia.
At the same time, the EU expanded restrictions against foreign banks, cryptocurrency platforms, oil traders, port terminals, and refineries. Notable examples include Indonesia’s Karimun oil terminal, linked to servicing Russian oil shipments, and Georgia’s Kulveli refinery, which processed Russian crude. Between January and August 2026, Georgia imported 643,000 tons of crude oil from Russia worth $ 270 million. Sanctions against the shadow fleet also continued to expand: by July 2026, EU restrictions covered 673 vessels, along with the companies servicing them.
Brussels is thus extending sanctions control to international supply chains, expanding its ability to influence foreign intermediaries and participants in Russian exports. Notably, amid mounting European pressure, the operator of the Kulveli refinery announced a shift to non-Russian feedstock.
Yet here lies a fundamental difference from the American approach. European restrictions rely primarily on EU jurisdiction: they deny access to the European market, financial services, and infrastructure, but do not automatically allow the EU to punish foreign buyers for any transaction involving Russian energy. The United States, by contrast, has mechanisms of secondary sanctions and trade tariffs to pressure companies and states beyond its jurisdiction.
This difference matters most for India and China, the largest buyers of Russian oil. The EU can restrict the participation of European insurers, shipping companies, and financial institutions in servicing deliveries, and it can sanction individual intermediaries. But where alternative carriers, insurers, and payment mechanisms are used, the scope for direct European leverage shrinks. American secondary sanctions and tariffs therefore complemented European restrictions precisely where Brussels’ capabilities fell short.
European sanctions policy also faces a serious test amid the energy crisis. EU countries, for instance, continue to purchase Russian LNG. In the first nine months of 2026, deliveries from the Yamal LNG project rose 9.5 percent year on year, reaching 12 million tons worth € 7.9 billion. Formally, these purchases do not violate existing restrictions: the import ban under certain long-term contracts

articles.title: Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees - The Guardian
articles.summary: Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees  The GuardianMastercard and Visa face new £5bn group claim  The Law Society GazetteInterchange fee claimants urge CAT to reject Visa’s bid to reopen pass-on findings  Global Competition ReviewMastercard, Visa targeted by planned UK mass claims over card fees  MLexUK files application for £5bn collective lawsuit against Visa and Mastercard — The Guardian  UA.NEWS
articles.full_text:
Visa and Mastercard are being threatened with a potential £5bn lawsuit for allegedly stifling competition and charging UK businesses excessive fees.
The law firms Harcus Parker and Hausfeld have lodged an application at the Competition Appeal Tribunal in hopes of pursuing a group claim that would compensate companies who, they claim, have been overcharged on customer card payments since October 2020.
The claim will centre on multilateral interchange fees, which are set by Visa and Mastercard and then paid by businesses through their banks every time a customer pays by card. The argument is that the lack of competition has left businesses at their mercy – and paying higher fees on debit, credit and prepaid cards – as a result.
The case will hope to claw back fees charged over the past six years, as well as interest on those losses. Sources close to the claim estimate that it could be worth about £5bn, based on the number of businesses allegedly overcharged between 2020 and 2026.
A spokesperson for Mastercard defended the interchange fees, saying the potential group claim was “speculative” and part of a “growing trend of opportunistic funder-backed litigation”.
The case is being funded by Bench Walk Advisors, a London-headquartered firm that launched in 2017 and makes money from backing lawsuits. It is being led by Stephen Allen, a British businessman and former travel sector executive who has been pursuing Visa and Mastercard through a number of group legal actions since 2021.
If the application is successful, an estimated 1m UK-based businesses, organisations and charities with less than £100m in revenues will be automatically included for compensation, unless they opt out. Their claims could be worth several thousands of pounds each.
Larger businesses would have to actively opt in to be included in the claim, and could be due tens of millions over the claim period.
However, it could take years for the case to reach a conclusion. Visa and Mastercard last year agreed to pay a combined $167.5m to settle a class action lawsuit in the US which accused the two companies of conspiring to keep ATM access fees artificially high. That lawsuit was originally filed in 2011.
Commenting on the latest group claim application, a Mastercard spokesperson said: “We strongly disagree with the basis of this claim. Interchange plays a vital role in supporting the UK payments ecosystem, and ensures people and businesses can pay and get paid quickly and securely.
“This speculative claim does nothing to support UK businesses or consumers and instead reflects the growing trend of opportunistic funder-backed litigation. It is exactly the type of claim the UK government’s recently announced proposed opt-out class action reforms [put out for consultation this summer] are directed at preventing.”
A Visa spokesperson said: “Visa continues to believe that interchange is a critical component to maintaining a secure digital payments ecosystem that benefits all parties, including consumers, merchants and banks.”

articles.title: Could Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU? | Catherine De Vries - The Guardian
articles.summary: Could Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU? | Catherine De Vries  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Europe is living through an autumn of unusual discontent. What protesters from Paris to Milan to Madrid share is a deepening anxiety about the future and a growing anger at the gap between what they expect from their governments and what they feel governments are delivering, whether the issue is unaffordable housing, stagnant wages, the spiralling cost of living or failing schools.
The electoral consequences of the failure to get a grip on this public anger are already with us. Spain goes to the polls next month in a snap election called after parliament voted down key housing reforms. France begins the process of electing a new president in April, while Poland, Italy and a string of smaller states will vote before the end of 2027. The stakes could not be higher.
At the same time, national leaders face mounting pressures from abroad. Issues such as Ukraine, uncertainty over US security guarantees and economic competition with China demand more European cooperation, even as national politics makes this increasingly difficult. Governments face popular demands to deliver security and prosperity, just as their capacity to do so independently is shrinking. This leaves Europe with a difficult question: how can countries whose leaders are increasingly struggling at home find the common ground needed to act together abroad?
If the EU did not exist, Europeans would have every reason to invent it. Together, its members form a market of 450 million people and an economy of almost €19tn, the third largest after the US and China. No individual EU country comes close to that weight on its own. Germany, the largest, has 84 million people and an economy about a sixth the size of the US’s. Twenty of the 27 member states have fewer than 12 million inhabitants, less than half of Shanghai’s. In a world of tariffs and export controls, it is scale that secures a seat at the table.
But this rationale for cooperation does not make the EU’s survival inevitable. This political project has often been declared on the brink of collapse; the most recent crises include Brexit, the pandemic and energy shocks. Yet it has proved remarkably durable, responding with improvised solutions that previously seemed impossible.
The very traits that infuriate Eurosceptics – slow decision-making, endless negotiations and messy compromises – are, counterintuitively, sources of strength for Europe. The dispersion of power between governments, parliaments, courts and EU institutions makes the system hard to capture and compromises tend to stick.
The EU’s staying power lies in its capacity to adapt despite disagreements, while helping countries achieve what is termed “effective sovereignty”. Nominal sovereignty is the right to decide alone, even when deciding alone – as the UK has discovered to its cost since it left the club supposedly to regain its sovereignty – changes little. Effective sovereignty is the capacity to shape outcomes on energy, trade, migration or defence that no European state can control by itself. And the EU has itself adapted: its fully paid-up members remain the core but non-members such as Norway and Switzerland participate on defence, security, energy and economic policy. The EU has an interest in bringing Britain back into closer cooperation too, even if not exactly as it looked pre-Brexit.
But the EU’s resilience should not be taken for granted. Negotiations over the next seven-year budget, worth almost €2tn, show just how hard it is to achieve consensus. While everyone agrees on the need for greater European security and economic competitiveness, countries can’t agree on who should foot the bill. France, for example, is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, which others resist.
Even so, growing domestic political instability does not necessarily mean there will be paralysis in Brussels. Quite the opposite – it creates an impetus to act. With France’s presidential election approaching, Emmanuel Macron has urged fellow leaders to strike a budget deal by Christmas, warning that political room for manoeuvre would shrink in the new year if Marine Le Pen succeeds him.
Le Pen no longer talks about taking France out of the euro or a Brexit-style referendum. But her platform would undermine the union from within, turning the EU into a “Europe of Nations” and threatening cuts to France’s contribution to the EU budget.
Whether political change comes through elections, protests or new compromises in Brussels, public discontent cannot simply be negotiated away. This brings us back to the streets. French, Italian and Spanish citizens want functioning public services, affordable housing, economic and national security, and a sense that they have some control over their futures.
Younger Europeans, in particular, face growing uncertainty about their economic prospects, from finding affordable housing to securing stable employment. So far, this pessimism has not translated into widespread rejection of the EU. Recent polling suggests that young Europeans remain among the EU’s strongest supporters, with 90% favouring greater unity among member states and 78% wanting the EU to have more resources to act.
This gives Europe an opportunity, but also a responsibility, to turn that support into tangible improvements in their lives. That is the real test in the years ahead. Decisions about defence, industrial policy and social protection will involve difficult trade-offs, and not everyone will benefit equally. But if European cooperation becomes better at preserving institutions than at responding to citizens’ concerns, the discontent now spilling on to the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself. The EU has repeatedly shown that it can survive political crises. Now it must ensure that the people living through them can do more than merely get by.
- Catherine De Vries is professor of political science at IE University in Madrid. She is the co-author with Alexandros Kentikelenis of How Europe Survives

articles.title: EU Digital Omnibus – the European Council adopts its position - Addleshaw Goddard LLP
articles.summary: EU Digital Omnibus – the European Council adopts its position  Addleshaw Goddard LLP
articles.full_text:
- Personal data and pseudonymisation: The Commission’s original draft of the Digital Omnibus (Commission draft) proposed amending the definition of personal data, making the relevant factor whether a specific entity can identify an individual, taking into account the means that entity is likely to use. 
The Council text has deleted the amended definition, but added a new Article 25a to clarify the rules on pseudonymised data:
- Controllers and processors may apply pseudonymisation in such a manner that personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information.
- Pseudonymised data shall not be considered personal data for a third party if that third party is unable to identify the natural person to whom the data relates.
- Where a third party discloses, transmits or otherwise makes pseudonymised data available to another third party who possesses or can obtain means reasonably likely to enable the data subject to be identified, both the transmission of the data to that other third party and the subsequent processing of the data by that other third party is processing of personal data.
- Where a processor processes personal data on behalf of a controller, that data shall be considered personal data for the processor.
- To determine whether a natural person is identifiable, including through personal data having undergone pseudonymisation, account shall be taken of all the means reasonably likely to be used to identify the natural person directly or indirectly.
- The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) must issue an opinion addressing the application of pseudonymisation and anonymisation, including related technical and organisational measures.
These amendments are intended to address the concerns raised by the EDPB and the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) in their joint opinion on the Digital Omnibus. The EDPB opinion will be critical to resolving the uncertainty caused by inconsistencies between recent case law of the CJEU, the Commission’s attempts to codify this in the Commission draft, and the EDPB/EDPS concerns.
- Scientific research: The Commission draft proposed amending the definition and relaxing the further processing and transparency rules relating to personal data used for this purpose. The Council text makes some changes to clarify the definition and the safeguards that must be applied when relying on the exemptions.
- Special category data: 
- Biometric verification: The Commission draft proposed introducing a new condition that permits the processing of special category data for biometric verification under the user's sole control, subject to safeguards. The Council text clarifies that this only permits a one-to-one comparison of biometric data provided by the data subject, as distinct from a “one-to-many” search of the data subject’s biometric data in a database.
- AI systems: The Commission draft proposed adding new conditions that permit the processing of special category data for the development and operation of an AI system or model. The Council text limits this to incidental processing of residual data and provides that this derogation only applies where erasing the data would be technically impossible or require manifestly disproportionate effort.
- Training AI models: The Commission draft proposed an amendment to the GDPR to explicitly provide that legitimate interest can be used as the lawful basis to process personal data to train AI models. The Council text removes the proposed GDPR amendment, but adds a new recital to the Digital Omnibus to clarify that the development and operation of an AI system or AI model does not in itself constitute a legitimate interest, and processing in the context of AI must be assessed on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the underlying purpose of the processing.
- DSARs: The Commission draft proposed extending the circumstances in which a controller may reject a data subject access request (DSAR) or charge a reasonable fee to where the data subject is abusing their GDPR rights for purposes other than protecting their data. The Council text limits this to where the controller can demonstrate abusive intention on the part of the data subject, and removes the reference to them abusing their GDPR rights for purposes other than protecting their data. An amended recital to the Digital Omnibus provides examples of where abusive intention may arise, such as:
- submitting excessive numbers of identical or largely similar requests with the sole intent of harming the controller;
- submitting a request, but at the same time offering to withdraw it in return for some form of benefit;
- submits a request with the sole purpose of obtaining compensation for an alleged infringement which is deliberately provoked by the data subject; or
- with the intention to adversely affect and burden public authorities, for instance by utilising AI agents for malicious automated requests.
- Privacy notices: The Commission draft proposed that controllers will not be required to provide a privacy notice in certain limited situations where they collect data directly from the individual. The Council text makes some amendments to limit when this exemption applies.
- Automated decision making (ADM): The Commission draft proposed amending Article 22 of the GDPR to: (i) change it from a right not to be subject to ADM to a provision setting out when ADM is permitted, and (ii) provide that solely automated decisions which have a legal or similarly significant effect on an individual can be taken when necessary for entering into or performing a contract with the data subject, regardless of whether the decision could be taken otherwise than by solely automated means. 
The Council text reinstates the right not to be subject to ADM unless an exception applies, deletes the reference to whether the decision could be taken by other means, inserted additional safeguards, and provides that ADM can only be based on special category data if the lawful basis of explicit consent or substantial public interest applies.
                
                    
- Data breach notifications: The Commission draft included a number of proposals: (i) controllers would only be required to report personal data breaches posing a high risk to data subjects; (ii) reports would be made via a single-entry point for reporting incidents under the GDPR, NIS2, DORA and the Critical Entities Resilience Directive; (iii) the reporting deadline would be increased from 72 hours to 96 hours; and (iv) the EDPB would need to establish a template for notifying breaches and a list of circumstances in which a breach is likely to result in a high risk.
The Council text retains the provision that breaches which do not result in a high risk to data subjects do not need to be reported. However, it makes a number of changes, including:
GDPR
- adding a requirement for the EDPB to prepare a list of circumstances in which a breach is likely or not likely to result in a high risk.
NIS2
- replacing the single-entry point with a requirement for each member state to create a national entry point for reporting incidents as required by EU law and endeavour to design their national entry point with a view to interoperability with other member states’ national entry points; and
- providing that ENISA (the EU Agency for Cybersecurity) will develop and maintain an incident reporting information point to support the identification and fulfilment of the obligation to report incidents and related events, including by enabling users to identify reporting obligations and be redirected to the appropriate national entry point.
                
                    Trade secrets: The Council text includes amendments to the Data Act to strengthen the “trade secrets handbrake” by providing that:
- trade secrets would have to be disclosed only once the data holder and the user have taken all necessary measures to preserve their confidentiality; and 
- data holders will not be required to disclose trade secrets if they can demonstrate that they are likely to suffer serious economic damage from the disclosure, or the disclosure poses a significant risk of unlawful transfer to third countries with weaker protection compared to that under EU law.
In addition, it imposes an obligation on the Commission to issue guidelines for data holders to apply the handbrake in practice.

articles.title: BoE and FCA publish joint report on AI in UK financial services - Global Regulation Tomorrow
articles.summary: BoE and FCA publish joint report on AI in UK financial services  Global Regulation Tomorrow
articles.full_text:
On 26 October 2026, the Bank of England (BoE) and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) jointly published a report on artificial intelligence (AI) in UK finance services (the Report).
Background
The BoE and FCA conducted a fourth survey on AI and machine learning in UK financial services. The Report provides a summary of the aggregate survey results. It reports how respondent firms are using, planning to use, governing and managing AI, and how they perceive the associated benefits, risks and constraints.
Summary
The Report provides an overview of the relevant survey results in relation to the following areas, in particular:
- AI adoption and use: AI adoption continues to increase, with 86% of firms reporting AI use, up from 75% in 2024. Adoption was highest among banks and insurers, and deployment is now almost universal among larger firms, with 94% operating at least one production AI system. AI use remains unevenly distributed, with a small number of firms accounting for a significant share of reported systems.
  - Use of AI systems by business area: AI use spans a wide range of business functions but remains concentrated in operations and IT, which accounted for 31% of reported systems, significantly higher than any other business area.
  - Use of Generative AI (GenAI): Generative AI has become mainstream, accounting for 56% of reported AI systems. Adoption is evident across all sectors, with the heaviest use in operations and IT and risk and compliance.
  - Use of AI systems by domain: Enterprise productivity remains the dominant use case, particularly coding assistants and summarisation tools. The strongest future growth is expected in operations, processing, compliance and regulatory activities.
  - Materiality of AI system: Only 7% of reported systems were classified as highly material, although the absolute number increased. High-materiality systems were concentrated in risk and compliance and operations and IT.
- AI agents: AI agent adoption is widespread, with 80% of firms already deploying agents and further growth expected. Enterprise and coding agents are most common, while multi-agent systems are expected to expand fastest. Most agents provide decision support rather than autonomous execution. Firms remain cautious about deploying highly autonomous agents in customer, payment or trading functions.
- Third-party implementation: Third-party AI systems account for 39% of all AI deployments and 53% of highly material systems. Cloud and compute providers are highly concentrated, creating dependency risks. Security, operational resilience and transparency concerns are the main challenges, although most firms apply enhanced due diligence, testing and governance controls to third-party AI products.
- Benefits and risks: Operational efficiency, automation and productivity remain the strongest realised benefits of AI. Firms expect benefits to increase significantly, particularly in cyber resilience and business growth. Key firm-level risks are data protection and security, third-party dependencies and GenAI-specific risks. Systemically, cyber risk amplification and concentration on critical providers are viewed as the greatest concerns.
- Constraints: AI adoption is shaped by both UK and international regulatory frameworks, including the EU AI Act, NIST standards and FCA guidance. Firms identified UK data protection requirements and international regulation as the most significant regulatory burdens, while integration challenges and legacy infrastructure remain the main non-regulatory barriers.
- Governance and accountability: Responsibility for AI most commonly sits with business owners and executive leadership. Most firms have formal AI governance frameworks, inventories and materiality assessments. Pre-deployment controls are well established, but post-deployment monitoring is less common. Governance challenges are concentrated around third-party AI oversight, model validation and ongoing monitoring.
- Frontier AI and cyber: Most firms expect frontier AI to have a material impact on cyber risk over the next two years. Management attention has focused on vulnerability management and patching, while firms increasingly expect to deploy AI-enabled cyber-defence tools.
- Sustainability: Over half of respondents consider the sustainability impacts of AI, but most do not yet report these externally. Some expect to begin disclosure within the next two years.
- Small firms: Among small firms, 73% reported using AI, predominantly through large language models. Operations was the leading use case. Data protection, governance and IT constraints were the most frequently cited barriers to wider adoption.

ams OSRAM

Computacenter provides technology sourcing and services to large corporate and public sector organizations across Europe and North America. The company reported FY25 adjusted diluted earnings per share growth of 9.5%, supported by gross invoiced income growth of 32% in constant currency.

articles.title: India-Netherlands semiconductor push: Why Piyush Goyal’s talks on chips, critical minerals matter - Open Magazine
articles.summary: India-Netherlands semiconductor push: Why Piyush Goyal’s talks on chips, critical minerals matter  Open Magazine
articles.full_text:
From the chips powering smartphones and data centres to the minerals needed for clean-energy technologies, the race to secure strategic supplies is reshaping global trade. India is looking to strengthen its position in that race, and the Netherlands could become an important partner.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal held talks with Dutch Minister of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy Heleen Herbert on October 26, focusing on cooperation in semiconductors, critical minerals, green hydrogen, clean energy and advanced manufacturing. In a post on X, Goyal said the two sides had also discussed using the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) to expand trade and build more resilient supply chains.
Why India wants deeper semiconductor cooperation with the Netherlands
Semiconductors are essential to smartphones, electric vehicles, telecommunications equipment, defence systems and artificial intelligence infrastructure. India has been working to expand domestic chip manufacturing and reduce dependence on overseas suppliers, but building a semiconductor ecosystem requires more than factories. It also depends on specialised equipment, technology, skilled workers and reliable supply chains.
The Netherlands has an important place in this ecosystem because of its advanced semiconductor equipment industry. Closer engagement could help Indian companies explore industrial partnerships, investment and technology-related opportunities. However, the latest announcement concerns discussions on cooperation; it does not, by itself, establish a new semiconductor manufacturing project or investment commitment.
Critical minerals and green hydrogen are also on the agenda
The talks extend beyond chips. Critical minerals are used in batteries, electronics, renewable-energy systems and other strategic industries. Securing dependable supplies and developing processing capabilities have become important priorities for countries seeking to expand clean technology manufacturing.
Green hydrogen, produced using renewable electricity, is another area of potential cooperation. India sees it as a possible source of cleaner energy for industries that are difficult to electrify, while partnerships with European companies could open avenues for technology development and investment.
For India, the wider objective is to build domestic manufacturing capacity while maintaining access to international expertise and materials. The discussions also covered the broader clean-energy transition and advanced manufacturing, according to Goyal’s statement.
How the India-EU FTA could change trade with the Netherlands
The meeting comes as India and the European Union move towards implementing their long-negotiated trade agreement. The two sides concluded FTA negotiations on January 27, 2026, after talks that were relaunched in 2022. On September 11, the European Commission submitted proposals to the EU Council for the agreement’s signature and conclusion.
The deal has not yet entered into force. It must pass the required approval process, including Council action, signature, European Parliament consent and the completion of India’s own procedures. Once implemented, it is expected to reduce trade barriers and create opportunities for businesses on both sides. The European Commission says goods trade between India and the EU reached €118 billion in 2025.
Goyal’s Netherlands visit brings businesses into focus
Goyal’s October 24–27 Netherlands visit is part of a wider effort to expand trade and industrial cooperation with European economies. According to the Commerce Ministry, around 100 Indian businesses and startups are accompanying him on his Germany and Netherlands trip.
The programme includes engagement with the Port of Rotterdam, a major European logistics hub, and an India-Netherlands Business Forum in The Hague, with discussions spanning high technology, renewable energy, logistics, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals and services.
The immediate outcome is a wider agenda for cooperation, rather than a confirmed package of new projects. For India, the test will be whether these discussions translate into investment, technology partnerships and more secure access to strategic supplies.
