articles.full_text:
A picturesque Spanish island popular with Brits is on the verge of collapse due to the massive influx of migrants. The situation on El Hierro, the smallest and most westerly island of the Canary Islands, is being described as "critical" following a significant increase in the number of small boats arriving from Africa in recent weeks. A total of 1,539 people have arrived on the island since last Monday aboard 20 canoes, straining the resources of a territory with just over 11,000 inhabitants. The figure increased on Monday (October 26) when a new cayuco arrived at the port of La Restinga with 59 people on board, including three women and four minors, all of sub-Saharan origin.
The magnitude of the crisis has led the president of the archipelago, Fernando Clavijo, to warn of the risk of the island hospital collapsing. He has slammed Madrid's lack of response and help and is demanding more resources and effective coordination to handle peak arrivals. His concerns have been echoed by the Independent El Hierro Group, with spokesman Javier Armas warning that guards have slipped and that the island is not prepared for a problem he considers chronic.
"The problem is that the means are insufficient to cope with this rate of arrival and it does not seem that anything has been done to mitigate both the intensity and all the necessary management with this whole issue," Mr Armas said. He went on to criticise the excessive dependence on citizens' goodwill.
"It cannot happen either that everything is in the hands or is again in the hands of volunteers," he added. "The local population is beginning to feel that the situation is unsustainable."
According to Mr Armas, the reception centres are in "deplorable conditions, even from a sanitary perspective," and he described the situation inside as "very, very, very, very lamentable".
"This state of affairs is causing growing concern among the island's inhabitants," he said. "The people who live in El Hierro are really beginning to fear that this is a permanent issue, that it is an issue that is going to change their lives for the future."
Mr Armas says the volume of arrivals far exceeds the capacity to respond.
This upturn has also shown the most tragic side of the Atlantic route. Last Wednesday, two young people who arrived lifeless on the island were buried in El Pinar. In addition, the Civil Guard is investigating the death of a child who, according to witnesses, was thrown overboard during the crossing of a cayuco that arrived on October 19 from Senegal.
Government delegate Anselmo Pestana has attributed the upturn to more favourable sea conditions and insists that overall, the arrival of migrants to the entire archipelago - which includes Tenerife, Lanzarote and Gran Canaria - has decreased.

articles.title: Canada-EU summit seeks deepened alliance as U.S. ties fray - CTV News
articles.summary: Canada-EU summit seeks deepened alliance as U.S. ties fray  CTV News
articles.full_text:
Canadian and European Union leaders meet in Montreal this week for a summit aimed at deepening their alliance as both sides navigate tumultuous relations with the United States.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said “Europe and Canada are stronger together,” in an address to the EU Parliament last month, after EU chief Ursula von der Leyen suggested Canada could become the 27-nation bloc’s first “associate member.”
Leaders at the two-day Montreal meeting will try to hammer out specifics for closer ties in areas including defence, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.
Beyond specifics, the push for new levels of Canada-EU closeness has highlighted the shifting geopolitical realities triggered by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Punished by U.S. tariffs, Canada is seeking new economic opportunities overseas to reduce its dependence on the United States.
Carney says the EU is a logical partner, quipping that his country is “the most European of non-European countries.”
For Timothy Snyder, the chair in modern European history at Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs, Carney’s outreach to Europe in response to U.S. hostility is tactically sound.
“If you can be arbitrarily, at any moment, cut off from the American market, then it makes sense to have as much in your back pocket as you can,” he told AFP.
“You look for something else, and that something else is Europe,” Snyder said, adding that if the US trade war ultimately subsides, Canada will be in a stronger, more diversified position.
The EU, repeatedly ridiculed by Trump and his top domestic allies, is also looking for reliable partnerships in a world dominated by China and the United States.
The bloc has let Canada into its defense procurement alliance and invited Carney and Canadian officials to attend key EU meetings.
The goal must now be to “move from writing each other love letters to real commitments,” said Tobias Cremer, a German member of the European Parliament who has backed deeper EU-Canada cooperation.
Associate member?
The contours of the “associate member” status are not fully clear. EU treaties do not outline such a possibility.
A draft joint declaration that could emerge from the summit, seen by AFP, indicates Canada could join the Erasmus student mobility program, the Galileo satellite navigation program or sit on a proposed European security council, a conceptual idea backed by the EU chief.
Trump threatened to cut off EU trade after the bloc proposed associate member status to Canada, calling the idea both “laughable” and “a hostile act.”
And Trump isn’t the only one to view the notion with scorn.
Angeline Furet, a member of the European Parliament from France’s far-right National Rally party, argued the current free trade with Canada is “ruining our agriculture sector.”
The Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, signed in 2016, eliminates import duties on 98 per cent of products but has not been fully implemented.
It’s hugely unpopular among French livestock farmers and has not been implemented by several members of the bloc, including France.
The idea of closer EU ties has also riled conservatives in Canada, stirring accusations that ordinary Canadians will become subject to onerous European bureaucracy.
“We will never be the 51st state of the US, but we will also never be the 28th state of the European Union,” Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre said, connecting EU ties with Trump’s annexation threats.

articles.title: Ripple alum’s Epoch raises $4.25M to help small importers meet EU deforestation rules - Tech Funding News
articles.summary: Ripple alum’s Epoch raises $4.25M to help small importers meet EU deforestation rules  Tech Funding News
articles.full_text:
- Epoch raised $4.25m in seed funding, led by Burnt Island Ventures and Sand River.
- The EU deforestation rules will apply to large and medium operators from 30th December 2026.
- Epoch’s self-serve tool uses supplier names rather than plot coordinates.
Jinal Surti began his career working on moving capital into emerging markets. In 2023, he co-founded Epoch to get capital to farmers at the very start of supply chains and to drive emissions reductions.
The London-based startup now verifies the origin of cocoa, coffee and rubber and has raised $4.25 million in seed funding, led by Burnt Island Ventures and Sand River, to provide this service to small importers. This brings total funding to $6.26 million.
The company also launched a self-serve product to automate compliance for SMBs, starting with the EU Deforestation Regulation.
From paying farmers to proving where goods are grown
Prior to founding Epoch, Surti was an early employee at Ripple and a founding exec at Menai. Co-founder and CTO William Ouellette previously co-founded Soilwatch, which helped developers design projects for the voluntary carbon market.
The company now focuses on the first-mile data layer for supply chains and lists carbon removal as one of five use cases, alongside EUDR compliance. That aligns with the regulatory timeline: the EU law came into force in June 2023 and now has enforcement dates in place.
Epoch uses geospatial AI and software agents to map the first mile of a supply chain, identifying the farms, plantations, and mines where raw materials originate. Users can start with a list of supplier names, and Epoch will find the supplier facilities, identify the relevant plots, and check for deforestation and legality risks.
The outcome is a due diligence statement with all the findings cited, which can be submitted to the EU’s TRACES system. Compliance teams can use the Epoch platform or work via assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. Epoch states that the customer’s sensitive business data remains in their own environment.
For example, a small coffee importer could upload the names of three exporters and, according to Epoch, receive a statement ready to file without waiting for any replies.
Small importers face the same regulations
The EUDR requires companies placing cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya or wood products on the EU market to demonstrate that their products are both deforestation-free and legally produced. This will involve tracing each product back to the plot of land where it was produced and submitting a due diligence statement.
The rules will apply to all large and medium operators from 30 December 2026 and to most micro and small operators from 30 June 2027. The big issue is getting the data.
“Supply chain compliance has been built on questionnaires, audits and certifications, and that toolkit is incomplete: regulations keep multiplying while suppliers increasingly can’t, or aren’t allowed to answer. We’ve built a compliance solution for the AI era. One sweep across a supply chain, using geospatial AI and agentic research, produces evidence that can be packaged for every regulation a company faces, including the ones not written yet. Enterprises get it inside the platforms they already run, and from today on, so does any SMB,” said Surti, Epoch’s co-founder and chief executive.
The Achilles heel is accuracy. In a June 2026 analysis, Epoch said the EU’s forest map incorrectly flagged 75% of the coffee plots it surveyed and that no single map should arbitrate compliance.
AI-driven compliance is attracting early investment across Europe. General Catalyst led an $11 million seed round for Complir in Copenhagen in September. Lifeline Ventures invested €1.4 million in Helsinki-based CRACI in May.
Market competition and what’s next
The category is very competitive. osapiens raised a $120 million Series B in July 2024, led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, for a platform in the EUDR space. Sourcemap closed a $20 million Series B in June 2023 and is in the EUDR software space. Meanwhile, Satelligence raised c.€1.9 million in a seed round in 2020.
Unlike rivals, Epoch provides the data that platforms such as Assent and Resilinc embed and now also has its own tool. The money will fund product development, infrastructure, and the commercial team.
“Large companies rely on their supply chains to operate their businesses, and they are often operating in the dark as to the local conditions around drought, flood, and forest health. The Epoch platform leverages AI, earth observation data and proprietary models to enable visibility into risk mitigation, and compliance. Epoch is a team of 14 that operates like a team of 140, punching way above their weight! It’s a transformative approach to managing supply chain risk and compliance,” said Christine Boyle, Burnt Island partner.
“A team of truly exceptional capability and experience underpins our belief that Epoch is best placed to be the single source of truth for the first mile. Compliance data becomes business intelligence and enables healthier, more resilient supply chains,” added Greg Robson, founding partner at Sand River.
The real test will be after Dec 30. If the authorities are prepared to accept satellite plot data from importers whose suppliers have not responded, then a 14-person company will have affected the compliance of smaller firms.

articles.title: "Fit for 55": how the EU's new plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions will work - ЭкоПолитика
articles.summary: "Fit for 55": how the EU's new plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions will work  ЭкоПолитика
articles.full_text:
The European Commission's new legislative package "Fit for 55" still needs to be approved by the EU member states and the European Parliament, but its main goals are already known and cover many key areas of the European Union's policy and economy.
This is stated in an article by Iryna Stavchuk, Deputy Minister of Environmental Protection and Natural Resources of Ukraine.
As is known, in July the European Commission published the "Fit for 55" legislative package aimed at revising the EU's current climate and energy targets for 2030. The package strengthens eight existing pieces of legislation and proposes five new initiatives across a range of policy areas and economic sectors: climate, energy and fuels, transport, buildings, land use and forestry, which will help achieve the set goal in the most effective way.
Revision of the EU Emissions Trading System
"Experience in recent years has shown that emissions trading is an effective and cost-efficient mechanism for reducing emissions, and the revenues it raises by auctioning emission allowances can be used by countries to support the transition to cleaner production and stimulate innovation," Stavchuk stressed.
As noted, the "Fit for 55" package includes a proposal to lower the overall emissions cap further and increase the annual rate of reduction by gradually cutting the number of CO2 emission allowances (including free ones) granted to companies under the EU ETS. This should lead to a higher price per tonne of emissions and thus encourage companies to reduce emissions. It is also proposed to phase out free emission allowances for steel companies and sectors covered by CBAM, as well as for airlines, while including maritime shipping in the system from 2023. The argument is that a single ship produces as much carbon emissions as 8,000 cars a day.
In addition, the EU intends to create a separate new emissions trading system for road transport and buildings heating and to start applying it from 2026.
Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)
One of the new proposals in the document is the creation of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which will set a price on imports of a limited number of polluting goods based on the carbon emissions generated during their production.
"This measure is aimed at protecting European businesses from environmental dumping and preventing "carbon leakage" in situations where European companies want to relocate outside the EU to avoid paying for CO2 emissions. The mechanism is also intended to encourage industry outside the EU and to encourage the EU's international partners to take steps in the same direction," the Deputy Minister emphasised.
She noted that CBAM will operate in addition to the European Emissions Trading System, but instead of allowances, special CBAM certificates will be introduced, which importers will buy in the EU according to the volume of emissions generated in the production of their goods. Certificate prices will be calculated on the basis of the average auction price of EU ETS allowances. CBAM will initially apply to imports of fertilisers, electricity, cement and metallurgical products (iron, steel, aluminium) and will take into account only direct emissions from production. As noted, these are the sectors with the highest CO2 emissions and high trade intensity, which creates a risk of "carbon leakage" to other countries.
CBAM applies to companies from all non-EU countries, except those that participate in the European Emissions Trading System or have a national ETS linked to the EU one. This applies to members of the European Economic Area and Switzerland.
At the same time, it is noted that Ukraine can count on special conditions, namely an exemption from CBAM in the energy sector.
"The preamble of the document notes that as soon as third countries are closely integrated into the EU electricity market through market coupling, technical solutions should be found to ensure the application of CBAM to electricity exported from such countries into the customs territory of the Union. If no technical solutions can be found, third countries with market coupling should benefit from a temporary exemption from CBAM until 2030 at the latest, only for electricity exports, provided certain conditions are met. However, these third countries must develop a roadmap and commit to introducing a carbon pricing mechanism with a price equivalent to the EU ETS, and must commit to achieving carbon neutrality by 2050, so as to align it with Union legislation on the environment, climate, competition and energy. This exemption should be withdrawn at any time if there are grounds to believe that the country concerned is not fulfilling its commitments or has not adopted an ETS equivalent to the EU ETS by 2030," Stavchuk said.
Changes in the transport sector
As noted, the EU wants to ban the registration of new petrol and hybrid cars in the EU from 2035. It also plans to tighten CO2 emission standards for cars and vans, which will accelerate the transition to zero-emission mobility. From 2030, average emissions of new cars must fall by 55%, and by 100% from 2035, compared to 2021 levels. As a result, all new cars registered as of 2035 will be zero-emission.
Under the revised Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation, the EU plans to ensure the necessary roll-out of interoperable and user-friendly infrastructure for charging and refuelling clean vehicles across the entire EU, keeping pace with market developments and guaranteeing that rural and remote areas are covered too. This is because consumers are increasingly buying electric vehicles. That is why it is proposed to build charging stations for electric vehicles every 60 kilometres along the EU's main motorways, and hydrogen refuelling stations every 150 kilometres.
"In addition, the revised Regulation aims to put an end to the current lack of pricing transparency and to facilitate cross-border payments when charging electric vehicles. The European Commission has already announced its intention to increase the number of electric vehicle charging points to 1 million by 2025 and to 3 million by 2030," Stavchuk added.
Changes in the energy and renewables sector
As reported, energy production and use account for 75% of emissions in the EU, so accelerating the transition to a clean energy system is crucial for cutting emissions. The Renewable Energy Directive performs two main functions: it defines which energy sources are considered "renewable" and sets binding targets for renewable energy in Europe's energy mix. The revised Directive proposes a higher target of producing 40% of energy in the EU member states from renewable sources by 2030, compared to the previous 32%. The action plan states that all EU member states should contribute to this goal, and specific targets are proposed for the use of renewable energy in transport, heating and cooling of buildings, and industry. The sustainability criteria for the use of bioenergy are also to be tightened.
In addition, the European Commission has revised the Energy Efficiency Directive, which aimed to achieve savings of at least 32.5% by 2030. At present this target is not binding, but the European Commission now plans to make it a legal obligation. During the latest revision of the Directive, the European Commission also set more ambitious annual targets for reducing energy consumption at EU level. The Directive will set out how national contributions are determined and will raise the annual obligation to reduce primary energy consumption for member states from the current 32.5% to 39%. The public sector will have to renovate 3% of its buildings every year to drive the renovation wave, create jobs and reduce energy consumption and costs for taxpayers.
Also, the new version of the Energy Taxation Directive in the "Fit for 55" package proposes to align the taxation of energy products with EU energy and climate policy, promoting clean technologies and removing outdated exemptions and reduced rates that currently encourage the use of fossil fuels.
"The new rules aim to reduce the harmful effects of energy tax competition and will help secure revenues for member states from green taxes, which are less detrimental to growth than taxes on labour," Stavchuk commented.
Aviation and maritime fuels
The ReFuelEU Aviation initiative aims to reduce carbon emissions from fuel by increasing the amount of green jet fuel used in the EU. To boost the supply of sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs), the EU intends to introduce a fuel blending mandate. All aircraft departing from EU airports will have to refuel with green aviation fuel, with a minimum share of 2% in 2025 and 5% in 2030.
"Similarly, the FuelEU Maritime initiative will stimulate the uptake of sustainable maritime fuels and zero-emission technologies by setting targets for reducing the carbon intensity of fuels used by ships calling at European ports. Over time, these limits will become increasingly strict," the official explained.
Social Climate Fund and effort sharing between member states
As noted, the European Commission plans to set up a Social Climate Fund, which will provide member states with funding of EUR 72.2 billion for the period 2025-2032, based on a targeted amendment to the multiannual financial framework. In total, the Fund will mobilise EUR 144.4 billion for a socially fair transition by 2032. The Fund will be financed from the EU budget, and from 2026 it will also receive 25% of the revenues from allowance trading for companies that will pay for emissions from heating buildings with fossil fuels and from road transport under the newly created emissions trading system for road transport and buildings heating.

articles.title: Fed Cuts Rates While ECB Holds Steady: Analyzing J. Safra Sarasin's Insights Amid Labor Risks - elciudadano.com

Original article: La Fed recorta y el BCE se queda quieto: la prudencia que anticipó J. Safra Sarasin choca con el riesgo laboral
The Swiss bank deemed it unnecessary to rush changes in October, anticipating a pause from the ECB; little did they realize, the Fed cut rates while the ECB remained steady: the caution predicted by J. Safra Sarasin collides with labor risks as financial system adjustments continue while supply chain demand and supply remain influenced.
By Bruno Sommer
Central banks from the two largest advanced economies concluded the week with contrasting messages. The Federal Reserve trimmed interest rates by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%–4.00%, while the European Central Bank kept all three of its benchmark rates unchanged for the third consecutive meeting. This U.S. decision stood in contrast to the cautious approach suggested by Karsten Junius, Chief Economist and Director of Economic Research at Bank J. Safra Sarasin, who believed neither central bank needed to hasten rate increases in October.
In a report leading up to the meetings, Junius argued that although inflation risks persisted, both the Fed and the ECB needed to weigh inflationary pressures stemming from energy prices and the impact of tightening financial conditions. According to him, this balance advised patience: the ECB would maintain rates, and the Fed could afford to wait. The Swiss bank even considered that the next move by the Fed could be an increase in December, targeting a terminal rate between 4.75%–5.00%.
However, the reality told a different story. The Fed implemented its second consecutive rate cut, justifying the decision by stating that while inflation «remains high,» downside risks to employment had increased. Unemployment was at 4.3%, and job growth had nearly stalled. The move was not unanimous: two members opposed it, one advocating for a 50 basis point cut and another in favor of maintaining rates. The U.S. CPI stood at 3.0% year-on-year, both overall and in the core reading, with gasoline prices rising 4.1% and energy index climbing 1.5%.
In contrast, the ECB adhered to the scenario anticipated by Junius. Keeping rates steady was consistent with an inflation rate in the Eurozone that dropped to 2.1% in October, near the target of 2%, influenced by a 1.0% decrease in energy prices. Additionally, spontaneous tightening of financial conditions in the Eurozone, due to fiscal concerns in France, raised sovereign debt yields and widened spreads for peripheral countries. This context diminished the urgency for further adjustments from Frankfurt.
This divergence sends a clear signal to markets: the Fed prioritized the nascent weakness in the labor market over inflation that still exceeds its target, while the ECB could afford a pause because inflation was nearing its goal and financial conditions were already tightening. Thus, the caution foretold by J. Safra Sarasin found its best expression in Frankfurt; in Washington, labor urgency took precedence.
Analysis | When Adjustment Comes from the Financial Core, Not Supply and Demand Balance
The divergence between the Fed and the ECB raises an uncomfortable question: to what extent does economic adjustment stem from a real rebalancing between supply and demand, and to what extent from conditions imposed by the financial system’s core? When interest rates, liquidity, risk premiums, and collateral move due to policy decisions or market stress, the cost of readjustment does not necessarily fall on those generating imbalances. It hits small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), indebted households, and long-term investment projects especially hard, while those with greater market power or privileged access to financing can better withstand and even expand their relative position.
The problem intensifies when supply and demand are already distorted by political interventions, military conflicts, or supply chain disruptions that favor certain actors over others. In this context, monetary policy can combat demand inflation, but it hardly resolves supply inflation. Raising rates does not unblock a port, replace an energy source, or diversify a supply chain; often, it just redistributes the cost of adjustment and may consolidate income for those in a better position.
This is not about attributing a generalized intent to every political or business decision, but rather highlighting a design risk: if adjustment is imposed from the financial core while supply and demand remain influenced, monetary policy gains in macroeconomic discipline but loses in distributional precision. The result could be more persistent inflation, higher credit costs for the productive economy, and greater market concentration. Thus, the critical reading does not invalidate the decisions made by the Fed and the ECB, but it does condition them: without fiscal, energy, competition, and supply diversification policies, financial adjustment risks replacing real adjustment rather than accompanying it.

The European Central Bank (ECB) meets on Thursday against a backdrop of upheaval in France and an Iran war that is keeping energy prices above $100, meaning inflation risks remain elevated.
"How do you set rates against that backdrop? It's incredibly difficult," David Coombs, head of multiasset investments at Rathbones Asset Management, said.
Here's a look at five key questions for markets ahead of the October meeting.
What will ECB do?
Leave its key interest rate unchanged at 2.5%.
A pause is widely anticipated after the ECB raised rates in June and September to counter rising inflation, as the Iran war pushed up energy prices.
Economists polled by Reuters expect a quarter-point rate hike in December.
"I don't think they've become materially less worried about inflation here," MUFG senior economist Henry Cook said.
What will ECB say about rate outlook?
It's likely to stick with a data-dependent approach.
Caught between high inflation, at 3.8% in September, and concerns that rising government bond yields could hurt growth, policymakers have recently argued for what ECB President Christine Lagarde called a "measured response."
"There will be a definite flag to the tightening in financial conditions and how it should slow growth and hence curb inflationary pressures," said Barclays' head of euro rates strategy Rohan Khanna.
"But also, plenty of uncertainty around the conflict and the outlook for energy prices."
How worried is ECB about energy-driven inflation rise?
Comments from officials such as ECB chief economist Philip Lane suggest the ECB is not overly worried, for now, about high energy costs leading to other prices and wages rising.
A muted increase in core inflation, which excludes food and fuel prices, to 2.5% last month from 2.4%, suggests that high energy costs have yet to generate the sort of second-round impacts that could set off a hard-to-break inflation spiral.
Still, with oil up 90% this year and headline inflation above its 2% target, the ECB will likely stress vigilance.
Eurozone consumers nudged up their inflation expectations for the next 12 months in September, a survey on Friday showed.
"If the war in Iran escalates, or if we see further pressure on energy prices, the risk is still more rate hikes in 2027," said Bas van Geffen, senior macro strategist at Rabobank, adding he did not have any penciled in for next year.
Markets price in at least two hikes by mid-2027.
What about French bond sell-off?
Well, the ECB is watching.
French 10-year borrowing costs just hit 24-year highs above 5% and a weakened government is grappling with violent protests that could undermine efforts to improve fragile finances.
Also, the premium investors demand to hold 10-year French bonds over safer Germany is at 167 bps, up from 92 bps when the ECB met last month.
But don't expect the ECB to act soon with measures such as the Transmission Protection Instrument that allows it to buy bonds from any member state experiencing an "unwarranted, disorderly" tightening of its financing conditions.
France should solve its own debt problems through fiscal consolidation, says Lagarde.
The ECB could hold back on rate hikes if it thinks a crisis in France could hurt economic growth materially, Berenberg chief economist Holger Schmieding said.
"If there are serious contagion effects from a hypothetical French crisis to other countries where the fiscal policy is much more sustainable, the ECB would probably use its TPI to shield these other countries, not France," he said.
Who will replace Lagarde?
The ECB chief, who could be appointed as the next World Economic Forum (WEF) chair as early as November, will likely be pressed on succession.
The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are seen as frontrunners.
Lagarde's exit would open a second vacancy on the ECB's six-member Executive Board after Isabel Schnabel's recent resignation. Chief economist Lane will step down in May.
Lagarde's term is scheduled to end next October. Leaving early allows time for a new ECB chief to be picked before France's spring presidential election. A snap Spanish election could also impact the politics around ECB succession, analysts said.

articles.title: European Steelmakers Criticize Prorated Allocation of EU Quota Duties - Металлургпром
articles.summary: European Steelmakers Criticize Prorated Allocation of EU Quota Duties  Металлургпром
articles.full_text:
European steel producers are unhappy with the EU’s administrative rules for tariff-rate quotas following their revision in July. In particular, Dow Jones Energy sources point to the prorated allocation of duties among shipments processed on a first-come, first-served basis.
In July, the EU tightened safeguards for the steel industry. The market is now in the second trading quarter since the new rules took effect.
Market participants have had time to assess the complexities of the new system. It roughly halved duty-free import volumes and raised the duty on imports above quota to 50%. Steel producers are increasingly saying that certain provisions can be exploited. In particular, they are concerned about how first-come, first-served quotas interact with duties when initial applications exceed the available volume.
EU quotas open at the start of each trading quarter. The first period, from July to September, was an exception: an 11-day transition period applied, during which customs clearance was blocked. Global quotas, which suppliers from different countries compete for, become available only after a country-of-origin quota has been exhausted. Importers whose goods are already at port typically try to clear them as quickly as possible to access duty-free volumes and avoid the 50% duty.
However, competition for duty-free volumes and the fragmented operation of customs authorities in the 27 EU member states mean that clearance applications submitted on the first day are treated equally. As a result, the duty is prorated across all eligible shipments. This allows volumes above the quota limit to be imported without paying the full 50% duty: the duty is applied to the entire volume at a reduced rate.
Under this approach, no shipment is entirely duty-free. But prorating the duty reduces import costs and could result in more steel entering the EU market than was envisaged when quotas were cut, at a price local producers may struggle to compete with.
How duty reduction works: Product Category 24
A case in point is the quota for Product Category 24, “other seamless tubes.” China has an annual duty-free limit of 52,635.36 t, or 13,158.84 t per quarter.
Market participants say that a significant volume of Chinese tubes was cleared into the EU after the fourth-quarter quota opened in October. As a result, the 50% duty was prorated across all shipments that cleared customs.
Data from the EU quota balance counter in the TARIC system show that China’s Category 24 quota has been exhausted. The last shipments recorded on October 8 were allocated 0% of the quota, indicating that at least some imports above quota are subject to the full 50% duty.
However, EU quota data do not make it possible to determine the duty actually paid. It can be calculated or estimated using the figures for “total volume awaiting allocation” and “quota share allocated in the latest allocation.” But this information is available only for the latest registered import declaration and is not retained in EU customs databases.
Without continually collecting and retaining TARIC data, market participants lose the ability to track not only volumes that may have exceeded the EU limits, but also the actual duty rate on those products.
In this case, weekly reports from the European Steel Tube Association (ESTA) on the use of the Category 24 quota help clarify the situation. They include up-to-date figures for the volume awaiting allocation. In ESTA’s October 2 report, the remaining Chinese quota stood at 13,159 t, while another 23,948 t was awaiting allocation—almost twice the EU limit.
However, ESTA’s report does not include data on the quota share allocated in the latest allocation. It is therefore impossible to confirm that the duty was in fact reduced through prorated allocation: some import declarations may have been withdrawn, as can happen, for example, in Italy. Nevertheless, a cost analysis points to the benefit of clearing such shipments.
If 23,948 t were cleared at once when the initial balance stood at 13,159 t, the quota would be exhausted and the 50% duty would have to be applied to 10,789 t. But EU member states’ customs authorities have no mechanism to distribute the quota fairly among all applications received on the first day. As a result, the 50% duty is prorated across the entire volume of 23,948 t, giving an effective rate of 22.53%.
Cost of deliveries
Market participants surveyed by Dow Jones Energy reported an offer from China at 568 euros per tonne FCA. Including delivery, the CIF price is 768 euros per tonne. With a prorated duty of 22.53% and costs under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), the total delivered cost reaches 1,071 euros per tonne. The offer estimate includes CBAM costs of 130 euros per tonne—the same figure shown by Dow Jones Energy’s CBAM default values calculator.
According to EU suppliers, the typical price for a comparable domestically produced product is 1,350 euros per tonne. Thus, even with tighter safeguards for the steel industry and CBAM costs calculated using default values, imports may cost almost 300 euros per tonne less than local offers. Moreover, even with the 50% duty applied to the CIF price, the total cost remains almost 100 euros per tonne below indicative domestic prices. This suggests that, at least for Category 24, the EU’s new measures do not fully protect producers from either import volumes or price competition.
Steel producers note that when a high duty is needed to close such a cost gap—as is often the case with shipments from China—it may not deter low-cost exports to the EU above quota, but instead encourage them.
Trader sources confirm that the opacity surrounding prorated duties and volumes awaiting allocation in the TARIC database makes it difficult to assess import availability after initial shipments have been registered.
“The EU does not keep this data publicly available, so we don’t even know how much volume is awaiting allocation—what has already been recorded and what has been withdrawn,” one trader said. “It is very difficult to assess the situation.”
Importers, however, consider the current system of prorated allocation the most workable option: with customs services fragmented across EU member states, it is difficult to track the order in which applications are submitted. In their view, it makes little sense to demand the full duty if quota space was clearly available when an application was filed.
Market participants say the combination of the first-come, first-served principle and prorated duty allocation has been in place for a long time and was also used under the previous safeguard system, introduced before July. However, its effects previously fell mainly on imports of flat-rolled products. Now that overall steel quota volumes have been reduced, lower duties could become a problem for new product categories as well. Producers would like to see this shortcoming addressed, especially if the new tariff-rate quotas become a permanent feature of EU steel trade policy.
By Benjamin Stephen

Hot-rolled coil (HRC) prices in Europe rose in the week to October 23, but trading activity remains low due to weak apparent demand.
European distributors have built up significant stocks of flat steel. In June, they cleared large volumes of products through customs ahead of the introduction of tighter quotas, which took effect after July. Demand has yet to recover, so inventories are being drawn down more slowly than usual.
Market participants say buyers are purchasing only the volumes they lack in their product ranges.
Despite the small number of deals, market sentiment is positive: tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) have made imports more expensive and restricted, increasing the share of European producers.
In Northwest Europe, locally produced HRC deals were concluded at EUR750–770/t ex-works. Offers for first-quarter deliveries reached EUR790–800/t delivered. Some steelmakers said they had already sold out of all HRC for first-quarter delivery.
Regional mills have also started discussing contracts for the first half of next year and for all of 2027. They are seeking price increases of EUR100–150/t compared with the second half of 2026. Market participants expect contracts will ultimately be concluded at a premium of around EUR50–80/t.
In Italy, locally produced HRC was assessed at EUR740–750/t ex-works and EUR740–770/t delivered. Some deals were still concluded at lower prices, at EUR730/t delivered.
Imported HRC prices are comparable to offers from European mills, ranging from EUR740/t DDP at Italian ports for material already there to EUR800/t DDP for new orders. Buyers also risk exceeding available quotas and facing duties of 50%. However, Dow Jones Energy analysis indicates that actual duties may be lower than expected.
On a CIF basis, HRC from the Far East, India and Turkey was offered at EUR740–750/t, including anti-dumping duties where applicable.
With imported coil availability limited, some traditional HRC importers have switched to buying steel slabs from outside the EU to use as feedstock for rolling at European facilities.
Green steel market
Demand for green coil in the spot market remains weak, with deals mainly involving small trial batches. Automakers and construction projects remain the main sources of demand for low-emissions steel. Most buyers are still focused on adapting to new trade restrictions and securing supplies of conventional steel.
Green HRC premiums vary depending on the producer, buyer and contract terms. Premiums of around EUR200/t have been reported for project sales and long-term contracts. A Southern European producer quoted the same premium—EUR200/t—for products from its electric arc furnace (EAF) mill. In the spot market, the premium for EAF-produced green HRC is typically around EUR100/t, which is roughly the level buyers consider acceptable.
Some steelmakers cite green steel premiums of up to EUR300/t, but confirmed levels are lower. Project deals were concluded at premiums of around EUR200/t, while trial sales by other producers reportedly came with premiums of about EUR150/t.
Distributors remain reluctant to keep low-emissions steel in stock and usually buy it against confirmed end-user orders. In the spot market, buyers are generally willing to pay around EUR100/t above the conventional price for green steel. This reflects weak demand and caution about paying extra for lower-emissions material.

Key Moments
- EUR/USD traded near 1.1220 in early Asian dealings on Monday as the pair attempted to recover recent losses.
- Ongoing unrest in France and mounting budget concerns were seen as potential headwinds for the Euro.
- Markets focused on upcoming ECB and Fed policy meetings, with investors largely expecting no immediate rate moves but monitoring guidance on future tightening.
Euro Attempts Recovery Amid French Political and Fiscal Concerns
EUR/USD edged higher toward 1.1220 in early Asian trading on Monday, retracing part of its recent decline. The advance came against a backdrop of lingering concerns about social unrest and political risks in France, which were seen as limiting the scope for further gains in the common currency. Market participants also awaited the latest round of Germany’s IFO data scheduled for release later on Monday.
According to CNBC, demonstrations across France over the rising cost of living and widening inequality turned violent for a second straight weekend. France’s Interior Ministry reported that about 410,000 people took part in protests across several major cities, including Paris. The persistence of these tensions, alongside worries about France’s deteriorating fiscal position, was cited as a potential source of selling pressure on the Euro in the near term.
ECB Outlook: Policy Steady Now, Further Tightening Still Priced In
The European Central Bank (ECB) was expected to keep its main interest rate unchanged at 2.5% at its October policy meeting on Thursday. However, Reuters indicated that markets had already factored in the likelihood of an additional rate increase before year-end. Traders were poised to study any guidance on the future policy path, particularly in light of ECB President Christine Lagarde’s comments in late September that a moderate policy response to inflation was appropriate.
Fed Expectations: October Pause, Focus Shifts to December
Across the Atlantic, investors widely anticipated that the US Federal Reserve would leave rates unchanged just days before the midterm elections. Data from the CME FedWatch tool showed that markets were pricing in a 90.6% probability that the Fed would hold rates steady at its October meeting on Wednesday, while assigning a 79.4% chance to a rate increase in December.

Analysts at Brown Brothers Harriman emphasized that “above target Eurozone inflation and a resilient growth outlook give the ECB scope to deliver additional hikes,” and pointed out that “the swaps curve implies nearly 75bps of tightening to 3.25% in the next twelve months.” They argued that this expected policy path “limits policy divergence with the Fed and the drag on EUR/USD.”
At the same time, Brown Brothers Harriman warned that “France’s fiscal troubles can drive EUR/USD down to 1.1000,” highlighting how country-specific concerns could offset the broader support stemming from Eurozone monetary policy expectations.
Fed Communication Keeps Dollar Support Intact
Fed Chair Warsh’s latest remarks were assessed with a score of 5.6/10 on the FXS Speechtracker, marginally below the historical mean of 6.1/10. This indicated a slightly less impactful but generally aligned message relative to past communications. The acknowledgment of being “over-scarred” by the global financial crisis reflected a cautious stance toward risk, even as Warsh discussed structural growth dynamics, an investment upswing spurred by “good policies,” and the role of AI as a near-term source of demand with uncertain implications for employment.
The speech underscored a continued focus on price stability, upcoming “crystalizing” FOMC meetings, and international spillovers, projecting a careful but constructive tone that maintained Dollar-friendly expectations without signaling a firm policy trajectory for the rest of 2026.
The FXS Fed Sentiment Index was unchanged, moving 0.00 points to 127.51, a level described as firmly hawkish. The unaltered yet elevated reading suggested that investors continued to view the Fed’s policy inclination as consistently hawkish. Warsh’s emphasis on output, labor markets, inflation, and financial stability risks reinforced the perception that the Fed would remain vigilant, a setting seen as supportive for the Dollar relative to other major currencies.

Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
“An athlete” is the surprise answer Charlie Nunn gives when I ask him what job he would have done if he were not the wonkish, whipsmart chief executive of Lloyds Banking Group.
But having faced him on the squash court, perhaps the response is logical enough: the breadth of Nunn’s shoulders not only generates a formidable forehand drive, but reflects a lifetime of athletic pursuits from rowing at Cambridge university to cycling (he recently scaled the seven mountain passes of the Italian Dolomites).
Either way, Nunn’s competitive spirit is crucial in his chosen profession, too. Lloyds, Britain’s biggest high street bank, must not only fend off resurgent adversaries, from NatWest (which is growing aggressively after shaking off government ownership) to Nationwide (the thriving mutual). Its most threatening rivals are arguably branchless banking apps such as Revolut and Monzo.
Nunn is also fighting to live up to the legacy of Lloyds’ golden years. On the face of it, he has little in common with the old-school, meat-and-no-veg attitude of the late Sir Brian Pitman, the legendary chief executive who made Lloyds the world’s biggest bank 30 years ago. But Pitman’s “great leadership and value creation” were exemplary, says Nunn.
If the black horse, as Lloyds has been known for more than a century, is to thrive as it did back then, Nunn will have to use his management nous and policy influence to the full. “What’s depressing to me,” he says in an interview at the bank’s City of London headquarters, “is that in the 1990s, when I started growing up in [finance], UK financial institutions were top in the world in virtually every sector — insurance, asset management, banking.”
In 1998, at the peak of Lloyds’ global dominance, its market capitalisation hit nearly $69bn. Today’s world beater, JPMorgan, is worth close to $890bn, more than 10 times Lloyds’ current size.
The 2008 financial crisis was pivotal in rejigging the pecking order. While Lloyds bought a failing bank (HBOS) just as the 2008 crisis was biting and suffered a near-death experience and state bailout as a result, JPMorgan benefited from opportunistic acquisitions.
But Nunn blames the gulf partly on the divergent policy environments in the US and Europe, including what he sees as a deliberate weakening of the City of London, the engine of UK growth. “It’s not the response that anywhere else in the world took. Most of the world realised that if you kill banking, you’re killing the ability of your economy to borrow and invest.”
Nunn had an unassuming upbringing — he attended a state comprehensive school in Hampshire, on England’s south coast, before studying economics at Cambridge. But most of his career has been spent abroad — first as a consultant with Accenture and McKinsey, before a decade at HSBC, much of it in Asia. Getting the biggest job of his career, as Lloyds’ CEO, five years ago, was oddly a comedown of sorts — the group is resolutely domestic in its focus, and its fortunes are tied inextricably to those of the broader UK economy. The nagging frustration he feels towards UK policymakers pervades much of our interview.
“In my 10 years at HSBC, working with 50 countries, typically the conversation I’d have with regulators and governments was what can you do to drive productivity and growth,” Nunn recalls. “They’d tell us what sectors, what parts of their country they were trying to grow [ . . .] The UK seems to have moved away from [that] since the financial crisis.”
Although financial services remains the largest single UK export sector (accounting for more than 11 per cent of total exports in the year to June), it remains unloved by policymakers. Even 18 years after the 2008 crisis, sector-specific taxes (a balance sheet “levy” and a profit “surcharge”) still bring in billions of pounds each year. There have been persistent rumours the surcharge will be increased in the government’s Budget this week.
“Tax is obviously a matter for the government,” Nunn says, though he disputes the moral case for a “windfall tax” (“we are not in an era . . . of windfall returns”). “We want to go faster . . . not slower” in fuelling economic growth, he adds. If only political leaders would “look at the UK economy as a CEO would”.
Not that Lloyds has been struggling. The bank made a 17 per cent return on tangible equity in the first half of 2026 (better than most European rivals), bringing in more than £3bn of profit after tax. A new strategic plan has set the goal of making a 20 per cent return by 2030. Its share price is up about 120 per cent in the five years since Nunn took over.
But the Lloyds boss is convinced an alignment of interests between the UK government and the country’s big banks could drive further mutual benefit. “The UK economy isn’t really taking enough risk [to] support scale-ups and entrepreneurs.” Far too much money is trapped in property and low-risk pension funds or is sitting uninvested in cash, he says. “Everything that the government wants to do around infrastructure, housing, driving better investment in the energy transition, [it] won’t be able to afford this without crowding in significant private finance.”
Nunn is more positive on the promise of regional devolution, a big passion of Prime Minister Andy Burnham. “When I came back to the UK to do this role, we realised that one of the best ways of getting things done was down at a local combined authority or mayoral level, because they could join the dots between the assets they had, like land, and businesses or universities . . . The devolution agenda done properly could unlock . . . the ability for government to actually get stuff done.”
Our conversation has been dominated by the challenging political and macroeconomic backdrop for banks such as Lloyds. But how does the rapid advance of technology fit in?
Some financial technology companies have already overtaken the big banks. Revolut, a decade-old private fintech most recently valued at a 40 per cent premium to 260-year-old Lloyds, is now a fully fledged bank in its home UK market with app-based operations in 40 countries and plans to be in 30 more by 2030.
AI technology is sure to disrupt traditional finance still more. The upbeat nerd in Nunn focuses excitedly on the consumer benefits: “You could have a digital twin of yourself helping you optimise your financial decisions every day. Every minute of every day.” That prospect has sparked fears at US banks of mass defections to high-interest-paying competitors, prompting some to ban AI agents from moving money. Nunn says “there hasn’t been enough thinking about the regulatory consequences if things go wrong for customers”, though he sounds sanguine on the risk that loyal bank clients (Lloyds has 28mn of them, about half Britain’s adult population) could be unshackled by the shop-around power of AI. “Most of the volume products in the UK,” he says, are already sold through intermediaries — mortgage brokers distribute 85 per cent of home loans, for example.
Overall, he insists, AI will be a boon for the bank and its customers, particularly in the area of investment advice, something current regulations have made it very difficult for banks to do without charging off-putting fees. “We can bring intelligence or advice to everyone in the country if they want it . . . anyone with £50 to invest.” Previously this would have required the bank to “hire millions of people”.
But from Lloyds’ point of view, won’t the biggest benefit of AI be huge cuts in staff costs? (It has more than 60,000 employees.) Another UK bank CEO controversially promised AI would allow him to cut back on “lower value human capital”. Nunn is more careful, and despite promising £2bn of gross cost savings in his 2030 strategy plan, he bats away questions about how many job losses that will mean. Instead, he suggests staff will be retrained for an AI world. “In agentic AI everyone’s a novice . . . So we’re seeing a massive opportunity to take our brilliant people, invest in them, reskill them.”
I wonder if an industry that has been plagued by the mis-selling of financial products — from payment protection insurance to car finance (Lloyds was a major offender in both) — is storing up the next scandal via an AI agent providing rogue advice. “If you look at what are classified as mis-selling scandals, it’s about the incentives,” he reasons, pointing to generous sales commissions paid on products such as PPI. “[But] you don’t have to incentivise an agent.”
As I make my way out past the builders at Lloyds’ HQ putting the finishing touches to an overhaul designed to make the old bank feel more like a fintech, it is hard to shake the suspicion that Nunn’s smooth exterior might be too good to be true. I check with rivals and colleagues, past and present, but struggle to find anyone who demurs from the view that HSBC was disappointed to lose him and that Lloyds’ staff are happier than under prior, more autocratic leaders.
How does Nunn see himself compared with the likes of Pitman, or the Portuguese banker António Horta-Osório, who was credited with saving the bank from potential collapse? “Many CEOs,” he responds, “are more about ROE [return on equity] optimisation, cost reduction, and portfolio shrinking [ . . .] with a strong ‘control’ leadership style.” He prefers “growth, innovation, empowered/talent-based organisations and strategic optionality for the longer term”. You can take the man out of McKinsey, but you can’t take McKinsey out of the man.

articles.title: Canada Considers a Subsea Power Cable to Europe - The Maritime Executive
articles.summary: Canada Considers a Subsea Power Cable to Europe  The Maritime Executive
articles.full_text:
Canada’s prime minister has expressed interest in exporting Canadian energy such as LNG to Europe, along with renewable energy. Other recent discussions have focused on a unique possibility: an undersea electric power cable extending across the North Atlantic to Northern Europe.
Introduction
The concept of transporting energy under the ocean dates back decades. Earlier examples of the concept involved undersea pipelines carrying natural gas and oil. While the first undersea electrical power cables carried telecommunications signals (telegraphs), modern undersea electrical power cables carry grid-scale electrical energy. Such cables are widely used to transmit electric energy from offshore wind turbines to shore-based power grids.
Discussions dating back some 15 years focused on the possibility of transmitting electric power from geothermal sources in Iceland to power grids located in Scotland and England.
During that period, Canada had commissioned a study on domestic coastal kinetic ocean energy potential. Every 24 hours, lunar gravity pulls several hundred cubic miles of ocean water from the North Atlantic into Hudson Bay and into the Bay of Fundy which has the highest tides in the world. Present technology can only convert a small portion of the hydrokinetic energy to electrical power. Several hundred uninhabited small islands located along the eastern side of Hudson Bay and the eastern side of Ungava Bay have potential to support wind turbines, with additional potential for offshore wind energy.
Northern Summers
Western Europe has endured several hot summers where demand for electric power exceeded electrical generating capacity. The combination of European wind and solar energy conversion has routinely been unable to meet peak summer demand for electric power. A transatlantic undersea electric power cable capable of transmitting 20 to 50-megawatts of electrical power offers potential for relief to overstressed European grids, providing additional power to run air conditioning and building cooling systems.
Transatlantic Power Cable
The development of geothermal electrical energy at Iceland, with undersea electric power cables extending to the UK and Europe, could provide a basis to extend an undersea power cable from Eastern Canada to southern Greenland, then to Iceland.
An undersea power cable connecting Iceland to the UK and Europe would need to carry the combined electrical energy coming from both Eastern Canada and Iceland. There is future potential to transmit a mix of hydroelectric power, ocean tidal power conversion, wind energy conversion and nuclear power between Canada and Western Europe.
During overnight hours after midnight with minimal market requirement for electric power across eastern Canada, the AM peak requirement for electric power would begin across the UK and Western Europe. Electric power from Canada and Iceland would assist UK and European electric power utilities in providing peak period electric power their customers.
When the midnight and overnight requirement for electric power is minimal across Europe, Eastern Canada and Northeastern United States would gain access to European power generation capacity during the Northeastern American and Eastern Canadian peak evening requirement for electric power.
Power Cable Economics
A transatlantic electric power cable would enhance the economics of electric power generation in both Eastern Canada/Northeastern United States and Western Europe. Excess wind power generation for which there is minimal demand in one region could be transmitted to another distant region. Nuclear power stations operate best when run at constant power output. An east-west undersea power cable allows for transmission of off-peak nuclear power in order to satisfy electric power demand in a distant region. Peak tidal power generation can occur when local demand for power is minimal, with peak demand for electric power across the Atlantic.
The usable service life of the undersea cable system would greatly exceed the usable service lives of electrical battery-based energy storage by several orders of magnitude. Electrical storage batteries incur a ‘round-trip’ loss of efficiency, with up to 30% of electrical energy being dissipated as heat. A cable operating on ultra-high voltage with low current would reduce loss of energy as heat, delivering more electrical energy to the market compared to a system that is heavily dependant on grid-scale chemical-battery energy storage or other methods – like compressed air energy storage, which also incurs a massive loss of energy as heat.
Ocean Tidal Energy
The conclusion of high tide across Hudson Bay causes a massive river of seawater to flow east through Hudson Strait, reaching peak velocity in the vicinity of the Button Islands where kinetic energy potential is estimated to exceed 2,000 megawatts. Turbulent seawater in the channels between the Button Islands generate extreme mechanical forces that require specially reinforced kinetic turbines of extreme strength, capable of cost-competitive operation in severe water current conditions. Turbine housing and support structure would need to deflect the occasional iceberg while ensuring that the turbines remain operational.
Further south, there is potential to build tunnels deep under the isthmus between the eastern end of the Bay of Fundy and the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Turbines installed in the tunnels would generate repeated daily cycles electric power, courtesy of the difference in water height across the isthmus.
There is also potential for Quebec to generate additional hydroelectric power, for export to Europe. The installation of wind turbines along the eastern side of Hudson Bay will slightly cool the humid air that winds blow toward Quebec, potentially increasing rainfall over hydroelectric dam watershed areas.

Conclusions
A future transatlantic undersea electric power cable connecting between Canada and Europe via Iceland and Greenland incurs both merit and drawbacks. It would make for more productive use of off-peak electric power while reducing the expense and energy loss of energy storage technologies. The cable would enhance the economics of ocean power conversion, nuclear power, hydroelectric power from Quebec and Labrador, and wind energy conversion. However, Canada and the USA would need to invest in developing new electrical power generation capacity for domestic demand, with potential to export future off-peak power over to Europe.

articles.summary: Defence start-up Helsing moves into missile interceptors  The TelegraphHelsing unveils interceptor missiles designed to chase Russia’s fast-flying Geran drones  Defense NewsDrone Designed to Counter Cruise Missiles: Helsing Unveils the AD-1 Inferno  МілітарнийRussia’s Jet Shaheds Are Scaling Fast—Helsing Just Unveiled an AI Air Defense Built to Hunt Them  UNITED24 MediaBritish tech gurus design cheap AI missiles to protect towns and cities across Europe fr...
articles.full_text:
A defence start-up backed by the founder of Spotify is expanding into interceptors as Europe scrambles to fortify itself against Russian-style mass drone and missile attacks.
Germany-based Helsing said on Monday that it had developed a new air defence system designed to shoot down targets with the help of artificial intelligence.
The company will use radar and other sensors to track where drones and missiles are headed before an AI then decides which ones to shoot down first and launches interceptor missiles from the ground.
Helsing said the Contra system will deploy two new kinds of interceptors: a smaller, loitering munition called the AD-1 Inferno, for destroying standard drones; and the larger, rocket-powered AD-2 Ambush, for shooting down high-speed drones and some cruise missiles.
The company’s move into interceptors comes amid surging demand as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East demonstrate how large numbers of cheap drones can overwhelm an enemy’s air defences and leave them vulnerable to missile strikes.
For example, the barrage of drone and missile attacks unleashed by Iran on the US and its Gulf allies this year has reportedly drained American stocks of Patriot interceptors to “beyond critical” levels.
Houthi rebels also succeeded in launching devastating missile strikes on Saudi Arabia’s largest airport this month after first overwhelming the kingdom’s air defences with waves of drones.
Russia continues to unleash massive volleys of cruise missiles and Iranian Shahed-style drones on Ukraine’s forces and cities.
Experts have said that cheaper, more easily-producible interceptors can spare militaries from having to use more precious, multimillion-pound missiles to shoot down drones that cost just tens of thousands of pounds.
Niklas Köhler, Helsing’s president, said on Monday: “Contra ends the air defence dilemma: slow, fair-weather drones, or million-euro missiles fired at cheap, mass-produced targets.
“Our AI links existing sensors and effectors in real time and adds our interceptors, AD-1 and AD-2.
“With jet and rocket propulsion, a low-cost all-weather radar seeker, and two independent European supply chains, they deliver autonomous fire superiority up to ten kilometres high – affordable and at industrial scale.”
Helsing – backed by Prima Materia, the venture capital firm of Daniel Ek, the Spotify founder – is the latest company to enter what is now a booming market for interceptors.
Defence primes including BAE Systems and Leonardo have also set out offerings for new “layered” air defences, combining artillery cannons with high-powered lasers and interceptor missile batteries to ensure militaries can repel enemy barrages.
Cambridge Aerospace, the British start-up recently valued at £2.5bn, also has a contract to supply the Ministry of Defence with drone-busting Skyhammer missiles.
In the UK, Helsing last year opened a “resilience factory” in Plymouth to test and produce maritime products including the company’s SG-1 Fathom undersea gliders.

articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing shows explosive growth, risks and staggering costs - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Anthropic’s IPO filing shows explosive growth, risks and staggering costs  Al JazeeraAnthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing  BBCGlobal markets rise as AI trade regains steam  Financial TimesAnthropic files for potentially record-breaking stock market valuation in key test for AI industry  The GuardianAnthropic, PBC - S-1 (Q2)  SEC.gov
articles.full_text:
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic has filed papers for what could be the biggest ever initial public offering (IPO) of stock, even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.
The filing on Monday sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86bn.
The filing comes weeks after chief executive and cofounder Dario Amodei argued in an essay for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models. An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as does its final valuation and offering price. But even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world’s most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and cofounder, Daniela, by billions of dollars.
The prospectus highlights the AI company’s rapid growth over the past year, fuelled by Big Tech’s breakneck spending that has driven a rally in AI stocks, while raising concerns about lofty valuations and rising debt.
The company also flagged growing risks from AI technology, underscoring concerns over its potential to cause harm, which had led Amodei to call for a slowdown in development of advanced models.
Anthropic’s net loss in the first half of 2026 widened sharply to $80.7bn, largely due to a rise in the fair value of bonds convertible into the company’s shares. Revenue in the period was about $16.3bn.
The company’s revenue grew a staggering 1,368 percent in the three months ended June 30 from a year ago, but warned in the prospectus that the revenue growth rate could decline over time and fluctuate occasionally.
The IPO, which is anticipated to be before Thanksgiving in the US, late next month, is expected to establish Anthropic, the AI lab behind the viral Claude models, as a benchmark for how Wall Street values leading AI companies, including rival OpenAI.
The IPO push comes despite a once-busy autumn listing calendar thinning out as choppy markets prompt companies to delay their offerings. Analysts said that would give Anthropic access to a deep pool of capital to fund its costly AI ambitions.
Growing investor unease with the debt-fuelled AI investment boom has led to a global selloff in AI and tech stocks, as they start to doubt whether the trillions spent on data centres, chips and computing capacity will generate fast returns to support lofty valuations. Higher borrowing costs and rising bond yields have added to their caution.
However, tech companies are still hungry for cash. Meta is aiming to raise up to $95bn in its largest-ever equity fundraising, while SpaceX has inked a $40bn deal with Apollo to lease AI chips and server hardware.
Some current and prospective investors are valuing Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion a week ago, after the AI startup disclosed some financial details at a recent investor event, Reuters reported.
The prospectus also details the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI, from potential misuse and security threats to concerns that advanced systems could produce outputs that “could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative”.
“Anthropic’s IPO will establish a benchmark for valuing leading AI labs, influencing both upcoming listings and confidence in the companies funding the AI infrastructure build-out,” IPOX research associate Lukas Muehlbauer said.
“Its success would not necessarily benefit every AI business equally,” he added.
Balancing AI’s promises and perils
Anthropic said that more than half of Fortune 500 companies and over 30 percent of Global 2000 firms were customers generating at least $100,000 each in revenue for the company over the 12 months ended September 30.
The IPO comes as Anthropic’s own research raises concerns about advanced AI systems, which in controlled tests have shown behaviours including code sabotage, fraud assistance and information manipulation.
The findings have fuelled concerns about how companies can keep powerful AI systems under control as they race to deploy them commercially.
The prospectus also highlighted risks associated with its AI models, which it said could exhibit “self-preserving behaviours”, including behaviour “resembling blackmail”.
“Our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate and implement corresponding safety, alignment and security measures,” it said.
The company said it relies on a limited number of cloud service providers, such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft and suppliers such as Broadcom for compute and critical parts of its infrastructure. These relationships can create “dependencies and potential vulnerabilities”, it said.
Anthropic will trade on the Nasdaq after the IPO closes under the ticker symbol “ANT”.
The filing did not reveal the terms of its offering, including the number of shares it plans to sell and the proposed price range.
Red-hot growth
Anthropic, founded in 2021 by a team of researchers, was valued at $965bn in May in a funding round that drew some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
Amazon and Google were among Anthropic’s early strategic partners, investing billions of dollars in the startup while providing the cloud infrastructure needed to train and deploy Claude models.
“We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialisation, electricity, semiconductors and the internet,” the prospectus said.
The company said it expects compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain its largest operating expense for the foreseeable future.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were named as the lead banks for the IPO alongside 20 others as underwriters. Morgan Stanley will act as a stabilisation agent, overseeing the stock’s early trading.
The roles mark another major win for Goldman and Morgan Stanley as they also led SpaceX’s IPO.

articles.title: Security concerns flagged within Japanese firm GMO before breach: CEO - Japan Today
articles.summary: Security concerns flagged within Japanese firm GMO before breach: CEO  Japan TodayJapanese companies compensate users as cyberattacks buffet economy  ReutersJapan Vows to Address Cyber Attack on FX with Urgency  Bloomberg.comJapanese virtual desktop cloud hacked so hard it asks to be banned  The RegisterGMO asks government to take active cyberdefense measures  The Japan Times
articles.full_text:
GMO Internet Group Inc CEO Masatoshi Kumagai admitted Sunday night that internal engineers had flagged security issues before unauthorized access occurred to a foreign exchange trading service it provides and that the company's response to the concerns was insufficient.
In a post on his blog, Kumagai said the internet services firm was warned by in-house white-hat hackers of "issues that needed improvement" regarding security but that its response was inadequate in both depth and speed and the attackers took advantage of that vulnerability. He apologized, saying, "I deeply regret it."
GMO has confirmed that customer information, including account passwords, was leaked externally and used in fraudulent transactions. On Saturday, it asked the government to take "active cyber defense" measures due to unauthorized access.
With cyberattacks against businesses growing increasingly severe, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and relevant cabinet ministers will hold a meeting on cyber security plans on Monday evening, according to the top government spokesman.
Under a law that took effect on Oct 1, the government can use its powers to infiltrate servers used by attackers and neutralize threats to prevent damage before it occurs. It is not designed, however, to be activated at the request of private companies.
While GMO is not among critical infrastructure operators designated under the framework, Kumagai said, the government should take a resolute stance that cybercrime will not be tolerated.
"If this is overlooked as just an isolated incident in the private sector, all kinds of social infrastructure and personal assets could be threatened next by similar methods," Kumagai said in his blog post.
The unauthorized access targeted the onamae.com desktop cloud service. A customer inquired about suspected unauthorized transactions on Oct 19 and GMO confirmed the next day that an unauthorized program had been installed on servers.
Although the servers were shut down on Wednesday, customers continued to report operations they said they did not recognize.
GMO said it will reimburse customers for losses from the unauthorized transactions and intends to pay 5,000 yen ($32) to all customers of the affected service, regardless of whether they suffered financial losses in the cyberattacks.
Speaking at a press conference in Tokyo, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said that "countermeasures are urgently needed" over the recent spate of data leaks and their misuse.
The ministerial meeting's attendees will share information and discuss future measures including further coordination between government agencies and ministries, he said.
